His will should be, and was, her delight. In a very short time, every thought was subdued. She even found her emotions rejoicing in God's will. Again, there was a lady who had a besetting sin, which in her emotions she dearly loved, but which in her will she hated. She believed she must control her emotions. So, she thought she couldn't conquer them unless her emotions changed first. But she learned a secret about the will. Going to her knees, she said, “Lord, You see that, with one part of my nature, I love this sin. But, in my true self, I hate it.” And now I put my will over on thy side in the matter. I will not do it anymore. Do you deliver me.” Immediately, God took over the will she had surrendered to Him. He began to work in her. His will then mastered her emotions. She found herself delivered, not by an outward command, but by an inward power. The Spirit of God working in her that which was well pleasing in His sight. And now, dear Christian, let me show you how to apply this principle to your difficulties. Stop considering your emotions. They are only servants. Your will is the real king in you. So, focus on it. Is that given up to God? Is that put into His hands? Does your will decide to believe? Does your will choose to obey? If this is the case, then you are in the Lord’s hands, and you decide to believe, and you choose to obey; for your will is yourself. And the thing is done. The transaction with God is as real, where only your will acts, as when every emotion coincides. It does not seem as real to you; but in God’s sight it is as real. When you find this secret, you need not attend to your emotions. Simply focus on your will. Then, all the Scripture commands become possible to you. They include: yielding to God, being a living sacrifice, abiding in Christ, walking in the light, and dying to self. You know your will can act and take God's side in all these. But if your emotions had to do it, you would despair, knowing they are uncontrollable. So, when you feel unreal or hypocritical, do not worry. It is just your emotions and not worth a moment's thought. Only ensure your will is in God's hands. Abandon yourself to His work. Choose His side, and there leave it. Your surging emotions, like a tossing vessel, must yield to a steady pull. This is the power of God, to which you chose to attach yourself. Your emotions must come into captivity, and give their allegiance to Him. You will prove true the say ing, “If any man will do His will, he shall know of the doctrine.” The will is like a wise mother in a nursery; the feelings are like a set of clamoring, crying children. The mother decides upon a certain course of action, which she believes to be right and best. The children clamor against it, and declare it shall not be. But the mother, knowing she is the mistress, remains calm. Unmoved by the children's clamors, she tries to soothe them. Eventually, the children must yield and accept her decision. Thus order and harmony are preserved. But if that mother thought the children were the mistresses, chaos would reign. Such instances have been known in family life! And how many souls, at this very moment, are confused? They are so because feelings govern, not the will! Remember, then, that your will decides what is real. Not your emotions. It is more dangerous to be a hypocrite by trusting your feelings than to stick to your will. If your will is on God's side, you are no hypocrite. So, claim as your own the blessed reality of belonging to Him. Your emotions may say otherwise, but they don't matter. I believe that, throughout the Bible, the “heart” does not mean emotions. It means the will, the man's true self. God's goal is to have this “I” yielded to Him, and to take full control of this central life. It is not the feelings of the man God wants, but the man himself. Have you given Him yourself, dear reader? Have you abandoned your will to His working? Do you consent to surrender the very centre of your being into His hands? Then, let your nature's outposts clamor as they may. You can, even now, say with the apostle, “I am crucified with Christ; nevertheless, I live; yet not I, but Christ lives in me. And the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave Himself for me.” After the chapter was sent to the printer, Pasteur T. Monod of Paris gave a remarkable, practical example of its teachings. It is a Presbyterian minister's experience. This pastor had kept it for many years. NEWBURGH, Sept. 26, 1842. Dear Brother, -- I take a moment of my time, devoted to the Lord, to write a short letter to you, His servant. It is sweet to feel we are wholly the Lord’s, that He has received us and called us His. Th is is religion. It is a giving up of self-ownership. It is a full embrace of the idea, “I am not my own, I am bought with a price.” Since I last saw you, I have been pressing on. Yet, there is nothing remarkable in my experience to share. I do not know if it is best to seek remarkable things. But I strive to be holy, as God is holy, pressing on toward the prize. I do not feel qualified to instruct you; I can only tell you the way in which I was led. The Lord deals differently with each soul. We should not copy others' experiences. But those seeking a clean heart must attend to certain things. We must personally consecrate all to God. We must make a covenant with Him to be wholly and forever His. I made this, using only my mind. My heart is hard and dark, full of sin and disbelief. I feel nothing. I covenanted to be the Lord’s, and laid all upon the altar, a living sacrifice, to the best of my ability. And after I rose from my knees, I was conscious of no change in my feeling. I was painfully conscious that there was no change. But I was sure I did. With all my sincerity, I made an eternal, complete dedication of myself to God. I did not consider the work done by any means. But, I engaged to be a living, perpetual sacrifice, wholly devoted to God. And now came the effort to do this. I knew that I must believe that God did accept me, and had come in to dwell in my heart. I was conscious that I did not believe this, and yet I desired to do so. I read with much prayer John’s First Epistle, and endeavored to assure my heart of God’s love to me as an individual. I was sensible that my heart was full of evil. I seemed to have no power to overcome pride or to repel evil thoughts, which I abhorred. But Christ was manifested to destroy the devil's works. The sin in my heart was the devil's work. I was enabled, therefore, to believe that God was working in me. He was to will and to do, while I worked out my own salvation with fear and trembling. I was convinced of unbelief, that it was voluntary and criminal. I clearly saw that unbelief was an awful sin; it made the faithful God a liar. The Lord showed me my besetting sins. They had dominion over me. They were, especially, preaching myself instead of Christ. I also indulged in complacent thoughts after preaching. I was enabled to make myself of no reputation, and to seek the honor which cometh from God only. Satan struggled hard to beat me back from the Rock of Ages. But thanks to God, I found a way to live in the moment. Then, I found rest. I trusted in the blood of Jesus as a full atonement for my past sins. I committed my future to the Lord, agreeing to do His will as He revealed it. I saw that I had to look to Jesus for grace. I had to trust Him to cleanse my heart and keep me from sin now. I felt a need to depend on the grace of Christ, if only for a moment. I would not let the enemy trouble me about the past or future. I expected, each moment, a supply for that moment. I agreed to be a child of Abraham. I would walk by faith in the Word of God, not by my feelings. I would seek to be a Bible Christian. Since that time the Lord has given me a steady victory over sins which before enslaved me. I delight in the Lord, and in His Word. I delight in my work as a minister: my fellowship is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ. I am a baby in Christ; I know my progress has been small compared with that made by many. My feelings vary. But when I feel, I praise God and trust His word. When I'm empty and feel nothing, I do the same. I have covenanted to walk by faith and not by feelings. The Lord is beginning to revive His work among my people. “Praise the Lord.” May the Lord fill you with all His fullness and give you all the mind of Christ. Oh, be faithful! Walk before God and be perfect. Preach the Word. Be instant in season and out of season. The Lord loves you. He works with you. Rest your soul completely upon that promise, “Look, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world.” Your fellow soldier, WILLIAM HILL There may be some who will object to this teaching, that it ignores the work of the blessed Holy Spirit. But I must refer such to the introductory chapter of this book, in which I have fully explained myself. I am not writing upon that side of the subject; I am considering man ’s part in the matter, and not the part of the Spirit. I know that all a man can do would be useless if the Holy Spirit did not work in him continually. I write as I do because I believe in the Spirit. It is a mighty, ever-present power, ready to do his work. But, like the wind that blows where it wants, you hear its sound. But you cannot tell where it comes from or where it goes. The Spirit's actions are beyond our control and understanding. The results we know, and the steps on our part which lead to those results, but we know nothing more. And yet, like a factory worker, we dare to urge men to act. They must, like the worker, trust an unseen power, called steam, behind their machinery. It can accomplish the impossible. We know the mighty Spirit will always provide the power needed for each moment's act. We boldly claim that we, as writers, can say, as earnestly as any other Christians, “We believe in the Holy Ghost.”

fields.title: Is God in Everything?
fields.body_html:
A major obstacle to living a life of total surrender is the difficulty of seeing God in everything.

People say, “I can submit to things from God. But, I cannot submit to man. “Most of my trials come through humans.” Or, “It's fine to talk of trusting. But, when I commit a matter to God, man is sure to come in and mess it up. I can trust God, but I see serious problems with trusting men.””

This is no imaginary trouble. It is of vital importance. If it cannot be met, it makes faith an impossible, visionary theory. Nearly everything in life comes to us through human means. Most of our trials result from someone's failure, ignorance, carelessness, or sin. We know God cannot be the author of these things. Yet, unless He is the agent, how can we say to Him, “Your will be done”? Besides, what good is it to trust our affairs to God, if man can come in and disrupt them? And, how can we live by faith if we can't trust humans? They will have too much influence on our lives.

Moreover, things in which we can see God’s hand always have a sweetness in them which consoles while it wounds. But, man's trials are full of bitterness. So, we must see God in everything. We must accept all things as His direct gifts, with no second causes. We must be brought to this. Only then can we know a lasting experience of total abandonment and perfect trust. Our abandonment must be to God, not to man, and our trust must be in Him, not in any arm of flesh, or we shall fail at the first trial.

The question is, “Is God in everything? “Do we have scripture to accept everything from Him? It was caused by other factors.”” I answer, unhesitatingly, yes. To the children of God, all comes from their Fath er's hand. It matters not who the apparent agents were. There are no “second causes” for them. The whole teaching of the Bible asserts and implies this. “Not a sparrow falls to the ground without our Father.” The very hairs of our head are all numbered. We are not to be careful about anything, because our Father cares for us. We are not to avenge ourselves, because our Father has charged Himself with our defence.

We are not to fear, for the Lord is on our side. No one can be against us, because He is for us. We shall not want, for He is our Shepherd. When we pass through the rivers, they shall not overflow us. When we walk through the fire, we shall not be burned. He will be with us. He shuts the mouths of lions, that they cannot hurt us. He delivers and rescues. He changes the times and the seasons; He removes kings and sets up kings. A man’s heart is in His hand, and, as the river of water, He turns it whithersoever He will.” “He rules over all the heathen kingdoms. In His hand is power and might. None can withstand Him.”

He rules the raging of the sea; when the waves thereof arise, He stills them. He brings the advice of the unruly to mischief; He makes the devices of the people of no effect. Whatsoever the Lord pleases that does Him in heaven, and in earth, in the seas, and all deep places. If you see the poor oppressed and justice perverted, don't marvel. For there is one higher than the highest. He sees all. These are a part of His ways, but how little a portion is heard of Him? But the thunder of His power, who can understand?”

“Have you not known, have you not heard? The everlasting God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, does not grow faint or weary. There is no searching of His understanding.

And this God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear. The earth may be removed. The mountains may be carried into the sea. The waters may roar and be troubled.

The mountains may shake with their swelling. I will say of the Lord, He is my refuge and my fortress, my God, in Him will I trust. Surely He shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noise of some pestilence. He shall cover me with His feathers, and under His wings shall I trust. His truth shall be thy shield and buckler. Do not be afraid of the terror by night, or the arrow that flies by day. Do not fear the pestilence that walks in darkness, or the destruction that wastes at noon.

“A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not c ome near you. You will only look with your eyes and see the recompense of the wicked. Because you have made the Lord your dwelling place, the Most High, who is my refuge, no evil shall be allowed to befall you, no plague come near your tent. For he will co mmand his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways.”

Psalms 91:7-11 These Scriptures, and others like them, settle, once and for all, the question of second causes in the lives of God's children. They are all under the control of our Father. Nothing can touch us except with His knowledge and by His permission. Man's sin may cause the action. So, it can't be called God's will. But by the time it reaches us, it is God's will. We must accept it as directly from His hands.

No man or group, no power on earth or in heaven, can touch the soul that abides in Christ. They must first pass through Him and get His permission. If God be for us, it matters not who may be against us; nothing can disturb or harm us, except He shall see that it is best for us, and shall stand aside to let it pass. An earthly parent’s care for his helpless child is a feeble illustration of this. If the child is in its father’s arms, nothing can touch it without that father’s consent, unless he is too weak to prevent it.

And even if this should be the case, he suffers the harm first in his own person, before he allows it to reach his child. If an earthly parent would thus care for his helpless child, how much more will our Heavenly Father! His love is infinite. His strength and wisdom are unfailing.

Some, even of God's children, doubt His love and care. They secretly blame Him for neglect they would not tolerate. But His care is far beyond human care. He counts the hairs on our heads and knows when a sparrow falls. He watches every small thing that affects His children's lives. He controls them all according to His will, no matter their origin.

The instances of this are numberless. Take Joseph. What could seem more a result of sin than his being sold into slavery? It was u tterly against God's will. And yet Joseph, in speaking of it, said, “ As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. ” Genesis 50:20.Now, do not be grieved or angry with yourselves for selling me. “ God sent me here to preserve life.” To the eye of sense, it was surely Joseph's wicked brethren who had sent him into Egypt.

Yet, with faith, Joseph could say, “God sent me.” His brothers had sinned. But by the time it reached Joseph, it was God's will. It was, though it didn't seem so at first, the greatest blessing of his life. So we see how the Lord can turn even man's anger to praise Him. And, how all things, even others' sins, shall work for good to those who love Him.

I learned this lesson, practically and experimentally, long before I knew the scripture. I was at a prayer meeting for scriptural holiness. A strange lady rose to speak. I wondered who she was, not knowing she would teach me a grand lesson. She said she had great difficulty in living a life of faith. The second cause that seemed to control everything about her caused it. Her confusion grew. She began to ask God to teach her the truth. Was he really in everything, or not?

After praying this for a few days, she had what she described as a vision. She thought she was in a dark place. Then, a body of light advanced towards her from a distance. It gradually surrounded and enveloped her and everything around her. As it approached, a voice seemed to say, “This is the presence of God; this is the presence of God.” This presence showed her all the great and awful things in life.

She saw fighting armies, wicked men, raging beasts, storms, and plagues. She saw every kind of sin and suffering. At first, she shrank back in terror. But, she soon saw that God's presence surrounded and enveloped each one of these. Not a lion could reach out its paw, nor a bullet fly through the air, except as His presence moved to permit it.

She knew that, if there were the thinnest of sheets of this glorious presence between her and the terrible violence, nothing could touch her. Not a hair on her head could be ruffled.

But, the presence must divide to let the evil through. Then, all the small annoyances of life flashed before her. She saw they were so wrapped in God's presence that nothing could touch her. Not a cross look, harsh word, or petty trial could reach her unless He let them through.

Her difficulty vanished. Her question was answered forever. God was in everything, and to her henceforth there were no second causes. She saw that her life came to her, day by day, and hour by hour, from His hand. It did not matter what seemed to control it. And, she never again found it hard to trust in His care. But if we focus on the seen things, we won't understand this secret. The children of God must “not look at the things which are seen: for the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” If we could see His unseen forces around us, we'd feel safe. We would walk through this world in an unbreakable fortress. For “the angel of the Lord encamped round about them that fear Him, and delivered them.”

We have a striking illustration of this in the history of Elisha. The king of Syria was at war with Israel.

His evil plans were foiled by a prophet. So, he sent his army to the prophet's city to capture him. We read, “He sent their horses and chariots and a great host; and they came by night and compassed the city about.” This was the seen thing. A nd the servant of the prophet, whose eyes had not yet been opened to see the unseen things, was alarmed. We read, “And when the man, God's servant, rose early and went forth, a host encompassed the city, with horses and chariots.” His servant said, “Alas, my master, how shall we do?” But his master could see the unseen things, and he replied, “Fear not; for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.” And then he prayed, saying, “Lord, I pray thee, open his eyes that he may see.

The Lord opened the young man's eyes, and he saw. The mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha. The presence of God is the fortress of His people. Nothing can withstand it. At His presence, the wicked perish. The earth trembles. The hills melt like wax. The cities crumble. “The heavens also dropped, and Sinai itself was moved at the presence of God.” In this secret, He has promised to hide His people from man's pride and from the strife of tongues. “My presence shall go with thee,” He says, “and I will give you rest.” I wish every Christian could see this truth as plainly as I do. It is the only clue to a completely restful life. Nothing else will let a soul live only in the present, as we are commanded to do. We must not think of tomorrow.

Nothing else will remove all the risks from a Christian's heart. It won't let him say, “Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.” Abiding in God’s presence, we run no risks. A soul like that can say: “I know not what it is to doubt. My heart is always gay. “I run no risks, for, come what will, God always has His way.” I once heard of a colored woman. She earned a precarious living by daily labor. But, she was a joyous, triumphant Christian.

“Ah!”Nancy,” said a gloomy Christian lady one day. She almost disapproved of her constant cheerfulness, yet envied it.

“Ah!” Nancy, it is all well enough to be happy now, but I should think the thoughts of your future would sober you. Only suppose, for instance, that you fell sick and couldn't work. Or, suppose your employers moved away, and no one else hired you. Or suppose -- “Stop!” cried Nancy, “I never supposes.

The Lord is my shepherd, and I know I shall not want. And, honey,” she added to her gloomy friend, “I know it’s all those things they’re suggesting that are making you so miserable . You should give them all up and just trust in the Lord. ” One text can end a believer's “suppose.” If only it is received and acted on with childlike faith. It is in Heb. 3:5-6 “ Now Moses was f aithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken later, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house, if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope . ” Be content with what you have. For He said, “Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, ' I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently say, the Lord is my Helper, I will not fear. What can man do to me?” Hebrews 13:5-6 What if dangers threaten you from every side? What if men's malice, foolishness, or ignorance combine to harm you?

You may face every contingency with these words: “The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.”

If the Lord is your helper, how can you fear what man may do unto you? No man, nor any company of men, can touch you. Unless, of course, your God, in whom you trust, allows it. “He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. The Lord is your keeper; the Lord is your shade on your right hand. The sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night. The Lord will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life. The Lord will keep you going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore.” (Psalm 121:3 - 8) Only seeing God in everything will make us loving and patient with those who annoy us.

They will be only instruments for His wise, tender purposes. We'll end up thanking them for the blessings they bring. Nothing else will completely put an end to all murmuring or rebellious thoughts.

Christians often feel a liberty to murmur against man when they would not dare to murmur against God. But this way of receiving things would make it impossible ever to murmur. If our Father allows a trial, it must be the best thing for us. We must accept it with thanks from His dear hand.

The trial itself may be hard to flesh out and blood, and I do not mean that we can like or enjoy the suffering of it. But we can and must love the will of God in the trial, for His will is always sweet, whether it be in joy or in sorrow. Our trials may be our chariots. We long for some victory over sin and self, and we ask God to grant it to us.

His answer comes in the form of a trial, which He means shall be the chariot to bear us to the longed for triumph. We may either let it roll over us and crush us like an unstoppable force. Or we may mount into it and ride triumphantly onward. Joseph's chariots, which raised him to glory, were his trials. They were being sold into slavery and unjustly imprisoned.

Our chariots may be less than these. They may be just annoying people or tough situations. But whatever they are, God means them to be our forces of triumph.

They shall bear us to the victories we have prayed for. If we are impatient and long to be patient, our chariot will probably be a trying person. Their ways or words will test our very souls. If we accept the trial as from God and submit, it will be the best discipline. It will give us the patience we seek.

God does not order the wrong thing. But, He uses it for our blessing. He did this with the cruelty of Joseph's wicked brethren. And, with Pharaoh's wife's false accusations. It makes life a long thanksgiving. It gives us a deep peace and a joy beyond words. Someone says, “God’s will on earth is always joy, always tranquility.” He must have His own way with His children. The soul that learns this secret finds green pastures and still waters. They offer rest and refreshment.

If the will of God is our will, and if He always has His way, then we always have our way also, and we reign in a perpetual kingdom. He who sides with God will win every time. Whatever the outcome, we can join the ap ostle's victory shout: “ But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains uplifted , because only through Christ is it taken away.”

(2Corinthians 2:14)

He counts the hairs on our heads and knows when a sparrow falls. He watches every small thing that affects His children's lives. He controls them all according to His will, no matter their origin. The instances of this are numberless. Take Joseph. What could seem more a result of sin than his being sold into slavery? It was u tterly against God's will. And yet Joseph, in speaking of it, said, “ As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today. ” Genesis 50:20.Now, do not be grieved or angry with yourselves for selling me. “ God sent me here to preserve life.” To the eye of sense, it was surely Joseph's wicked brethren who had sent him into Egypt. Yet, with faith, Joseph could say, “God sent me.” His brothers had sinned. But by the time it reached Joseph, it was God's will. It was, though it didn't seem so at first, the greatest blessing of his life. So we see how the Lord can turn even man's anger to praise Him. And, how all things, even others' sins, shall work for good to those who love Him. I learned this lesson, practically and experimentally, long before I knew the scripture. I was at a prayer meeting for scriptural holiness. A strange lady rose to speak. I wondered who she was, not knowing she would teach me a grand lesson. She said she had great difficulty in living a life of faith. The second cause that seemed to control everything about her caused it. Her confusion grew. She began to ask God to teach her the truth. Was he really in everything, or not? After praying this for a few days, she had what she described as a vision. She thought she was in a dark place. Then, a body of light advanced towards her from a distance. It gradually surrounded and enveloped her and everything around her. As it approached, a voice seemed to say, “This is the presence of God; this is the presence of God.” This presence showed her all the great and awful things in life. She saw fighting armies, wicked men, raging beasts, storms, and plagues. She saw every kind of sin and suffering. At first, she shrank back in terror. But, she soon saw that God's presence surrounded and enveloped each one of these. Not a lion could reach out its paw, nor a bullet fly through the air, except as His presence moved to permit it. She knew that, if there were the thinnest of sheets of this glorious presence between her and the terrible violence, nothing could touch her. Not a hair on her head could be ruffled. But, the presence must divide to let the evil through. Then, all the small annoyances of life flashed before her. She saw they were so wrapped in God's presence that nothing could touch her. Not a cross look, harsh word, or petty trial could reach her unless He let them through. Her difficulty vanished. Her question was answered forever. God was in everything, and to her henceforth there were no second causes. She saw that her life came to her, day by day, and hour by hour, from His hand. It did not matter what seemed to control it. And, she never again found it hard to trust in His care. But if we focus on the seen things, we won't understand this secret. The children of God must “not look at the things which are seen: for the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” If we could see His unseen forces around us, we'd feel safe. We would walk through this world in an unbreakable fortress. For “the angel of the Lord encamped round about them that fear Him, and delivered them.” We have a striking illustration of this in the history of Elisha. The king of Syria was at war with Israel. His evil plans were foiled by a prophet. So, he sent his army to the prophet's city to capture him. We read, “He sent their horses and chariots and a great host; and they came by night and compassed the city about.” This was the seen thing. A nd the servant of the prophet, whose eyes had not yet been opened to see the unseen things, was alarmed. We read, “And when the man, God's servant, rose early and went forth, a host encompassed the city, with horses and chariots.” His servant said, “Alas, my master, how shall we do?” But his master could see the unseen things, and he replied, “Fear not; for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.” And then he prayed, saying, “Lord, I pray thee, open his eyes that he may see. The Lord opened the young man's eyes, and he saw. The mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha. The presence of God is the fortress of His people. Nothing can withstand it. At His presence, the wicked perish. The earth trembles. The hills melt like wax. The cities crumble. “The heavens also dropped, and Sinai itself was moved at the presence of God.” In this secret, He has promised to hide His people from man's pride and from the strife of tongues. “My presence shall go with thee,” He says, “and I will give you rest.” I wish every Christian could see this truth as plainly as I do. It is the only clue to a completely restful life. Nothing else will let a soul live only in the present, as we are commanded to do. We must not think of tomorrow. Nothing else will remove all the risks from a Christian's heart. It won't let him say, “Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.” Abiding in God’s presence, we run no risks. A soul like that can say: “I know not what it is to doubt. My heart is always gay. “I run no risks, for, come what will, God always has His way.” I once heard of a colored woman. She earned a precarious living by daily labor. But, she was a joyous, triumphant Christian. “Ah!”Nancy,” said a gloomy Christian lady one day. She almost disapproved of her constant cheerfulness, yet envied it. “Ah!” Nancy, it is all well enough to be happy now, but I should think the thoughts of your future would sober you. Only suppose, for instance, that you fell sick and couldn't work. Or, suppose your employers moved away, and no one else hired you. Or suppose -- “Stop!” cried Nancy, “I never supposes. The Lord is my shepherd, and I know I shall not want. And, honey,” she added to her gloomy friend, “I know it’s all those things they’re suggesting that are making you so miserable . You should give them all up and just trust in the Lord. ” One text can end a believer's “suppose.” If only it is received and acted on with childlike faith. It is in Heb. 3:5-6 “ Now Moses was f aithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that were to be spoken later, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house, if indeed we hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope . ” Be content with what you have. For He said, “Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, ' I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently say, the Lord is my Helper, I will not fear. What can man do to me?” Hebrews 13:5-6 What if dangers threaten you from every side? What if men's malice, foolishness, or ignorance combine to harm you? You may face every contingency with these words: “The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what man shall do unto me.” If the Lord is your helper, how can you fear what man may do unto you? No man, nor any company of men, can touch you. Unless, of course, your God, in whom you trust, allows it. “He will not let your foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep. The Lord is your keeper; the Lord is your shade on your right hand. The sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night. The Lord will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life. The Lord will keep you going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore.” (Psalm 121:3 - 8) Only seeing God in everything will make us loving and patient with those who annoy us. They will be only instruments for His wise, tender purposes. We'll end up thanking them for the blessings they bring. Nothing else will completely put an end to all murmuring or rebellious thoughts. Christians often feel a liberty to murmur against man when they would not dare to murmur against God. But this way of receiving things would make it impossible ever to murmur. If our Father allows a trial, it must be the best thing for us. We must accept it with thanks from His dear hand. The trial itself may be hard to flesh out and blood, and I do not mean that we can like or enjoy the suffering of it. But we can and must love the will of God in the trial, for His will is always sweet, whether it be in joy or in sorrow. Our trials may be our chariots. We long for some victory over sin and self, and we ask God to grant it to us. His answer comes in the form of a trial, which He means shall be the chariot to bear us to the longed for triumph. We may either let it roll over us and crush us like an unstoppable force. Or we may mount into it and ride triumphantly onward. Joseph's chariots, which raised him to glory, were his trials. They were being sold into slavery and unjustly imprisoned. Our chariots may be less than these. They may be just annoying people or tough situations. But whatever they are, God means them to be our forces of triumph. They shall bear us to the victories we have prayed for. If we are impatient and long to be patient, our chariot will probably be a trying person. Their ways or words will test our very souls. If we accept the trial as from God and submit, it will be the best discipline. It will give us the patience we seek. God does not order the wrong thing. But, He uses it for our blessing. He did this with the cruelty of Joseph's wicked brethren. And, with Pharaoh's wife's false accusations. It makes life a long thanksgiving. It gives us a deep peace and a joy beyond words. Someone says, “God’s will on earth is always joy, always tranquility.” He must have His own way with His children. The soul that learns this secret finds green pastures and still waters. They offer rest and refreshment. If the will of God is our will, and if He always has His way, then we always have our way also, and we reign in a perpetual kingdom. He who sides with God will win every time. Whatever the outcome, we can join the ap ostle's victory shout: “ But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read the old covenant, that same veil remains uplifted , because only through Christ is it taken away.” (2Corinthians 2:14)

fields.title: Growth
fields.body_html:
After a believer fully surrenders and trusts, they find a life of happy communion and peace. This raises the question, “Is this the end? “I answer emphatically “No, it is only the beginning.” But, this is so little understood that many oppose the faith advocates. They claim the advocates do not believe in growth in grace. They are to teach that the soul can reach a perfect state. There is no further advance beyond it. This teaching voids all the Scriptural calls for growth and development.

Since the opposite is true, I must, next, consider this subject. I want to, if possible, fully answer such objections. I also want to show the scriptural place and way for the soul to grow. The most quoted text is 2 Pet 3:18. It says, “ But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen. “ This text expresses our belief in God's will for us. It also reflects our belief that He has made it possible for us to experience it. We accept, in their fullest meaning, all commands and promises. They concern our growth into Christ in all things, until we are perfect, and measure up to His fullness.

We are glad that we don't always have to be like babies, needing milk. We may, by use and growth, become skilled in the word of righteousness. We should then be able to discern good from evil and need strong meat. And none would grieve more than we at the thought of an end to the Christian life.

There could be no advance beyond it. But, we believe in a growth that produces maturity. We believe in a development that, in fact, bears ripe fruit. We expect to reach the aim set before us, and if we do not, we feel sure there must be some fault in our growing. No parent would be satisfied if, year after year, their child remained a helpless babe. And no farmer would be pleased if his grain grew only to the blade, but never produced the ear or the full corn in the ear.

Growth, to be real, must be progressive. The days, weeks, and months must bring a maturity in the thing growing. But is this the case with a large part of that which is called growth in grace?

Doesn't the very Christian who longs for it, too often find that, at year's end, he is not as far in his Christian experience as at the beginning? His zeal, devotion, and separation from the world are not as complete as when his Christian life began.

I was urging a group of Christians to take an immediate, definite step into the Promised Land. A very intelligent lady interrupted me. She thought her words would completely rebut my argument. She exclaimed, “Ah! But, my dear friend, I believe in growing in grace.” “How long have you been growing?” I asked. “About twenty - five years,” was her answer. “And how much more unworldly and devoted to the Lord are you now than w hen you began your Christian life?” I continued, “Sadly!” was the answer. “I fear I am not nearly so much so.” Her eyes opened to see that, at least, her growth had failed. It had done the opposite.

The trouble with her, and every other such case, is simply this, they are trying to grow into grace, instead of in it. They are like a rosebush. The gardener should plant it in the hard, stony path to grow into the flower-bed. But, it would reduce and wither instead of flourishing. The children of Israel wandering in the wilderness are a perfect picture of this sort of growing. They had traveled for forty years. They took many weary steps. They found little rest from their wanderings. Yet, at the end, they were no nearer the Promised Land than at the start. At Kadesh Barnea, they were at the land's borders.

A few steps would have taken them into it.

Upon ending their wanderings in the plains of Moab, they were at its borders. But now there was a river to cross, which there hadn't been at first. Their wanderings and fights in the wilderness had not won them an inch of the Promised Land. To possess this land, one must first be in it. To grow in grace, one must first be planted in it. But, once in the land, their conquest was very rapid. Once planted in grace, the soul will grow in one month more than in years in any other soil. For grace is a most fruitful soil, and the plants that grow therein are plants of a marvelous growth.

A Divine Gardener takes care of them. The Sun of Righteousness warms them. The dew from Heaven waters them. Surely, it is no wonder they bear fruit. “Some a hundred-fold, some sixty-fold, some thirty-fold.” But, what does “growing in grace” mean? Few people understand what the grace of God is. So, it is hard to answer this question. To say that it is free, unmerited favor, only expresses a little of its meaning. It is God's wondrous, boundless love, poured out upon us without measure. It is not based on our worthiness, but on His infinite, unfathomable love. Its heights and depths surpass all knowledge. I sometimes think we change the meaning of “love” with God. We understand it well in its human use.

But, if ever human love was tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted; if it could bear and forbear; if it could gladly suffer for its loved ones; if it would pour itself out for their comfort and pleasure, then Divine love is far more so. It is infinitely more tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted. It is glad to bear and forbear, to suffer, and to lavish its best gifts on those it loves.

Take all the tenderness and love you know of, dear reader. Add the deepest love you have ever felt.

Then add the strongest love ever given to you. Next, pile on the love of all the world's loving hearts.

Now multiply it by infinity. You might then faintly glimpse the love of God in Christ Jesus. And this is grace. To be planted in grace is to live in love. It means to envelop yourself in it, steep yourself in it, and revel in it. It means to know nothing but love, and to grow in knowledge and faith in it. It means to trust it completely and have no doubt that it will order all things well.

To grow in grace is opposed to all self-dependence, to all self-effort, to all legality of every kind. It is to put our growing, as well as everything else, into the hands of the Lord and leave it with Him. We should trust our Husbandman. His skill and wisdom are perfect. So, we won't question His methods or His cultivation plan. It is to grow as the lilies or babes grow. To grow, without a care or anxiety. To grow by a life force that must grow. To grow because we live and must grow. To grow because He who planted us made us to grow.

Surely, this is what our Lord meant. He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?” Or, when He says again, “And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?” There is no effort in the growing of a child or of a lily. They do not toil or spin. They do not stretch or strain.

They make no effort to grow. They are not even aware that they are growing. But, by an inner life force, they grow. God's providence, a gardener, the sun, and the rain nurture them.

And the result is sure. Even Solomon, our Lord, says, in all his glory, was not arrayed like one of these.

Solomon's array cost much toil and gold, but the lily's cost none of these. We may toil to make ourselves beautiful spiritual garments. We may strain for spiritual growth. But we will achieve nothing. No man can add a cubit to his stature by thinking. Our efforts can't match the beautiful dress the great Husbandman gives His garden's plants. They grow under His care.

If I could make my readers see how helpless we are in growing, I believe it would relieve many lives.

Imagine a child obsessed with growing. He would not grow unless he tried to. He insisted on a combination of rope and pulleys to stretch himself to the desired height. He might, it's true, waste his days in a weary strain. But, there would be no change in the fact, “No man can add to his stature by thinking.” His years of labor would be wasted if they did not hinder the longed-for end.

Imagine a lily trying to clothe itself in beauty. It stretched its leaves and stems to grow. It tried to manage the clouds and sunshine, to meet its needs. Yet, these two pictures show a truth. Many Christians want to grow. They know they should. They feel a deep instinct to grow. But, they try to do it by toiling and spinning. They wear themselves out with endless self-effort.

It is wear ying to watch. Grow, dear friends. But, please, grow in God’s way, the only true way. Be sure to be rooted in grace. Then, let the Divine gardener cultivate you in His own way.

Expose yourselves to His presence in the sunshine. Let the dew of heaven fall on you. Then, see what will happen. Leaves, flowers, and fruit must come in their season. Your Husbandman is a skilled one.

He never fails in His harvesting. Just don't hinder the shining of the Sun of Righteousness or the falling of the dew from Heaven. A very thin covering may block the heat or moisture. The plant may wither even in their midst. A slight barrier between your soul and Christ may cause you to fade like a plant in a cellar or under a bushel. Keep the sky clear. Open every part of you to receive the blessings our Divine Husbandman may bring.

Bask in the sunshine of His love. Drink in the waters of His goodness. Keep your face upturned to Him.

Look, and your soul shall live. You need to make no efforts to grow, but let your efforts instead be all concentrated on this, that you abide in the Vine. The gardener who tends the vine will care for its branches too. He will prune, purge, water, and tend them. They will grow and bear fruit that will last.

Like the lily, their glory will surpass even Solomon's.

What if you seem to yourselves to be planted at this moment in a desert soil where nothing can grow!

Trust fully in the great gardener. He will make that desert blossom and create springs in its sands. The promise is sure. The man who trusts in the Lord, “He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit.”(Jeremiah 17:8)It i s the great prerogative of our Divine gardener. He can turn any soil into the soil of grace, the moment we put our growing into His hands. He does not need to move us to a different field. Right where we are, with just the circumstances around us, He makes His sun to shine and His dew to fall on us. He turns our greatest obstacles into the best means of our growth. I care not what the circumstances may be, His wonder-working power can accomplish this. And we must trust Him with it all.

Surely He is a man we can trust.

If He sends storms, winds, rains, or sunshine, we must accept it. We must trust, with unwavering faith, that He will cultivate us and bring us to maturity. He knows the best way to do this. He controls the elements to ensure our rapid growth. Let me entreat of you, then, to give up all your efforts after growing, and simply to let yourselves grow. Leave it all to the Gardener, whose responsibility it is, and who alone can manage it. No difficulties in your case can baffle Him.

Nothing in your past can mar His perfect work. Not the limiting of your growth, the dryness of your life, or any deformity. If you will, put yourselves completely in His hands and let Him have His way with you. His own gracious promise to His backsliding children a ssures you of this. “ I will heal their apostasy ,” He says: “I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them.

I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon.

His shoots shall sp read out; his beauty shall be like the olive, and his fragrance like Lebanon.”(Hosea 14:4-6) “They shall return and dwell beneath my shadow; they shall flourish like the grain; they shall blossom like the vine; their fame shall be like the wine of Lebanon.” (Hosea 14:7) And again He says, “ Fear not, you beasts of the field, for the pastures of the wilderness are green; the tree bears its fruit; the fig tree and vine give their full yield.”(Joel 2:22-26) And the floors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil. I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopper, the destroyer, and the cutter, my great army, which I sent among you. You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and praise the name of the Lord your God, who has dealt wondrously with you. And my people shall never again be put to shame.” (Joel 2:25 -26) Oh! You could. But, you know what your Lord meant when He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin”(Mathew 6:28 ).

These words show a life and a growth far different from the ordinary life and growth of Christians.

They show a life of rest and growth without effort. Yet, this life and growth have glorious results. To every soul that becomes a lily in the Lord's garden, and grows as the lilies do, the same glorious array will be given. They will know a mystical passage about their Beloved: “He feeds among the lilies.”

We who fully trust believe in a growth in grace. It is a growth that brings desired results. It blossoms into a flower and fruit, becoming a tree planted by rivers of water. It bears fruit in season. Its leaves do not wither. It prospers in all it does. We rejoice to know that, in the Lord's heritage, many such plants are growing up now. As the lilies grow by seeing the sun, they are changed into the same image by beholding the Lord's glory, from glory to glory, by the Lord's spirit.

If you ask them how they grow so fast and well, they would say they don't worry about it. They hardly notice their growth. Their Lord told them to abide in Him. He promised that if they did, they would bear much fruit. They focus only on abiding, which is their part. They leave the rest to their good Husbandman, who alone can manage it. You will find that such souls are not engaged in watching self, but in looking unto Jesus.

They do not toil nor spin for their spiritual clothes. They leave it to the Lord to dress them as He pleases.

Self-effort and self-dependence are at an end with them. Their interest in self is gone, transferred over into the hands of another. Self has become really nothing, and Christ alone is all in all to such as these.

And the blessed result is, that not Even Solomon, in all his glory, was arrayed like these will be. Let us examine this subject practically.

We all know that growing is not a thing of effort, but is the result of an inward life, a principle of growth. All the stretching and pulling in the world could not make a dead oak grow. But a live oak grows without stretching. It is plain, then, that the key is to get within you the growing life. Then you cannot help but grow. And this life is the life hid with Christ in God, the wonderful divine life of an indwelling Holy Ghost. Be filled with this, dear believer. You must grow, whether you know it or not.

Do not worry about your growth. Just ensure you have the growing life.

Abide in the Vine. Let the life from Him flow through all your spiritual veins. Interpose no barrier to His mighty life-giving power, working in you all the good pleasure of His will. Surrender completely to His gentle guidance. Put your growing into His hands, as completely as you have put all your other affairs. Suffer Him to manage it as He will. Do not concern yourself about it, nor even think of it.

Trust Him without reservation, and at all times.

Accept each moment's gift, from His dear hands. It is the needed sunshine or dew for your growth. Say a continual “Yes” to your Father's will. Until now, you may have tried, as many do, to be both the lily and the gardener, both the vineyard and the gardener. You have taken on the burdens and duties that belong only to the Divine gardener. Only He can bear them. Henceforth consent to take your rightful place and to be only what you really are. Say to yourself, “If I am only the garden, not the gardener; if I am only the vine, not the gardener, then I must keep the garden and act its part.”” I must not usurp the gardener's place or try to act his part.”

Do not choose your own soil or set your borders. Do not plant your own seeds, prune, or tend your vines. Be content with what the Divine Husbandman arranges for you, and with the care He gives. Let Him choose which plants and fruits to cultivate. If He wills it, let Him grow a potato as gladly as a rose. And, let Him value everyday virtues as much as exalted passions. Be content with the seasons He sends, and the sun and rain. Accept your growth, whether fast or slow. In short, be satisfied with all His ways, even if we don't understand them.

There is infinite repose in this. As the violet rests in its nook, it contentedly accepts its daily portion. It lets the rains fall, the suns rise, and the earth whirl, without one anxious pang. So, we must repose in the present as God gives it to us. We should accept, without worry, our daily portion in His grand plan.

It is creative and redemptive.

The wind that blows can never kill the tree God plants. It blows east, it blows west. The tender leaves have little rest. But any wind that blows is best. The tree God plants Strikes deeper root, grows higher still, spreads wider boughs. For God's goodwill meets all its wants. No frost can blight the tree God shields. The roots are warm beneath the soft snows. When spring comes, it knows, and every bud will blossom. The tree God shields Grows on apace by day and night, Till, sweet to taste and fair to sight, its fruit it yields.

No storm can blast the tree, God knows. No thunder, rain, lightning, or hurricane can. When they spend, it remains. The tree God knows. Through every tempest, it stands fast. From its first day to its last, it grows ever fairer.

If in the soul's still garden, a seed God sows a little seed, it will soon grow. And, all men will know it.

For heavenly land, He bids it blow. A seed God sows, and up it springs by day and night; through life, through death, it grows right, forever grows.
