The children of Israel wandering in the wilderness are a perfect picture of this sort of growing. They had traveled for forty years. They took many weary steps. They found little rest from their wanderings. Yet, at the end, they were no nearer the Promised Land than at the start. At Kadesh Barnea, they were at the land's borders. A few steps would have taken them into it. Upon ending their wanderings in the plains of Moab, they were at its borders. But now there was a river to cross, which there hadn't been at first. Their wanderings and fights in the wilderness had not won them an inch of the Promised Land. To possess this land, one must first be in it. To grow in grace, one must first be planted in it. But, once in the land, their conquest was very rapid. Once planted in grace, the soul will grow in one month more than in years in any other soil. For grace is a most fruitful soil, and the plants that grow therein are plants of a marvelous growth. A Divine Gardener takes care of them. The Sun of Righteousness warms them. The dew from Heaven waters them. Surely, it is no wonder they bear fruit. “Some a hundred-fold, some sixty-fold, some thirty-fold.” But, what does “growing in grace” mean? Few people understand what the grace of God is. So, it is hard to answer this question. To say that it is free, unmerited favor, only expresses a little of its meaning. It is God's wondrous, boundless love, poured out upon us without measure. It is not based on our worthiness, but on His infinite, unfathomable love. Its heights and depths surpass all knowledge. I sometimes think we change the meaning of “love” with God. We understand it well in its human use. But, if ever human love was tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted; if it could bear and forbear; if it could gladly suffer for its loved ones; if it would pour itself out for their comfort and pleasure, then Divine love is far more so. It is infinitely more tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted. It is glad to bear and forbear, to suffer, and to lavish its best gifts on those it loves. Take all the tenderness and love you know of, dear reader. Add the deepest love you have ever felt. Then add the strongest love ever given to you. Next, pile on the love of all the world's loving hearts. Now multiply it by infinity. You might then faintly glimpse the love of God in Christ Jesus. And this is grace. To be planted in grace is to live in love. It means to envelop yourself in it, steep yourself in it, and revel in it. It means to know nothing but love, and to grow in knowledge and faith in it. It means to trust it completely and have no doubt that it will order all things well. To grow in grace is opposed to all self-dependence, to all self-effort, to all legality of every kind. It is to put our growing, as well as everything else, into the hands of the Lord and leave it with Him. We should trust our Husbandman. His skill and wisdom are perfect. So, we won't question His methods or His cultivation plan. It is to grow as the lilies or babes grow. To grow, without a care or anxiety. To grow by a life force that must grow. To grow because we live and must grow. To grow because He who planted us made us to grow. Surely, this is what our Lord meant. He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?” Or, when He says again, “And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?” There is no effort in the growing of a child or of a lily. They do not toil or spin. They do not stretch or strain. They make no effort to grow. They are not even aware that they are growing. But, by an inner life force, they grow. God's providence, a gardener, the sun, and the rain nurture them. And the result is sure. Even Solomon, our Lord, says, in all his glory, was not arrayed like one of these. Solomon's array cost much toil and gold, but the lily's cost none of these. We may toil to make ourselves beautiful spiritual garments. We may strain for spiritual growth. But we will achieve nothing. No man can add a cubit to his stature by thinking. Our efforts can't match the beautiful dress the great Husbandman gives His garden's plants. They grow under His care. If I could make my readers see how helpless we are in growing, I believe it would relieve many lives. Imagine a child obsessed with growing. He would not grow unless he tried to. He insisted on a combination of rope and pulleys to stretch himself to the desired height. He might, it's true, waste his days in a weary strain. But, there would be no change in the fact, “No man can add to his stature by thinking.” His years of labor would be wasted if they did not hinder the longed-for end. Imagine a lily trying to clothe itself in beauty. It stretched its leaves and stems to grow. It tried to manage the clouds and sunshine, to meet its needs. Yet, these two pictures show a truth. Many Christians want to grow. They know they should. They feel a deep instinct to grow. But, they try to do it by toiling and spinning. They wear themselves out with endless self-effort. It is wear ying to watch. Grow, dear friends. But, please, grow in God’s way, the only true way. Be sure to be rooted in grace. Then, let the Divine gardener cultivate you in His own way. Expose yourselves to His presence in the sunshine. Let the dew of heaven fall on you. Then, see what will happen. Leaves, flowers, and fruit must come in their season. Your Husbandman is a skilled one. He never fails in His harvesting. Just don't hinder the shining of the Sun of Righteousness or the falling of the dew from Heaven. A very thin covering may block the heat or moisture. The plant may wither even in their midst. A slight barrier between your soul and Christ may cause you to fade like a plant in a cellar or under a bushel. Keep the sky clear. Open every part of you to receive the blessings our Divine Husbandman may bring. Bask in the sunshine of His love. Drink in the waters of His goodness. Keep your face upturned to Him. Look, and your soul shall live. You need to make no efforts to grow, but let your efforts instead be all concentrated on this, that you abide in the Vine. The gardener who tends the vine will care for its branches too. He will prune, purge, water, and tend them. They will grow and bear fruit that will last. Like the lily, their glory will surpass even Solomon's. What if you seem to yourselves to be planted at this moment in a desert soil where nothing can grow! Trust fully in the great gardener. He will make that desert blossom and create springs in its sands. The promise is sure. The man who trusts in the Lord, “He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit.”(Jeremiah 17:8)It i s the great prerogative of our Divine gardener. He can turn any soil into the soil of grace, the moment we put our growing into His hands. He does not need to move us to a different field. Right where we are, with just the circumstances around us, He makes His sun to shine and His dew to fall on us. He turns our greatest obstacles into the best means of our growth. I care not what the circumstances may be, His wonder-working power can accomplish this. And we must trust Him with it all. Surely He is a man we can trust. If He sends storms, winds, rains, or sunshine, we must accept it. We must trust, with unwavering faith, that He will cultivate us and bring us to maturity. He knows the best way to do this. He controls the elements to ensure our rapid growth. Let me entreat of you, then, to give up all your efforts after growing, and simply to let yourselves grow. Leave it all to the Gardener, whose responsibility it is, and who alone can manage it. No difficulties in your case can baffle Him. Nothing in your past can mar His perfect work. Not the limiting of your growth, the dryness of your life, or any deformity. If you will, put yourselves completely in His hands and let Him have His way with you. His own gracious promise to His backsliding children a ssures you of this. “ I will heal their apostasy ,” He says: “I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them. I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon. His shoots shall sp read out; his beauty shall be like the olive, and his fragrance like Lebanon.”(Hosea 14:4-6) “They shall return and dwell beneath my shadow; they shall flourish like the grain; they shall blossom like the vine; their fame shall be like the wine of Lebanon.” (Hosea 14:7) And again He says, “ Fear not, you beasts of the field, for the pastures of the wilderness are green; the tree bears its fruit; the fig tree and vine give their full yield.”(Joel 2:22-26) And the floors shall be full of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil. I will restore to you the years that the swarming locust has eaten, the hopper, the destroyer, and the cutter, my great army, which I sent among you. You shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and praise the name of the Lord your God, who has dealt wondrously with you. And my people shall never again be put to shame.” (Joel 2:25 -26) Oh! You could. But, you know what your Lord meant when He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin”(Mathew 6:28 ). These words show a life and a growth far different from the ordinary life and growth of Christians. They show a life of rest and growth without effort. Yet, this life and growth have glorious results. To every soul that becomes a lily in the Lord's garden, and grows as the lilies do, the same glorious array will be given. They will know a mystical passage about their Beloved: “He feeds among the lilies.” We who fully trust believe in a growth in grace. It is a growth that brings desired results. It blossoms into a flower and fruit, becoming a tree planted by rivers of water. It bears fruit in season. Its leaves do not wither. It prospers in all it does. We rejoice to know that, in the Lord's heritage, many such plants are growing up now. As the lilies grow by seeing the sun, they are changed into the same image by beholding the Lord's glory, from glory to glory, by the Lord's spirit. If you ask them how they grow so fast and well, they would say they don't worry about it. They hardly notice their growth. Their Lord told them to abide in Him. He promised that if they did, they would bear much fruit. They focus only on abiding, which is their part. They leave the rest to their good Husbandman, who alone can manage it. You will find that such souls are not engaged in watching self, but in looking unto Jesus. They do not toil nor spin for their spiritual clothes. They leave it to the Lord to dress them as He pleases. Self-effort and self-dependence are at an end with them. Their interest in self is gone, transferred over into the hands of another. Self has become really nothing, and Christ alone is all in all to such as these. And the blessed result is, that not Even Solomon, in all his glory, was arrayed like these will be. Let us examine this subject practically. We all know that growing is not a thing of effort, but is the result of an inward life, a principle of growth. All the stretching and pulling in the world could not make a dead oak grow. But a live oak grows without stretching. It is plain, then, that the key is to get within you the growing life. Then you cannot help but grow. And this life is the life hid with Christ in God, the wonderful divine life of an indwelling Holy Ghost. Be filled with this, dear believer. You must grow, whether you know it or not. Do not worry about your growth. Just ensure you have the growing life. Abide in the Vine. Let the life from Him flow through all your spiritual veins. Interpose no barrier to His mighty life-giving power, working in you all the good pleasure of His will. Surrender completely to His gentle guidance. Put your growing into His hands, as completely as you have put all your other affairs. Suffer Him to manage it as He will. Do not concern yourself about it, nor even think of it. Trust Him without reservation, and at all times. Accept each moment's gift, from His dear hands. It is the needed sunshine or dew for your growth. Say a continual “Yes” to your Father's will. Until now, you may have tried, as many do, to be both the lily and the gardener, both the vineyard and the gardener. You have taken on the burdens and duties that belong only to the Divine gardener. Only He can bear them. Henceforth consent to take your rightful place and to be only what you really are. Say to yourself, “If I am only the garden, not the gardener; if I am only the vine, not the gardener, then I must keep the garden and act its part.”” I must not usurp the gardener's place or try to act his part.” Do not choose your own soil or set your borders. Do not plant your own seeds, prune, or tend your vines. Be content with what the Divine Husbandman arranges for you, and with the care He gives. Let Him choose which plants and fruits to cultivate. If He wills it, let Him grow a potato as gladly as a rose. And, let Him value everyday virtues as much as exalted passions. Be content with the seasons He sends, and the sun and rain. Accept your growth, whether fast or slow. In short, be satisfied with all His ways, even if we don't understand them. There is infinite repose in this. As the violet rests in its nook, it contentedly accepts its daily portion. It lets the rains fall, the suns rise, and the earth whirl, without one anxious pang. So, we must repose in the present as God gives it to us. We should accept, without worry, our daily portion in His grand plan. It is creative and redemptive. The wind that blows can never kill the tree God plants. It blows east, it blows west. The tender leaves have little rest. But any wind that blows is best. The tree God plants Strikes deeper root, grows higher still, spreads wider boughs. For God's goodwill meets all its wants. No frost can blight the tree God shields. The roots are warm beneath the soft snows. When spring comes, it knows, and every bud will blossom. The tree God shields Grows on apace by day and night, Till, sweet to taste and fair to sight, its fruit it yields. No storm can blast the tree, God knows. No thunder, rain, lightning, or hurricane can. When they spend, it remains. The tree God knows. Through every tempest, it stands fast. From its first day to its last, it grows ever fairer. If in the soul's still garden, a seed God sows a little seed, it will soon grow. And, all men will know it. For heavenly land, He bids it blow. A seed God sows, and up it springs by day and night; through life, through death, it grows right, forever grows.

fields.title: Service
fields.body_html:
Perhaps, no part of Christian experience knows a greater change than in service. This is upon entering into the life hid with Christ in God. In lower forms of Christian life, service can feel binding. It is often a duty, and a trial and a cross. At first, some things may bring joy. But, they become weary tasks. They are done faithfully, but with secret disinclination. There are many wishes, both confessed and unconfessed, that they need not be done, or at least, not so often. The soul finds itself saying, instead of the “May I” of love, the “Must I” of duty. The yoke, which was at first easy, begins to gall, and the burden feels heavy instead of light.

One dear Christian expressed it once to me in this way. “After my conversion,” she said, “I was full of joy and love. I was so glad and thankful to do anything for my Lord. So, I eagerly entered every open door.” But, as my early joy faded and my love cooled, I began to regret my eagerness. I found myself in services that were becoming very distasteful and burdensome. I could not give them up, since I had begun them. It would excite great remark. Yet, I increasingly longed to do so. I was expected to visit the sick, and pray beside their beds.

I was expected to attend prayer-meetings, and speak at them. I was expected to be always ready for every effort in Christian work. The weight of these expectations bowed me down continually. At last, it became unbearable to live the Christian life I had begun, and that everyone expected of me. I would have infinitely preferred to scrub all day on my hands and knees rather than endure my daily Christian work. I envied,” she said, “the servants in the kitchen, and the w omen at the wash-tubs.”

This may seem a strong statement. But, does it not evoke some of your own experiences, dear Christian?

Have you never gone to your work as a slave to his daily task, knowing it was your duty? You must do it. But, like a rubber ball, you bounced back to your real interests and pleasures the moment your work was done.

You know this was the wrong way to feel. You are ashamed of it, but you can't help it. You have not loved your work. If you could have, you would have gladly given it up. Or, if this does not describe your case, perhaps another picture will. You love your work in the abstract. But, in doing it, you find many cares and responsibilities. You have doubts about your ability. This makes it a heavy burden.

You go to it, weary and bowed down, before the work has even begun.

You also distress yourself about your work. You are troubled if the results are not what you want. This, too, is a constant burden. Now, the soul is entirely delivered from all these forms of bondage. It enters fully into the blessed life of faith. First, it delights in any service. It has surrendered its will to the Lord.

He works in it to desire and do His pleasure. The soul now wants to do what God wants. It is always nice to do what we want, no matter how hard or tiring it is. If a man is truly set on a thing, he will. He'll ignore the obstacles in his way. He'll laugh at the idea of any opposition or difficulties hindering him.

How many men have, gladly and thankfully, searched the earth for wealth or to fulfill their ambitions?

They scorned any thoughts of the cross connected with it! How many mothers have congratulated themselves on their sons' promotions to powerful government jobs? They have rejoiced. But, it may have meant years of separation and hardship for their dear ones. Yet, these men and their mothers would have called it an unbearable cross if Christ's service had required the same sacrifice of home, friends, and ease.

It is altogether the way we look at things, whether we think they are crosses or not. I am ashamed to think that any Christian would mourn for doing a thing for Christ, which a worldly man would do for money.

What we need in the Christian life is to get believers to want to do God’s will, as much as other people want to do their own will. And this is the idea of the Gospel. It is what God intended for us; and it is what He has promised. In describing the new covenant in Heb. 8:6-13 “ But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.”

“And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord, for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest. For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more. “In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.

“He says it shall no more be the old covenant made on Sin ai. That is, a law given from the outside, controlling a man by force. But it shall be a law written within, constraining a man by love. “I will put my laws,” He says, “in their mind, and write them in their hearts.” This can mean nothing but that we shall love His law, for anything written on our hearts we must love.

Putting it into our minds is the same as God working in us to “For it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. ” (Philippians 2:13)It means we will want what God wills. We will obey His commands, not out of duty, but because we want to do what He wants. Nothing could possibly be conceived more effectual than this. How often have we thought, “If I could get inside my kids and make them want to do what I want, managing them would be so easy!” We have found, in practice, that to deal with cross-grained people, we must avoid suggesting our wishes to them. We must instead induce them to suggest their own. Then, we will face no opposition. We, a stiff-necked people by nature, always rebel against an outside law. But we embrace a law that springs up within us.

God's plan is to possess a man's inner self. He wants to control and manage his will, and work it for him. Then, obedience is easy and a delight. Service becomes perfect freedom. The Christian must exclaim, “This happy service!” Who could dream earth had such liberty?” Then, dear Christian, if you are in bondage, you must surrender your will to your Lord. Give Him complete control of it. Say, “Yes, Lord, YES !” To everything. Trust Him to work in you to will. To bring your wishes and affections into harmony with His lovely will. I have seen this done over and over, in cases where it looked beforehand an utterly impossible thing.

In one case, a lady had long feared and hated a thing she knew was right. I saw her, in despair and without feeling, give her will to her Lord. She began to say to Him, “Your will be done; your will be done!” And in one short hour that very thing began to look sweet and precious to h er. It is wonderful what miracles God works in wills that are utterly surrendered to Him. He turns hard things into easy and bitter things into sweet. It is not that He puts easy things in the place of the hard, but He actually changes the hard thing into an easy one. And this is salvation. It is grand. Do try it. You, who find daily Christian living hard, will find that your Master will transform your bondage into the most delicious liberty!

Or, if you love His will in theory, but find it hard to do, there is deliverance in the wonderful life of faith. For in this life no burdens are carried, nor anxieties felt. The Lord is our burden-bearer, and upon Him we must lay off every care. He says, in effect, be careful for nothing, but just make your requests known to me, and I will attend to them all. Be anxious for nothing, He says, not even your service.

Above all, I should think, our service. We are utterly helpless in this. So, even if we were careful, it would not matter. What have we to do with thinking whether we are fit or not!

The Master has the right to use any tool for His work. It is not the tool's place to decide if it is the right one. He knows; and if He chooses to use us, of course we must be fit. And in truth, if we only knew it, our chief fitness is in our utter helplessness. His strength can only be made perfect in our weakness. I can give you a convincing illustration of this.

I once visited an asylum for people with intellectual disabilities. I watched the children doing dumbbell ex ercises. We know that it’s hard for people with intellectual disabilities to control their movements.

They are usually strong, but they lack the skill to use that strength. So, they can’t do much. In the dumbbell exercises, this problem was very clear. They made all sorts of awkward movements.

Occasionally, they would move in time with the music and the teacher’s instructions, but most of the time, it was all out of sync .

One little girl, however, I noticed, who made perfect movements. Not a jar nor a break disturbed the harmony of her exercises. And the reason was, not that she had more strength than the others, but that she had no strength at all. She could not close her hands over the dumb-bells, nor lift her arms. The master had to stand behind her and do it all. She yielded up her members as instruments to him, and his strength was made perfect in her weakness. He knew how to do those exercises. He had planned them. So, when he did them, they were done right. She did nothing but yield herself up utterly into his hands, and he did it all.

The yielding was her part, the responsibility was all his. It was not her skill that was needed to make harmonious movements, but only his. The question was not of her capacity, but of his. Her utter weakness was her greatest strength. If this shows our Christian life, it's no wonder. Paul could say, “Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.”

Who would not glory in being so weak and helpless, that the Lord Jesus Christ should find no hindrance to the perfect working of His mighty power through us and in us?

Then, too, if the work is His, the responsibility is His, and we have no room left for worrying about it.

Everything in reference to it is known to Him, and He can manage it all. Why not leave it all with Him then, and consent to be treated like a child and guided where to go. The most effective workers I know have no anxiety about their work. They commit it to their dear Master. They ask Him to guide them and trust Him for the wisdom and strength they need, moment by moment.

One might think they were too carefree, with such at stake. But, when you learn God's secret of trusting, you will see the beauty and power of a life yielded to His work. You will cease to condemn. You will wonder how any of God's workers can dare to bear burdens or responsibilities that He alone can bear.

There are one or two other bonds of service from which this life of trust delivers us. We find out that we are not responsible for all the work in the world. The commands cease to be general, and become personal and individual.

The Master does not map out a general course of action for us and leave us to get along through it by our own wisdom and skill as best we may. He leads us step by step, giving us each hour the special guidance needed for that hour.

His blessed Spirit in us brings to mind, when needed, the command. So, we need not think ahead. We should simply take each step as it is revealed to us, following our Lord wherever He leads. “The steps of a good man are ordered of the Lord, ” not his way only, but each separate step in that way. Many Christians make the mistake of expecting to receive God’s commands all in a lump, as it were. They think, because He tells them to give a tract to one person on a train, that they must always give tracts to everyone. They burden themselves with an impossible command.

Once, a young Christian met a soul on a walk. The Lord had sent her to deliver a message. She took it as a command to speak to everyone she met about their souls. This was, of course, impossible, and as a consequence, she was soon in hopeless bondage about it. She was terrified to go outside. She lived in constant shame.

At last, she told her distress to a friend. This friend, a servant of God, said she was mistaken. The Lord has a special work for each worker. In a well-run household, each servant must not try to do the others' work. The same goes for the Lord's servants. They are not obliged to do everything. He told her to seek the Lord's guidance on her work. She should trust Him to show her whom to speak to. He assured her that He guides His own sheep. He goes before them and makes a way for them.

She followed this advice. She laid her work on the Lord. The result was a happy path of daily guidance.

She was led into much blessed work for her Master. She did it all without a care, for He prepared the way before her. Trusting God is like connecting the machinery to the steam engine. The power is not in the machinery, but in the steam. The machinery is useless, disconnected from the engine. But if you connect them, the machinery will run easily. It has great power behind it. So, the Christian life becomes easy and natural. It develops the divine work within.

Most Christians are tense. Their wills clash with God's. The connection is not perfect. It takes effort to move the machinery. But when the connection is made, the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus can work in us with all its power. We are then free from the law of sin and death. We shall know the glorious liberty of the children of God. We shall lead frictionless lives.

Another form of bondage is to service. The life of faith delivers the soul from it. It refers to the after reflections that always follow any Christian work. These self-reflections are of two sorts. The soul both congratulates itself on its success and is uplifted. Or, it is distressed over its failure and is cast down.

One of these is sure to come. Of the two, I dread the first more. The last causes greater suffering at the time. But in the life of trust, neither will trouble us. We have committed ourselves and our work to the Lord. We will be satisfied to leave it to Him and not think about ourselves at all.

Years ago, I found this sentence in an old book: “Never indulge, at the end of an action, in any self-reflection, whether of self-congratulation or despair.” Forget the things that are behind, the moment they are past. Leave them with God.” It has been of unspeakable value to me. When the temptation comes, as it always does, to indulge in these reflections, I turn from them at once. I refuse to think about my work at all. I leave it to the Lord to overrule the mistakes and bless it as He chooses.

In short, for happy and effective service, just trust your work to the Lord and leave it there. Do not pray, “Lord, guide me; give me wisdom; arrange for me.” Then, rise from your knees and take back the burden. Don't try to guide and arrange for yourself. Leave it with the Lord, and remember that what you trust to Him, you must not worry over nor feel anxious about. Trust and worry cannot go together.

If your work is a burden, it is because you are not trusting it to Him. If you trust it to Him, you will find the yoke He puts on you is easy. The burden He gives you is light. Even amid a life of ceaseless activity, you will find rest for your soul.

But some may say that this teaching would make us into mere puppets. I answer, No, it would simply make us into servants. A servant must not plan, arrange, decide, or supply materials. He must only obey. It is for the Master to do all the rest. The servant is not responsible, either, for results. The Master alone knows what results he wished to have produced, and so he alone can judge of them. Intelligent service must, of course, sympathize with the Master's plans. But, there cannot be a full understanding.

The Master cannot shift his responsibility to the servant. With our limited view and great ignorance, we can do little but accept God's will. We shouldn't expect to fully understand it. We must leave all results to Him.

What seems like failure on the surface is often, on the unseen side, a great success. If we allow ourselves to lament and worry, we will be foolish. We should be singing and rejoicing, not weeping. It is far better to avoid all self-reflection. We should not think about ourselves at all, whether for good or ill.

We are not our own property, nor our own business. We belong to God. We are His instruments and His business. He always attends to His own business. So, He will, of course, attend to us.

I once heard of a slave on a ship during a violent storm. While everyone else was scared, he whistled happily. Finally, someone asked if he was afraid of drowning. He smiled and said, “Well, maybe I am.

But I don’t belong to myself, and it will only be my master’s loss.” This attitude could help us avoid many worries in our work. With a group of people fully dedicated to serving and trusting in our Master, imagine what He could do. One person like this could defeat a thousand, and two could put ten thousand to flight. Nothing would be impossible for them because, with the Lord, it doesn’t matter whether we have many or few.

May God quickly raise such an army! And may you, my dear reader, enroll in this army today. Yield yourself to God as one alive from the dead. May every part of you be His instrument of righteousness, to be used by Him as He wishes.
fields.body_text: Perhaps, no part of Christian experience knows a greater change than in service. This is upon entering into the life hid with Christ in God. In lower forms of Christian life, service can feel binding. It is often a duty, and a trial and a cross. At first, some things may bring joy. But, they become weary tasks. They are done faithfully, but with secret disinclination. There are many wishes, both confessed and unconfessed, that they need not be done, or at least, not so often. The soul finds itself saying, instead of the “May I” of love, the “Must I” of duty. The yoke, which was at first easy, begins to gall, and the burden feels heavy instead of light. One dear Christian expressed it once to me in this way. “After my conversion,” she said, “I was full of joy and love. I was so glad and thankful to do anything for my Lord. So, I eagerly entered every open door.” But, as my early joy faded and my love cooled, I began to regret my eagerness. I found myself in services that were becoming very distasteful and burdensome. I could not give them up, since I had begun them. It would excite great remark. Yet, I increasingly longed to do so. I was expected to visit the sick, and pray beside their beds. I was expected to attend prayer-meetings, and speak at them. I was expected to be always ready for every effort in Christian work. The weight of these expectations bowed me down continually. At last, it became unbearable to live the Christian life I had begun, and that everyone expected of me. I would have infinitely preferred to scrub all day on my hands and knees rather than endure my daily Christian work. I envied,” she said, “the servants in the kitchen, and the w omen at the wash-tubs.” This may seem a strong statement. But, does it not evoke some of your own experiences, dear Christian? Have you never gone to your work as a slave to his daily task, knowing it was your duty? You must do it. But, like a rubber ball, you bounced back to your real interests and pleasures the moment your work was done. You know this was the wrong way to feel. You are ashamed of it, but you can't help it. You have not loved your work. If you could have, you would have gladly given it up. Or, if this does not describe your case, perhaps another picture will. You love your work in the abstract. But, in doing it, you find many cares and responsibilities. You have doubts about your ability. This makes it a heavy burden. You go to it, weary and bowed down, before the work has even begun. You also distress yourself about your work. You are troubled if the results are not what you want. This, too, is a constant burden. Now, the soul is entirely delivered from all these forms of bondage. It enters fully into the blessed life of faith. First, it delights in any service. It has surrendered its will to the Lord. He works in it to desire and do His pleasure. The soul now wants to do what God wants. It is always nice to do what we want, no matter how hard or tiring it is. If a man is truly set on a thing, he will. He'll ignore the obstacles in his way. He'll laugh at the idea of any opposition or difficulties hindering him. How many men have, gladly and thankfully, searched the earth for wealth or to fulfill their ambitions? They scorned any thoughts of the cross connected with it! How many mothers have congratulated themselves on their sons' promotions to powerful government jobs? They have rejoiced. But, it may have meant years of separation and hardship for their dear ones. Yet, these men and their mothers would have called it an unbearable cross if Christ's service had required the same sacrifice of home, friends, and ease. It is altogether the way we look at things, whether we think they are crosses or not. I am ashamed to think that any Christian would mourn for doing a thing for Christ, which a worldly man would do for money. What we need in the Christian life is to get believers to want to do God’s will, as much as other people want to do their own will. And this is the idea of the Gospel. It is what God intended for us; and it is what He has promised. In describing the new covenant in Heb. 8:6-13 “ But as it is, Christ has obtained a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is enacted on better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no concern for them, declares the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts, and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” “And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord, for they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest. For I will be merciful toward their iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more. “In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away. “He says it shall no more be the old covenant made on Sin ai. That is, a law given from the outside, controlling a man by force. But it shall be a law written within, constraining a man by love. “I will put my laws,” He says, “in their mind, and write them in their hearts.” This can mean nothing but that we shall love His law, for anything written on our hearts we must love. Putting it into our minds is the same as God working in us to “For it is God who works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure. ” (Philippians 2:13)It means we will want what God wills. We will obey His commands, not out of duty, but because we want to do what He wants. Nothing could possibly be conceived more effectual than this. How often have we thought, “If I could get inside my kids and make them want to do what I want, managing them would be so easy!” We have found, in practice, that to deal with cross-grained people, we must avoid suggesting our wishes to them. We must instead induce them to suggest their own. Then, we will face no opposition. We, a stiff-necked people by nature, always rebel against an outside law. But we embrace a law that springs up within us. God's plan is to possess a man's inner self. He wants to control and manage his will, and work it for him. Then, obedience is easy and a delight. Service becomes perfect freedom. The Christian must exclaim, “This happy service!” Who could dream earth had such liberty?” Then, dear Christian, if you are in bondage, you must surrender your will to your Lord. Give Him complete control of it. Say, “Yes, Lord, YES !” To everything. Trust Him to work in you to will. To bring your wishes and affections into harmony with His lovely will. I have seen this done over and over, in cases where it looked beforehand an utterly impossible thing. In one case, a lady had long feared and hated a thing she knew was right. I saw her, in despair and without feeling, give her will to her Lord. She began to say to Him, “Your will be done; your will be done!” And in one short hour that very thing began to look sweet and precious to h er. It is wonderful what miracles God works in wills that are utterly surrendered to Him. He turns hard things into easy and bitter things into sweet. It is not that He puts easy things in the place of the hard, but He actually changes the hard thing into an easy one. And this is salvation. It is grand. Do try it. You, who find daily Christian living hard, will find that your Master will transform your bondage into the most delicious liberty! Or, if you love His will in theory, but find it hard to do, there is deliverance in the wonderful life of faith. For in this life no burdens are carried, nor anxieties felt. The Lord is our burden-bearer, and upon Him we must lay off every care. He says, in effect, be careful for nothing, but just make your requests known to me, and I will attend to them all. Be anxious for nothing, He says, not even your service. Above all, I should think, our service. We are utterly helpless in this. So, even if we were careful, it would not matter. What have we to do with thinking whether we are fit or not! The Master has the right to use any tool for His work. It is not the tool's place to decide if it is the right one. He knows; and if He chooses to use us, of course we must be fit. And in truth, if we only knew it, our chief fitness is in our utter helplessness. His strength can only be made perfect in our weakness. I can give you a convincing illustration of this. I once visited an asylum for people with intellectual disabilities. I watched the children doing dumbbell ex ercises. We know that it’s hard for people with intellectual disabilities to control their movements. They are usually strong, but they lack the skill to use that strength. So, they can’t do much. In the dumbbell exercises, this problem was very clear. They made all sorts of awkward movements. Occasionally, they would move in time with the music and the teacher’s instructions, but most of the time, it was all out of sync . One little girl, however, I noticed, who made perfect movements. Not a jar nor a break disturbed the harmony of her exercises. And the reason was, not that she had more strength than the others, but that she had no strength at all. She could not close her hands over the dumb-bells, nor lift her arms. The master had to stand behind her and do it all. She yielded up her members as instruments to him, and his strength was made perfect in her weakness. He knew how to do those exercises. He had planned them. So, when he did them, they were done right. She did nothing but yield herself up utterly into his hands, and he did it all. The yielding was her part, the responsibility was all his. It was not her skill that was needed to make harmonious movements, but only his. The question was not of her capacity, but of his. Her utter weakness was her greatest strength. If this shows our Christian life, it's no wonder. Paul could say, “Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.” Who would not glory in being so weak and helpless, that the Lord Jesus Christ should find no hindrance to the perfect working of His mighty power through us and in us? Then, too, if the work is His, the responsibility is His, and we have no room left for worrying about it. Everything in reference to it is known to Him, and He can manage it all. Why not leave it all with Him then, and consent to be treated like a child and guided where to go. The most effective workers I know have no anxiety about their work. They commit it to their dear Master. They ask Him to guide them and trust Him for the wisdom and strength they need, moment by moment. One might think they were too carefree, with such at stake. But, when you learn God's secret of trusting, you will see the beauty and power of a life yielded to His work. You will cease to condemn. You will wonder how any of God's workers can dare to bear burdens or responsibilities that He alone can bear. There are one or two other bonds of service from which this life of trust delivers us. We find out that we are not responsible for all the work in the world. The commands cease to be general, and become personal and individual. The Master does not map out a general course of action for us and leave us to get along through it by our own wisdom and skill as best we may. He leads us step by step, giving us each hour the special guidance needed for that hour. His blessed Spirit in us brings to mind, when needed, the command. So, we need not think ahead. We should simply take each step as it is revealed to us, following our Lord wherever He leads. “The steps of a good man are ordered of the Lord, ” not his way only, but each separate step in that way. Many Christians make the mistake of expecting to receive God’s commands all in a lump, as it were. They think, because He tells them to give a tract to one person on a train, that they must always give tracts to everyone. They burden themselves with an impossible command. Once, a young Christian met a soul on a walk. The Lord had sent her to deliver a message. She took it as a command to speak to everyone she met about their souls. This was, of course, impossible, and as a consequence, she was soon in hopeless bondage about it. She was terrified to go outside. She lived in constant shame. At last, she told her distress to a friend. This friend, a servant of God, said she was mistaken. The Lord has a special work for each worker. In a well-run household, each servant must not try to do the others' work. The same goes for the Lord's servants. They are not obliged to do everything. He told her to seek the Lord's guidance on her work. She should trust Him to show her whom to speak to. He assured her that He guides His own sheep. He goes before them and makes a way for them. She followed this advice. She laid her work on the Lord. The result was a happy path of daily guidance. She was led into much blessed work for her Master. She did it all without a care, for He prepared the way before her. Trusting God is like connecting the machinery to the steam engine. The power is not in the machinery, but in the steam. The machinery is useless, disconnected from the engine. But if you connect them, the machinery will run easily. It has great power behind it. So, the Christian life becomes easy and natural. It develops the divine work within. Most Christians are tense. Their wills clash with God's. The connection is not perfect. It takes effort to move the machinery. But when the connection is made, the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus can work in us with all its power. We are then free from the law of sin and death. We shall know the glorious liberty of the children of God. We shall lead frictionless lives. Another form of bondage is to service. The life of faith delivers the soul from it. It refers to the after reflections that always follow any Christian work. These self-reflections are of two sorts. The soul both congratulates itself on its success and is uplifted. Or, it is distressed over its failure and is cast down. One of these is sure to come. Of the two, I dread the first more. The last causes greater suffering at the time. But in the life of trust, neither will trouble us. We have committed ourselves and our work to the Lord. We will be satisfied to leave it to Him and not think about ourselves at all. Years ago, I found this sentence in an old book: “Never indulge, at the end of an action, in any self-reflection, whether of self-congratulation or despair.” Forget the things that are behind, the moment they are past. Leave them with God.” It has been of unspeakable value to me. When the temptation comes, as it always does, to indulge in these reflections, I turn from them at once. I refuse to think about my work at all. I leave it to the Lord to overrule the mistakes and bless it as He chooses. In short, for happy and effective service, just trust your work to the Lord and leave it there. Do not pray, “Lord, guide me; give me wisdom; arrange for me.” Then, rise from your knees and take back the burden. Don't try to guide and arrange for yourself. Leave it with the Lord, and remember that what you trust to Him, you must not worry over nor feel anxious about. Trust and worry cannot go together. If your work is a burden, it is because you are not trusting it to Him. If you trust it to Him, you will find the yoke He puts on you is easy. The burden He gives you is light. Even amid a life of ceaseless activity, you will find rest for your soul. But some may say that this teaching would make us into mere puppets. I answer, No, it would simply make us into servants. A servant must not plan, arrange, decide, or supply materials. He must only obey. It is for the Master to do all the rest. The servant is not responsible, either, for results. The Master alone knows what results he wished to have produced, and so he alone can judge of them. Intelligent service must, of course, sympathize with the Master's plans. But, there cannot be a full understanding. The Master cannot shift his responsibility to the servant. With our limited view and great ignorance, we can do little but accept God's will. We shouldn't expect to fully understand it. We must leave all results to Him. What seems like failure on the surface is often, on the unseen side, a great success. If we allow ourselves to lament and worry, we will be foolish. We should be singing and rejoicing, not weeping. It is far better to avoid all self-reflection. We should not think about ourselves at all, whether for good or ill. We are not our own property, nor our own business. We belong to God. We are His instruments and His business. He always attends to His own business. So, He will, of course, attend to us. I once heard of a slave on a ship during a violent storm. While everyone else was scared, he whistled happily. Finally, someone asked if he was afraid of drowning. He smiled and said, “Well, maybe I am. But I don’t belong to myself, and it will only be my master’s loss.” This attitude could help us avoid many worries in our work. With a group of people fully dedicated to serving and trusting in our Master, imagine what He could do. One person like this could defeat a thousand, and two could put ten thousand to flight. Nothing would be impossible for them because, with the Lord, it doesn’t matter whether we have many or few. May God quickly raise such an army! And may you, my dear reader, enroll in this army today. Yield yourself to God as one alive from the dead. May every part of you be His instrument of righteousness, to be used by Him as He wishes.

fields.title: Difficulties Concerning Guidance
fields.body_html:
You have now begun, dear reader, the life of faith. You have given yourself to the Lord, to be His wholly. He has taken you and begun to mold you into a vessel of His honor. Your deepest desire is to be very flexible in His hands. You want to follow Him wherever He may lead you.

You trust Him to work in you to will and to do of His good pleasure. But you find a great difficulty here. You do not know the voice of the Good Shepherd. So, you are in doubt about His will for you.

God is calling you to certain paths. Your friends express strong disapproval. And, these friends may be older than you in the Christian life. They seem much more advanced, too. You can hardly bear to differ from or distress them. You also feel very unsure about yielding to any duty they might disapprove of.

Yet, you cannot shake these impressions. You plunge into doubt and unease. There is a way out of all these difficulties, to the fully surrendered soul. I would repeat, fully surrendered. Any will to resist makes it hard to know God's mind on that point. So, first, ensure you truly want to obey the Lord in all respects. If this is the case, your soul only needs to know God's will to consent to it.

Then, you cannot doubt His desire to make it known and to guide you.

There are many very clear promises in reference to this. Take, for instance, John 10:3-4 “To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, when he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. ” John 14:26: But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.” Also, James 1:56: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. ” With such passages as these, and many more like them, we must believe that Divine guidance is promised to us, and our faith must confidently look for and expect it.

This is essential; for in James 1:6-7, we are told, “ But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord .

First, settle this point. Divine guidance has been promised. You will surely have it if you ask for it.

Let no doubt turn you from this.

Next, remember that our God has all knowledge and wisdom. Therefore, He may guide you to paths where great blessings await you. But, to the short-sighted human eyes around you, those paths may seem to lead to confusion and loss.

You must accept that God's thoughts and ways differ from man’s . Only He, who knows the end from the beginning, can judge the results of any action. You must realize that His love for you may lead you to go against your dearest friends' wishes.

You must learn from Luke 14 and similar passages, “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.” ( Luke 14:26-33.)

To be a disciple of your Lord, you may need to forsake all you have. You may have to turn your back on your family, or even your own life. If this is not clearly recognized, the soul may suffer. Often, a child's path of obedience will displease those he loves most. If he cannot trust the Lord through this, he will be lost.

Of course, this is in harmony with our duties of honor and love to one another in our various life relationships. The closer we are to Christ, the more we will show His meekness and gentleness. We will also be tender to our natural guardians and counselors. The Master's guidance will always show itself by the Master's Spirit. If, in obeying Him, we act against our friends' wishes, our love and patience will prove our motive. But, this point settled, we now ask how God's guidance will come to us. How shall we know His voice?

There are four special ways God speaks: 1. the voice of Scripture, 2. the inward impressions of the Holy Spirit, 3. our higher judgment, and 4. providential circumstances. If these four align, it is safe to say that God speaks. I lay it down as a principle, which none can dispute. His voice will always be in harmony with itself, no matter how many ways He may speak.

The voices may be many, the message can be but one. If God tells me in one voice to do or to leave undone anything, He cannot possibly tell me the opposite in another voice. If there is a contradiction in the voices, the speaker cannot be the same.

My rule for distinguishing the voice of God is to test it against this harmony. If I have an impression, I must check if it aligns with Scripture. I must also see if my higher judgment approves it, and, as we Quakers say, if “way opens” to carry it out. If either test fails, it is not safe to proceed. I must wait in quiet trust until the Lord shows me the point of harmony. He will, if it is His voice that has spoken. For we must not overlook the fact that there are other voices that speak to the soul. There is the loud and clamoring voice of self that is always seeking to be heard. And there are the voices of evil, deceiving spirits. They lie in wait to entrap every traveler who enters these higher regions of the spiritual life.

In the same epistle which tells us that we are seated in “ and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus , ” (Eph. 2:6) , we are also told that we shall have to fight there with spiritual enemies. “ For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places.” (Eph. 6:12). These spiritual enemies, whoever they are, must communicate with us through our spiritual faculties. Their voices, therefore, will be, like God's, an inward impression on our spirits.

So, just as the Holy Spirit may tell us, by impressions, the will of God, so will these spiritual enemies.

They will, by impressions, tell us their will, though not giving their name. It is plain, therefore, that we need a test. We must try these inner impressions. It is to know whose voice is speaking. And that test will always be the harmony to which I have referred. In a misguided attempt to honor the Divine Spirit, some earnest Christians have ignored and even violated the Bible. They have disregarded clear signs from Providence and outraged their own better judgment. God, who sees their sincere hearts, can and does forgive. But, the consequences in this life are often very sad.

We must first test any voice claiming to be divine. It must align morally with God's mind and will, as revealed in the Gospel of Christ. Whatever is contrary to this, cannot be Divine, because God cannot contradict Himself. We cannot expect a direct revelation until we seek and obey God's will, as revealed in the Bible. A great many fatal mistakes are made in this matter of guidance, by the overlooking of this simple rule. If our Father has given us clear directions, He won't reveal anything more. No man needs or could expect a direct revelation to tell him not to steal. God has already, in the Scriptures, plainly declared His will about it. It seems so obvious that I would not mention it. But, I have met Christians who overlooked it and became fanatical.

For the Scriptures are far more explicit even about details than most people think. And there are not many important affairs in life for which a clear direction may not be found in God’s book.

Take the matter of dress, and we have 1 Pet. 3:3-4 “ Do not let your adorning be external — the braiding of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear — but let your adorning be the hidden person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is very precious .” and 1 Tim. 2:9 - 10 “ likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with what is proper for women who profess godliness —with good works.”

Take the matter of conversation, and we have Eph. 4:29 “ Let no corrupting talk come out of your mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those who hear . ” , and 5:4 “ Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place, but instead let there be thanksgiving .” Take the matter of avenging injuries and standing up for your rights, and we have (Romans.12:19-21) “ Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” To the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will hear burning coals on his head.” Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good ,” and (Matthew. 5:38 - 48) “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also.

And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the one who would borrow from you. You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward do you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? And if you greet only your brothers, what more are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? You therefore must be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect.”

“ For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God. For to this you have been called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps .”(1Peter.

2:19-21) Take the matter of forgiving one another, and we have (Ephesians.4:32) “ Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.”

Mark 11:25-26 “And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses .” Take the matter of conformity to the world, and we have (Romans 12:20) “ Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and acceptable and perfect. ” and (1 John 2:15-17) “ Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world — the desires of the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life — is not from the Father but is from the world. And the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.

“ You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God?

Therefore, whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.”(James 4:4) Take the matter of anxieties of all kinds, and we have (Matthew 6:25-34) “Therefore I tell you, do not be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you will put on. Isn't life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air: they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not of more value than they? And which of you, by being anxious, can add a single hour to his span of life?

And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore, do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’

or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. “Therefore , do not be anxious about tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.

“ Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.”( Philippians 4:6-7) I only give these as examples to show how very full and practical the Bible guidance is. If you are confused, first, check if the Bible addresses your question. Ask God to reveal His will to you through the Scriptures. And whatever shall seem to you to be plainly taught there, that you must obey. Reading and meditating on this record of God's mind and will enlightens us. The inspiring Spirit will do so. Our obedience will then be, as if, a present, living word. It will be as if our Lord spoke it to us today from Heaven. The Bible is an ancient message from God, sent to us long ago. It is also a present message, sent to us now each time we read it.

“My words are spirit and life. You must obey them. It's a command, personal and present.” But we must remember, the Bible is a book of principles. It is not a group of unrelated sayings . Isolated texts may be used to sanction things. These are opposed by Scripture's principles.

I recently heard of a Christian woman at a Western meeting. The text, “For we walk by faith, and not by sight,” brought it to mind. She felt it was a command to be literally obeyed. So, she blindfolded herself and insisted on walking up and down the aisle to illustrate the walk of faith. She soon stumbled and fell against the stove, burning herself. Then, she wondered at the mysterious dispensation.

Applying Scripture and her common sense would have saved her from the delusion.

The second test, therefore, is our own higher judgment, or common sense. It is as true now as in Solomon's time. A “man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels.” His exhortation still binds us: “Get wisdom, the principal thing. “Wi th all you're getting, get understanding.” The Scriptures say it is vital for God's children to use all their abilities on their journey through this world. They are to use their outward faculties for their outward walk, and their inward faculties for their inward walk. They might as well expect to be “kept” from stubbing their toes if they walk blindfolded. It's the same as expecting to be “kept” from spiritual stumbling if they ignore their judgment and common sense.

I asked a “sound mind” Christian how she told false spirits from the Holy Spirit. She replied, “I rap them over the head and see if they have any common sense.” Some may say, “But we should not depend on our human understanding in divine things.” I answer that we should not depend on our unenlightened understanding. We should rely on our judgment and common sense, which the Spirit of God has enlightened. That is, God will speak to us through the faculties He has Himself given us, and not independently of them. We must use our eyes when we walk, no matter how faithful we are.

Similarly, we must use our minds in our inner lives.

The third and last test is that of providential circumstances. If a “leading” is of God, a way will always open for it. Our Lord assures us of this in John 10:4. It says, “When he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. ” Notice here the expressions “goes before,” and “ follows .” He goes before to open a way, and we are to follow in the way thus opened. A Christian should not force his way and trample opposition. That is never a sign of a Divine leading. If the Lord “goes before” us, He will open all doors for us, and we shall not need ourselves to hammer them down.

The fourth point is this: We must test our impressions by the other three voices. We must also test those voices by our inward impressions. If we feel a “stop in our minds” about anything, we must wait until it is removed before acting. A Christian, who had quickly advanced in the Divine life, gave me this secret: “I always mind the checks.” We must not ignore our inner voice, nor ride roughshod over it, any more than we must the other three voices of which I have spoken.

These four voices, then, will always be found to agree in any truly Divine leading. The voice of our impressions, the voice of Scripture, the voice of our own sanctified judgment. The voice of providential circumstances. If these four do not agree at first, we must wait until they do.

A divine sense of “oughtness,” derived from the harmony of all God’s various voices, is the only safe foundation for any action. I have guarded the points of danger. So, please let me out. I long for the joy of this direct communication of God's will to us. It seems to me to be the grandest of privileges. In the first place, that God should love me enough to care about the details of my life is perfectly wonderful.

And that He would tell me all about it. And, to know how to live and walk to perfectly please Him, seems almost too good to be true.

We never care about the little details of people’s lives unless we love them. We don't care what most people do or how they spend their time. But when we love someone, we start to care. God's care for us proves His love. It's a great blessing that He speaks to us about everything in our lives. This includes our duties, pleasures, friendships, and all we do, think, or say.

You must know this in your own experience, dear reader. Only then will you find the joy and privilege of a life hid with Christ in God. It is one of its most precious gifts. God promises to work in us to will and to do of His good pleasure.

This means He will take control of our will and work it for us. His suggestions will come to us as desires, not commands. They will originate in our will; we shall feel as though we wanted to do so and so, not as though we must. This makes it a service of perfect liberty. For it is always easy to do what we desire, no matter how difficult the circumstances. Every mother knows she could get perfect obedience from her child. She just needs to control his will, making him want to do what she wants.

And this is what our Father does for His children in the new dispensation.

He writes His laws on our hearts and minds. We love them. Our affections and judgment, not our fears, draw us to obey. The Holy Spirit usually guides by impressing a desire to do or avoid certain things.

In prayer, the soul feels a sudden suggestion about a duty. “I would like to do this or the other,” it thinks, “I wish I could.” Or the suggestion may come as a question, “I wonder whether I had not better do so and so?” Or it may be only at first in the way of a conviction that such is the right and best thing to be done. The matter should be committed to the Lord. We must instantly choose to obey Him. If the suggestion agrees with the Scriptures, a holy judgment, and the circumstances, we should obey it.

Immediate obedience is the safest and easiest course. When the Spirit speaks, it is easy to obey. But if the soul hesitates and reasons, it becomes harder to obey.

The first convictions are usually right in a fully surrendered heart. God is faithful and will make His voice heard above all others. Such convictions, therefore, should never be met by reasoning. Prayer and trust are the only safe attitudes of the soul. But even these should be brief.

We must act before the time passes and we miss the blessing.

If the suggestion is unclear and doubt arises, we should wait for further insight. This is especially true if our friends disagree. The Scripture rule is, “Whatsoever is not of faith is sin” which means plainly that we must never act in doubt. A clear conviction of right is the only safe guide. But we must wait in faith. We must fully surrender, saying, “Yes,” to our Lord's will, whatever it may be.

Our troubles stem from a lack of will. Next, many doubt any real Divine guidance. God's children are very skeptical here. They read the promises and feel the need. But, they cannot believe that someone will guide them.

It's as if God wants us to obey His voice, but didn't know how to make us hear and understand Him. It is, thus, very possible for God to speak, but for the soul not to hear, because it does not believe He is speaking. No earthly parent or master could guide his children or servants if they did not believe him or accept his voice as his true will. God, who spoke to the fathers in many ways, still speaks. He wants to see if any souls will obey His will.

Every moment of our lives our Father is seeking to reveal Himself to us. “ Jesus said to her, “I who speak to you am he.”(John 4:26) I that speak in your heart, in your circumstances, in your losses, in your gains, in your sorrows, and in your joys, am He. “I speak everywhere and in everything.” So, we must have perfect faith that the Lord's voice is speaking to us. It will teach and lead us. He will give us wisdom for our guidance. After asking for guidance, we must follow our strongest sense of what we should do. A few rules can help us with this.

I. We must believe that God will guide us.

II. We must surrender our own will to His guidance.

III. We must hearken for the Divine voice.

IV. We must wait for the divine harmony.

fields.body_text: You have now begun, dear reader, the life of faith. You have given yourself to the Lord, to be His wholly. He has taken you and begun to mold you into a vessel of His honor. Your deepest desire is to be very flexible in His hands. You want to follow Him wherever He may lead you. You trust Him to work in you to will and to do of His good pleasure. But you find a great difficulty here. You do not know the voice of the Good Shepherd. So, you are in doubt about His will for you. God is calling you to certain paths. Your friends express strong disapproval. And, these friends may be older than you in the Christian life. They seem much more advanced, too. You can hardly bear to differ from or distress them. You also feel very unsure about yielding to any duty they might disapprove of. Yet, you cannot shake these impressions. You plunge into doubt and unease. There is a way out of all these difficulties, to the fully surrendered soul. I would repeat, fully surrendered. Any will to resist makes it hard to know God's mind on that point. So, first, ensure you truly want to obey the Lord in all respects. If this is the case, your soul only needs to know God's will to consent to it. Then, you cannot doubt His desire to make it known and to guide you. There are many very clear promises in reference to this. Take, for instance, John 10:3-4 “To him the gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, when he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. ” John 14:26: But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.” Also, James 1:56: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. ” With such passages as these, and many more like them, we must believe that Divine guidance is promised to us, and our faith must confidently look for and expect it. This is essential; for in James 1:6-7, we are told, “ But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord . First, settle this point. Divine guidance has been promised. You will surely have it if you ask for it. Let no doubt turn you from this. Next, remember that our God has all knowledge and wisdom. Therefore, He may guide you to paths where great blessings await you. But, to the short-sighted human eyes around you, those paths may seem to lead to confusion and loss. You must accept that God's thoughts and ways differ from man’s . Only He, who knows the end from the beginning, can judge the results of any action. You must realize that His love for you may lead you to go against your dearest friends' wishes. You must learn from Luke 14 and similar passages, “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple. Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.” ( Luke 14:26-33.) To be a disciple of your Lord, you may need to forsake all you have. You may have to turn your back on your family, or even your own life. If this is not clearly recognized, the soul may suffer. Often, a child's path of obedience will displease those he loves most. If he cannot trust the Lord through this, he will be lost. Of course, this is in harmony with our duties of honor and love to one another in our various life relationships. The closer we are to Christ, the more we will show His meekness and gentleness. We will also be tender to our natural guardians and counselors. The Master's guidance will always show itself by the Master's Spirit. If, in obeying Him, we act against our friends' wishes, our love and patience will prove our motive.
