If these four align, it is safe to say that God speaks. I lay it down as a principle, which none can dispute. His voice will always be in harmony with itself, no matter how many ways He may speak. The voices may be many, the message can be but one. If God tells me in one voice to do or to leave undone anything, He cannot possibly tell me the opposite in another voice. If there is a contradiction in the voices, the speaker cannot be the same. My rule for distinguishing the voice of God is to test it against this harmony. If I have an impression, I must check if it aligns with Scripture. I must also see if my higher judgment approves it, and, as we Quakers say, if “way opens” to carry it out. fields.title: Concerning Temptation
fields.body_html:
Some very big mistakes are made about temptation in this life of faith. First, people expect that, after the soul rests in God, temptations will cease. They believe the promised salvation is from both temptation and being tempted. When they find the Canaanite still in the land, and see the great, walled cities, they are discouraged. They think they must have gone wrong and that this cannot be the true land after all.

Next, they mistakenly see temptation as sin. They blame themselves for it, but it's the enemy's fault.

This leads to condemnation and discouragement. If it continues, it ends in sin. The enemy makes an easy prey of a discouraged soul; so that we fall often from the very fear of having fallen. To solve the first difficulty, I must refer to Scripture. It says the Christian life is a constant warfare. It also says we must, especially when seated in heavenly places in Christ Jesus, wrestle against spiritual enemies there.

Their power and skill to tempt us must be far superior to any we've ever encountered.

Temptations usually grow tenfold in strength after we start the interior life, not decrease. Their power must not lead us to doubt that we have found the true, abiding place. Strong temptations are generally a sign of great grace, rather than of little grace. When the Israelites first left Egypt, the Lord did not lead them through the Philistines' land, the nearest route. God said, “When Pharaoh let the people go, God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, “Lest the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt.” But, when they learned to trust Him, He allowed their enemies to attack. In their wilderness journey, they met few enemies and fought few battles. In the land, they faced seven great nations and thirty-one kings. They had to conquer walled cities and defeat giants.

They could not have fought the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites until they had entered their land. Your temptations, dear Christian, may prove you are in the land you seek to enter. They are unique to that land. Never let your temptations make you doubt that you are in the promised “heavenly places.”

The second mistake is not quite so easy to deal with. It's almost pointless to say that temptation is not sin. Yet, most distress comes from not understanding this. The very suggestion of wrong seems to bring pollution with it. The evil agency not recognized, the poor, tempted soul fears it must be very bad, and far from God, to have had such thoughts. It is as though a burglar broke into a man's house to steal.

When the owner began to resist him, the burglar accused him of being the thief. It is the enemy's clever trick to trap us.

He comes and whispers evil ideas to us: doubts, blasphemies, jealousy, envy, and pride. Then he says, “Oh, how wicked you must be to think of such things!” It is plain that you do not trust the Lord. If you did, these things would not have entered your heart. This reasoning seems true, so the soul accepts it.

It then feels condemned and discouraged. From there, it is easy to fall into sin. One of the most fatal things in the life of faith is discouragement.

One of the most helpful is cheerfulness. A wise man once said that, in overcoming temptations, cheerfulness was the key. It was the first, second, and third thing. We must expect to conquer. That is why the Lord often told Joshua, “Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go ” (Joshua 1:9). And it is also the reason He says to us, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John14:27) .

The power of temptation is in the fainting of our own hearts. The enemy knows this. He always tries to discourage us at the start of his assaults, if he can.

Sometimes, we feel discouraged. We think it's righteous grief and disgust at ourselves for being tempted. But it's really an embarrassment . We are ashamed because we secretly congratulated ourselves. We believed our tastes were too pure and our separation from the world too complete for such things to tempt us. We expected something from ourselves. We are disappointed to find it lacking.

As a result, we are discouraged. This embarrassment and discouragement are worse than the temptation. They seem humble, but they only stem from wounded self-love.

True humility can bear to see its own weakness and foolishness revealed. It never expected anything from itself. It knows its only hope must be in God. So, instead of discouraging the soul from trusting, it drives it to a deeper and more utter trust. But counterfeit humility, born of self, plunges the soul into despair. It drives it into the very sin it so despises. I remember once hearing an allegory that illustrated this to me wonderfully. Satan called together a council of his servants to consult how they might make a good man sin. One evil spirit started up and said, “I will make him sin.” “How will you do it?” asked Satan. “I will set before him the pleasures of sin,” was the reply; “I will tell him of its delights and the ri ch rewards it brings.” “Ah,” said Satan, “that will not do; he has tried, it, and knows better than that.”

Then another spirit started up and said, “I will make him sin.”

“What will you do?” asked Satan. “I will tell him of the pains and sorrows of v irtue. I will show him that virtue has no delights, and brings no rewards.” “Ah, no!” exclaimed Satan, “That will not do at all.

He has tried it. He knows, 'wisdom's ways are pleasant, and her paths are peace.' Another said, I will make him sin. And what will you do? Asked Satan, again. I will discourage his soul, was the short reply. Ah, that will do,” cried Satan, “that will do! We shall conquer him now.” And they did. An old writer says, all discouragement is from the devil. I wish every Christian would remember this and keep it as a pocket-piece. We must fly from discouragement as we would from sin. But this is impossible if we fail to recognize the true agency in temptation. For if the temptations are our own fault, we cannot help being discouraged. But they are not.

The Bible says, “Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him. ”(James 1:12) It urges us to “count it all joy when we fall into diverse temptations.” Temptation, therefore, cannot be sin. It is no more a sin to hear evil whispers in our souls than to hear the swearing of bad men as we pass along the street. The sin only comes in either case by our stopping and joining in with them. If, when the wicked thoughts come, we turn from them at once, as we would from wicked talk, and ignore them, we do not sin. But if we carry them on in our minds, and roll them under our tongues, and dwell on them with a half consent of our will to them as true, then we sin.

We may be enticed by evil a thousand times a day without sin, and we cannot help these enticing. But if the enemy can make us think his temptations are our sin, he will have won half the battle. He will then likely win completely.

A dear lady once came to me under great darkness, simply from not understanding this. She had been very happy in her faith for some time. She had been free from temptation, and thought she would never be tempted again. But suddenly a very peculiar form of temptation had assailed her, which had horrified her. She found that the moment she began to pray, dreadful thoughts of all kinds would rush into her mind. She had lived a very sheltered, innocent life. These thoughts seemed so awful to her, that she felt she must be one of the wicked of sinners to have them. She began by thinking she could not have entered into the rest of faith. She ended by concluding that she had never been born again.

Her soul was in an agony of distress.

I told her that these dreadful thoughts were the enemy's doing. He came to her the moment she kneeled in prayer and filled her mind with them. She was not to blame for them at all. She could not help them any more than she could help hearing a wicked man blaspheme in her presence. I urged her to see them as from the enemy. She should not blame or discourage herself. Instead, she should turn to Jesus and commit them to Him. I showed her how much the enemy had gained. They made her think these thoughts were her own. This condemned and discouraged her. I assured her she would win quickly if she ignored them. She should turn her back on them and look to the Lord.

She grasped the truth, and the next time these thoughts came she said to the enemy, “I have found you out now. It is you who are suggesting these dreadful thoughts to me, and I hate them, and will have nothing to do with them. The Lord is my Saviour; take them to Him, and settle them in His presence.”

The baffled enemy, found out, fled in confusion. Her soul was perfectly delivered.

Another thing also. The enemy knows that if a Christian sees a hint of evil as his, he will reject it. He will do so more quickly than if it seems to be his own mind's suggestion. If Satan began each temptation with, “I am Satan, your enemy; I have come to make you sin,” we would likely resist. He has to hide himself in order to make his baits attractive. Our victory will be easier if we are not ignorant of his tricks. We must recognize him at his first approach. We also make a mistake about temptations. We think that all time spent fighting them is wasted. Hours pass, and we seem to have made no progress, because we have been so beset with temptations. But, we may have served God more truly during these hours than in our freer times, when we faced fewer temptations.

Temptation is really more the devil’s wrath against God, than against us. He cannot touch our Saviour.

But, he can wound Him by conquering us. Our ruin matters to him only as it does this. So, we fight our Lord's battles when we resist temptation. In these cases, an hour is worth a day's time. We read, “Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him .”(James 1:12).I am sure this means to endure its continuance and frequent recurrence.

Nothing cultivates the grace of patience like enduring temptation. And, nothing drives the soul to depend on the Lord Jesus like it. And finally, nothing brings more glory to our Lord than the trial of our faith, which comes through many temptations. It is said to be more precious than gold, though tested by fire. We, who endure the trial, shall receive a reward. It is “the crown of life” which the Lord has promised to those who love Him.”

We cannot wonder at the Holy Ghost's urging at the start of the Book of James: “ Count it all joy, my brothers, when you meet trials of various kinds, for you know that the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing. ”(James 1:2)Temptation is God's tool to complete our perfection. So, the enemy's own weapons are turned against him. We see that all things, even temptations, can work for good to them that love God.

To resist temptations, I don’t need to tell my audience: it is by faith. For this is, of course, the foundation upon which the whole interior life rests. Our one great motto is throughout, “We are nothing, and Christ is all.” A nd always and everywhere we have started to stand, and walk, and overcome, and live by faith. We have found our own helplessness. We cannot help ourselves. Our only way, therefore, is to hand the temptation over to our Lord and trust Him to conquer it for us.

But when we put it into His hands, we must leave it there. We must commit to Him for victory as we did for salvation. He must do all for us in the one case, as completely as in the other. It was faith only then, and it must be faith only now.

The Lord works miracles in conquering the temptations of those who trust Him. Thousands can testify to this. But I cannot expand on this now. I aimed to show temptation in its true light, not to detail the way to overcome it. I want to free good, faithful souls from bondage. They will be trapped if they confuse temptation with sin. They must understand temptation's true nature and use. I want them to know that temptations are vital for our souls' growth. Whatever their source, God uses them to build in us graces of character that would otherwise be missing.

Wherever temptation is, there is God also, superintending and controlling its power. “Where were you, Lord I, while I was being tempted?” cried the saint of the desert. “Close beside you, my son, all the while,” was the tender reply. Temptations try us. We are worth nothing if we are not tried. They develop our spiritual strength and courage and knowledge, and our development is the one thing God cries for.

How shallow would all our spirituality be if it were not for temptations? “Blessed is the man who endures temptation. He will receive the crown of life, which the Lord has promised to those who love Him.” This “crown of life” will be worth all the trials and endurance it costs to obtain it; without those, it could not be attained.

A sick woman once bought a cocoon . It held a very beautiful butterfly with magnificent wings. She hoped to see it emerge from the cocoon in her chamber. She watched it eagerly as spring drew on.

Finally, she was delighted to see the butterfly beginning to emerge. But it seemed to have great difficulty. It pushed, and strained, and struggled. It made so little headway that she concluded it must need help. With a pair of delicate scissors, she clipped the tight cord that bound the cocoon's opening.

Immediately the cocoon opened wide, and the butterfly escaped without any further struggle. She congratulated herself on her experiment's success. But, something was wrong with the butterfly.

It was all out of the cocoon, it's true. But, its great wings were lifeless and colorless. They dragged behind it, a useless burden. For a few days it lived a miserable sickly life, and then died, without having once lifted its powerless wings. The lady was sorely disappointed and could not understand it. But when she related the circumstance to a naturalist, he told her that it had all been her own fault. That it took just that pushing and struggling to send the life fluid into the wings' veins. Her misguided kindness in shortening the struggle had left the wings lifeless and colorless.

So, our spiritual wings need the struggle of resisting temptation. To save us from it would weaken our souls' power to “mount up with wings as eagles.” It would also deny us the “crown of life” promised to those who endure.

fields.title: Failures
fields.body_html:
The very title of this chapter may startle some. “Failures,” they will say; “we thought t here were no failures in this life of faith!” To this I would answer that there ought not to be, and need not be; but, as a fact, there sometimes are. And we have got to deal with facts, and not with theories. No teacher of this inner life says we can't sin. They only insist that we don't have to. A chance for constant victory is now possible. Few deny that, at times, they have given in to temptation.

Of course, in speaking of sin here, I mean conscious, known sin. I do not touch on the sins of ignorance.

Nor do I discuss the so-called inevitable sin of our nature. Both are covered by the atonement and do not disturb our fellowship with God. I have no desire or ability to discuss the doctrines of sin. I will leave that to the theologians. I will speak only of the believer's experience. I want it to be clear that I will refer only to what is within our consciousness. Misunderstanding, then, on this point of known sin, is dangerous to the higher Christian life. A believer, who trusts he is on the highway of holiness, may be surprised into sin. He is then tempted to either give up, or to hide his sin. To preserve doctrine, he may call it an “infirmity” and refuse to be honest.

Either of these courses is equally fatal to any real growth and progress in the life of holiness. We must face the sad truth. We must name it and find, if we can, its cause and cure. This life of union with God requires the utmost honesty with Him and with ourselves. The sin would only momentarily disturb the communion. But, any dishonesty with it would surely destroy it. A sudden failure is no reason for being discouraged and giving up all as lost. Neither is the integrity of our doctrine touched by it. We are not preaching a state, but a walk. The highway of holiness is not a place, but a way. Sanctification is not a thing to be gained at a certain stage of our experience and forever possessed. It is a life to be lived day by day and hour by hour.

We may briefly stray from a path. But our wandering does not erase it. We can quickly return. In this life of faith, we may fail at times. These failures are sad and to be deplored. But, if met rightly, they need not disturb our complete trust in God. They should not interrupt our happy communion with Him for long.

The great point is an instant return to God. Our sin is no reason for ceasing to trust, but only an unanswerable argument why we must trust more fully than ever. No matter the cause of our failure, discouragement won't help. A child learning to walk might despair after a fall. He might refuse to try again. A believer, learning to live by faith, must not give up for having sinned. The only way in both cases is to get right up and try again. After a disastrous defeat.

“Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the Lord until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads. And Joshua said, “Alas, O Lord God, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us? Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan! O Lord, what can I say when Israel has turned their backs before their enemies? For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?”(Joshua 7:6-9) What a wail of despair this was! And how it is repeated by many a child of God today. Their hearts melt, like water, because of a defeat. They cry, “And Joshua said, 'Alas, Lord GOD , why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all — to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us?

Oh, that we had been content, and dwelt on the other side of the Jordan !” They predict further failures and even defeat by their enemies. No doubt, Joshua thought, as we now do. After such a failure, discouragement and despair seemed the only safe response. But God thought otherwise. “ So the L ORD said to Joshua: “Get up! Why do you lie thus on your face? “ They should not surrender to despair, however humble it might seem. They must face the evil and get rid of it. They must “sanctify themselves” at once.”

“Up, sanctify the people,” is always God’s command. “Lie down and be discouraged” is always the enemy’s temptation. We feel it is presumptuous, even impertinent, to go at once to the Lord after having sinned against Him. We should suffer our sins' consequences for a while and endure our guilty consciences. We can hardly believe the Lord would want to welcome us back into His loving fellowship. A little girl once expressed the feeling to me, with a child's honest straightforwardness. She asked if the Lord Jesus always forgave our sins if we asked Him. I said, “Yes, of course He does.””

“Just as soon” she repeated, doubtingly. “Yes,” I replied, “the very minute we ask, He forgives us.”

“Well,” she said deliberately, “I cannot believe that. I should think He would make us feel sorry for two or three days first. And then I should think He would make us ask Him a great many times, and in a very pretty way too, not just in common talk. I believe that is how He does. You need not try to make me think He forgives me at once, no matter what the Bible says.”

She only said what most Christians think. Worse, most act on it. Their remorse now separates them from God more than their sin would.

It is so contrary to how we want our children to act, that I wonder how we could have conceived such an idea of God. A mother grieves when her naughty child goes off alone in despair. She doubts her willingness to forgive. But, her heart welcomes the darling who runs to her and begs forgiveness!

Surely, our God knew this love when He said, “ Return, O faithless sons; I will heal your faithlessness.

Behold, we come to you, for you are the Lord our Go d.”(Jeremiah3:22) The same moment that reveals sin, should reveal forgiveness. This is vital for a steadfast walk on the holy path. Here, we cannot tolerate an instant of separation from God. We can only walk this path by looking to Jesus, moment by moment. If we take our eyes off Him to see our sin and weakness, we will leave the path at once. The believer, who trusts he is on this path, must flee to the Lord if sin overcomes him. He must act on ( 1 John 1:9) “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and j ust to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” He must not hide his sin and seek to salve it over with excuses, or to push it out of his memory by the lapse of time. But he must do as the children of Israel did. He must rise up “early in the morning,” and “run” to where the evil thing is hidden. Then, he must take it from its hiding place and lay it “out before the Lord.”

He must confess his sin. Then he must stone it, burn it, and put it away. Then, he must raise a great heap of stones to hide it forever. He must, then and there, believe that God is. He must believe, according to His word, that God is faithful and just to forgive him his sin, and that He does do it. He must also believe that God cleanses him from all unrighteousness. He must, by faith, claim an immediate forgiveness and cleansing. Then, he must trust more than ever.

Once Israel's sin was uncovered and removed, God's word came. It was a message of great encouragement: “ And the LORD said to Joshua, “Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land. ”(Joshua 8:1) Our courage must rise higher than ever. We must trust the Lord more. Then, His mighty power can work in us to fulfill His will. Moreover, we must forget our sin as soon as it is thus confessed and forgiven. We must not dwell on it, and examine it, and indulge in a luxury of distress and remorse. We must not idolize it, then walk around and view it. That would make it a mountain that hides our God from us. We must follow Paul's example. We must “forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before.” Then, we must “press toward the ma rk for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.””

He was suddenly overcome by a temptation to treat a brother unkindly. He thought it impossible to sin again. So, he was deeply discouraged. He concluded he was wrong. He had never truly trusted. His discouragement grew into despair. He concluded he had never been born again, and gave himself up for lost. He spent three years in misery. He drifted further from God and fell into one sin after another. His life became a curse to himself and to those around him.

His health failed under the terrible burden. Fears arose for his reason. At the end of three years, he met a Christian lady, who understood the truth about sin that I had been trying to explain. After a brief chat, she learned his trouble. She said, “You sinned in that act, no doubt. Don't try to excuse it.”

But have you never confessed it to the Lord and asked Him to forgive you?” “Confessed it!” He exclaimed, “I have done nothing but confess it. I have begged God to forgive me for these three dreadful years.” “And you have never believed He did forgive you?” asked the lady. “No,” said the poor man, “how could I, for I never felt as if He did?” “But suppose He had said He forgave you, would not that have done as well as for you to feel it?”

“Oh, yes,” replied the man, “if God said it, of course I would believe it.” “Very well, He does say so,” was the lady’s answer, and she turned to the verse we have taken above. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness . ”(1 John 1:9) and read it aloud. “Now,” she continued, “for three years you've confessed your sin. All the while, God's record has declared He is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse you. Yet, you have never once believed it.”

You have been ‘making God a liar’ all this while by refusing to believe His record.”

The poor man saw the whole thing. He was dumbfounded and alarmed. When the lady suggested they kneel, he obeyed like one in a maze. She wanted him to confess his past sins and claim, then and there, forgiveness and cleansing. But the result was glorious. In a few moments, the light broke in, and he burst out into praise at the wonderful deliverance. In three minutes, his soul, by faith, traversed the long, weary journey of three years. He found himself resting in Jesus, rejoicing in His full salvation.

The other illustration was of a Christian lady. She had been in salvation for about two weeks. She had a bright, victorious experience. Suddenly, at the end of that time, she was overcome by a violent burst of anger. For a moment, a flood of discouragement swept over her soul. The enemy said, “There, now, that shows it was all a mistake. Of course, you have been deceived about the whole thing, and have never entered into the life of full trust at all.

You might as well give up. You can't consecrate or trust yourself more than you did this time. So, it is plain this life of holiness is not for you!” These thoughts flashed through her mind in a moment. But she was well-taught in God's ways. So, she said, “Yes, I have sinned, and it is very sad.” But the Bible says that if we confess our sins, God will forgive us. He is faithful and just. He will also cleanse us from all unrighteousness. I believe He will do it.” She did not delay. Still boiling with anger, she ran, not walked, into a room to be alone. Kneeling by the bed, she said, “Lord, I confess my sin.” I have sinned, I am even at this very moment sinning.

I hate it, but I cannot get rid of it. I confess it with shame and confusion of face to God. And now I believe that, according to your word, you do forgive and you do cleanse.” She said it out loud, for the inward turmoil was too great for it to be said inside. As the words “You do forgive and you do cleanse” passed her lips, the deliverance came. The Lord said, “ And he awoke and rebuked the wind and said to the sea , ' Peace! Be still!” And the wind ceased, and there was a great calm ,” ( Mark 4:39) and there was a great calm. A flood of light and joy burst on her soul, the enemy fled, and she was more than a conqueror through Him that loved her. It had taken only five minutes, the sin and its cure. Now, her feet trod more firmly than ever on the blessed highway of holiness. So, the valley of anchor became a door of hope. She sang her song of deliverance, with deeper m eaning: “Then Moses and the people of Israel sang this song to the LORD, saying, 'I will sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:1 ) In every crisis, the only remedy is to trust in the Lord. If this is all we can do, is it not better to do it at once? I have often been brought up short by the question, “Well, what can I do but trust?” I realized at once the folly of seeking deliverance any other way. I thought, “I will have to trus t in the end. “Then, why not do it now?” We have entered a life of faith. If we fail, our only recovery must be an increase in faith, not a decrease.

Let every failure, if any occur, drive you to the Lord. Abandon yourself to Him and trust Him completely. Though sad, these failures won't end your rest or your sweet communion with Him. I have shown the way to escape failure. Now, I want to discuss the causes of failure in this life of full salvation.

The causes do not lie in the strength of the temptation, our own weakness, or, above all, any lack in our Saviour's power or will to save us. The promise to Israel was positive, “ No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you. ” (Joshua1:5). And the promise to us is equally positive, “ No temptation has overtaken you that is not common to man. God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide a way of escape, that you may be able to endure it.” 1 Corinthians 10:13) So about three thousand men went up there from the people. And they fled before the men of Ai It was not the strength of their enemy, neither had God failed them. Their defeat had another cause, which the Lord declares: “Israel hath sinned. They have also transgressed my covenant which I commanded them.

They have taken of the accursed thing. They have also stolen and dissembled, and put it among their own stuff.”

“So, the children of Israel could not stand before their enemies. They turned their backs upon their enemies.”” It was a hidden evil that conquered them. Deep beneath the earth, in a tent in that vast army, was something against which God had a controversy.

This hid den thing made the whole army helpless before their enemies. “Israel, there is something wrong among you . You cannot stand before your enemies until you remove it.””

The teaching is this: Any hidden evil in our hearts, no matter how small, will cause us to fall before our enemies. Any cherished bitterness, harsh judgments, or slackness in obeying the Lord will cripple our spiritual life. So will any doubtful habits or surroundings. We may have hidden the evil in our hearts.

We may have covered it up, refusing to see it. But, we are secretly aware of it.

We may ignore it and declare our full trust. We may be more earnest in our religious duties. We may see more truth and beauty in the life of faith. We may seem to have won, both to ourselves and others.

Yet, we may suffer bitter defeats. We may wonder, question, despair, and pray. But, nothing will help until the accursed thing is dug up, brought to light, and laid before God. If a believer living an inner life is defeated, he must seek the cause. It is not the enemy's strength. It is a hidden lack of dedication at his core.

A headache is not a disease, but a symptom of one. It is in some other part of the body. So, in a Christian, sin is only a symptom. It reveals an evil that likely exists in another part of his being.

Sometimes, one may hide evil even in what, at a cursory glance, looks like good. Hidden behind a strong desire for the truth, there may be a tendency to judge or favor our own opinions . Clear Christian faithfulness may hide an absence of Christian love. Beneath a seemingly rightful care for our affairs, we may hide a great want of trust in God. Our blessed Guide, the indwelling Holy Spirit, is. He secretly discovers these things to us. He does so through little twinges and pangs of conscience. So, we are left without excuse. It is easy to ignore His gentle voice. We convince ourselves that all is well. This will hide a fatal evil among us, causing unexpected defeats.

A capital illustration of this occurred to me once in my housekeeping. I moved into a new house. In checking it for readiness, I found a very clean cider cask in the cellar. It was headed up at both ends. I debated whether to take it from the cellar and open it. It seemed empty and looked nice. So, I decided to leave it, as it would have been a lot of work to get it up the stairs. I didn't feel completely comfortable, but I pushed aside my doubts and left it. Every spring and fall, during house-cleaning time, I would remember that cask. A twinge of my housewifely conscience nagged at me. I could not rest in a perfectly cleaned house while it remained unopened. For how did I know it did not hide some evil beneath its fair exterior?

Still, I eased my doubts. I feared the trouble of investigating it. For two or three years, the harmless-looking barrel sat in my basement. Then, most unaccountably, moths began to fill my house. I used every possible precaution against them and made every effort to eradicate them, but in vain. They increased rapidly and threatened to ruin everything I had.

I suspected my carpets were the cause, and subjected them to a thorough cleaning. I suspected something was wrong with my furniture, so I had it redone. I suspected all sorts of impossible things.

At last, the thought of the cask flashed on me. I had it brought up from the cellar, and the head knocked in.

I think it's safe to say that thousands of moths poured out. The previous occupant must have left something that bred moths. This was the cause of all my trouble.

I now believe that some habit or indulgence, some safe, minor thing, causes us little twinges of conscience. It's not been fairly examined under God's searching eye. I think it lies at the root of most failures in this higher life. All is not given up. Some secret corner is kept locked against the entrance of the Lord. And therefore, we cannot stand before our enemies, but find ourselves smitten down in their presence.

To prevent failure, or to find its cause if we do, we must keep this prayer before us: “Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me and know my thoughts; and see if there be any evil way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.””

There may be something very deceptive in our sufferings over our failures. We may think we are focused on God's glory. Yet, our souls may be troubled by self alone. We are not as saintly as we thought. This discovery hurts our self-love. Our frustration can be a bigger mistake than the original wrongdoing. The only safe way to treat our failures is to avoid justifying or condemning ourselves.

We should, instead, lay them quietly before the Lord. We should look at them in peace and with love.

The old mystic writers say that a simple, peaceful turning to God helps us more than regretting our straying from Him. “Only be faithful,” they say. “Turn only to Him, the moment you see your sin. His presence will free you from the snares that have trapped you.” To look at self-plunges you deeper into the slough, for this very slough is after all nothing but self; while a simple look towards God can calm and comfort your heart.

Finally, let us never forget, no matter our failures. The Lord Jesus is able, as declared, to save us from our enemies. Then, we may “That we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.”(Luke1:74-75). Let us pray, each of us, day and night: “ Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me .”(Psalm19:13). “ But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”(Acts 1:8). We must be so pliable in His hands, and trust Him. Then He will “ Equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.” (Hebrews 13:21)

We may have covered it up, refusing to see it. But, we are secretly aware of it. We may ignore it and declare our full trust. We may be more earnest in our religious duties. We may see more truth and beauty in the life of faith. We may seem to have won, both to ourselves and others. Yet, we may suffer bitter defeats. We may wonder, question, despair, and pray. But, nothing will help until the accursed thing is dug up, brought to light, and laid before God. If a believer living an inner life is defeated, he must seek the cause. It is not the enemy's strength. It is a hidden lack of dedication at his core. A headache is not a disease, but a symptom of one. It is in some other part of the body. So, in a Christian, sin is only a symptom. It reveals an evil that likely exists in another part of his being. Sometimes, one may hide evil even in what, at a cursory glance, looks like good. Hidden behind a strong desire for the truth, there may be a tendency to judge or favor our own opinions . Clear Christian faithfulness may hide an absence of Christian love. Beneath a seemingly rightful care for our affairs, we may hide a great want of trust in God. Our blessed Guide, the indwelling Holy Spirit, is. He secretly discovers these things to us. He does so through little twinges and pangs of conscience. So, we are left without excuse. It is easy to ignore His gentle voice. We convince ourselves that all is well. This will hide a fatal evil among us, causing unexpected defeats. A capital illustration of this occurred to me once in my housekeeping. I moved into a new house. In checking it for readiness, I found a very clean cider cask in the cellar. It was headed up at both ends. I debated whether to take it from the cellar and open it. It seemed empty and looked nice. So, I decided to leave it, as it would have been a lot of work to get it up the stairs. I didn't feel completely comfortable, but I pushed aside my doubts and left it. Every spring and fall, during house-cleaning time, I would remember that cask. A twinge of my housewifely conscience nagged at me. I could not rest in a perfectly cleaned house while it remained unopened. For how did I know it did not hide some evil beneath its fair exterior? Still, I eased my doubts. I feared the trouble of investigating it. For two or three years, the harmless-looking barrel sat in my basement. Then, most unaccountably, moths began to fill my house. I used every possible precaution against them and made every effort to eradicate them, but in vain. They increased rapidly and threatened to ruin everything I had. I suspected my carpets were the cause, and subjected them to a thorough cleaning. I suspected something was wrong with my furniture, so I had it redone. I suspected all sorts of impossible things. At last, the thought of the cask flashed on me. I had it brought up from the cellar, and the head knocked in. I think it's safe to say that thousands of moths poured out. The previous occupant must have left something that bred moths. This was the cause of all my trouble. I now believe that some habit or indulgence, some safe, minor thing, causes us little twinges of conscience. It's not been fairly examined under God's searching eye. I think it lies at the root of most failures in this higher life. All is not given up. Some secret corner is kept locked against the entrance of the Lord. And therefore, we cannot stand before our enemies, but find ourselves smitten down in their presence. To prevent failure, or to find its cause if we do, we must keep this prayer before us: “Search me, O God, and know my heart; try me and know my thoughts; and see if there be any evil way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting.”” There may be something very deceptive in our sufferings over our failures. We may think we are focused on God's glory. Yet, our souls may be troubled by self alone. We are not as saintly as we thought. This discovery hurts our self-love. Our frustration can be a bigger mistake than the original wrongdoing. The only safe way to treat our failures is to avoid justifying or condemning ourselves. We should, instead, lay them quietly before the Lord. We should look at them in peace and with love. The old mystic writers say that a simple, peaceful turning to God helps us more than regretting our straying from Him. “Only be faithful,” they say. “Turn only to Him, the moment you see your sin. His presence will free you from the snares that have trapped you.” To look at self-plunges you deeper into the slough, for this very slough is after all nothing but self; while a simple look towards God can calm and comfort your heart. Finally, let us never forget, no matter our failures. The Lord Jesus is able, as declared, to save us from our enemies. Then, we may “That we, being delivered from the hand of our enemies, might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him all our days.”(Luke1:74-75). Let us pray, each of us, day and night: “ Keep back your servant also from presumptuous sins; let them not have dominion over me .”(Psalm19:13). “ But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”(Acts 1:8). We must be so pliable in His hands, and trust Him. Then He will “ Equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.” (Hebrews 13:21)

fields.title: Doubts
fields.body_html:
A great number of Christians are slaves to the habit of doubting. No drunkard was ever more completely bound by the chains of his fatal habit than they are by those chains. Their whole Christian life is a constant battle. An army of doubts lies in wait to attack at any chance. Their lives are wretched. Their doubts hinder their usefulness and break their communion with God.

The soul's entry into the life of faith, which this book discusses, often banishes doubts. But, they sometimes resurge. They can cause stumbling and despair. They can't fully turn the believer back to the dreary wilderness.

We all remember, doubtless, the childish mix of fascination and horror in that story. It was about Christian's imprisonment in Doubting Castle by the wicked giant Despair. We felt extremely happy in his escape from those massive gates and that cruel tyrant. We did not suspect then that we would be imprisoned by the same giant, in the same castle. And yet I fear to every member of the Church of Christ there has been at least one such experience. If it's not fresh in your minds, please read the account again. You may find there experiences of your own. They were very hard to bear and sorrowful to remember.

It's strange that people called Believers must confess such doubts. Their name suggests their only trait is belief. It is such a universal habit that, if the Church were renamed, “Doubters” would be the only fitting name. Most Christians have accepted their doubts. They see them as a painful, inevitable illness.

They must resign themselves to it as part of life's discipline. They complain about their doubts as a man might complain about his aches and pains. They want to be seen as an “interesting case” of rare trial, needing deep sympathy and great care.

This is often true of believers. They long to live by faith and have taken many steps towards it. They may have lost their old doubts. They once tormented them. They wondered if their sins were forgiven and if they'd reach Heaven. But, they still doubt. They have simply shifted the habit to a higher platform. They are saying, perhaps, “Yes, I believe my sins are forgiven, and I am a child of God through faith in Jesus Christ. I dare not doubt this anymore.

But then, and this “but then” includes doubts about every promise our Father has made to His children.

They fight with them, refusing to believe until they have better proof of their truth than God's word.

They wonder why they can walk in such darkness. They see themselves as martyrs. They groan under the unique spiritual conflicts they must endure. Spiritual conflicts! Far better would they be named did we call them spiritual rebellions! Our fight is to be a fight of faith, and the moment we doubt, our fight ceases and our rebellion begins.

I desire to put forth, if possible, one vigorous protest against this whole thing. I might as well join in with a drunkard's complaints. I might as well pray with him for grace to endure his fatal indulgence. It is as foolish as to console the enslaved souls with their weak complaints. I can do nothing else but proclaim to them the perfect deliverance the Lord Jesus Christ has for them. I implore, entreat, and command them, with all my being, to accept it and be free. Not for one moment would I listen to their despairing excuses. You ought to be free, you can be free, and you must be free!

Will you undertake to tell me that it is an inevitable necessity for God to be doubted by His children?

Is it an inevitable necessity for your children to doubt you? Would you tolerate their doubts a single hour? Would you pity your son if he said, “Father, I cannot believe your word, I cannot trust your love”? Would you find him an interesting case? I remember once seeing the indignation of a mother I knew, stirred to its very depths by a little doubting on the part of one of her children. She had brought two little girls to my house to leave them while she did some errands. One of them, with a child's happy confidence, abandoned herself to my nursery. She found all the pleasures there. She sang and played until her mother returned.

The other one, with unfortunate caution of maturity, sat alone in a corner. She wondered if her mother would remember to come back for her. She feared being forgotten. She imagined her mother would be glad to get rid of her, since she was a naughty girl. In the end, she worked herself into a perfect frenzy of despair. I shall not easily forget the look on that mother's face. It was after her weeping little girl returned and told her what the matter was. Grief, wounded love, indignation, and pity, all strove together for mastery. But indignation gained the day, and I doubt if that little girl was ever so vigorously dealt with before. That scene has come before me a hundred times since. It has taught me deeply. It has compelled me to refuse doubts about my Heavenly Father's love. Those doubts have clamored at my heart's door for entrance.

I am convinced that, for many, doubting is a luxury. To deny themselves that would be the hardest self-denial they know. It is a luxury that, like all other luxuries, brings sorrowful results. Perhaps, seeing the sadness it has caused in your own Christian life, you may be tempted to say, Sad! This is no luxury to me, but only a fearful trial.” But pause for a moment. Try gi ving it up, and you will soon find out whether it is a luxury or not. Don't your doubts come to you like a group of friends? They sympathize with your troubles and want to comfort you.

Is it not a luxury to sit with them, entertain them, and listen to their arguments? To join in their condolences? Would it be no self-denial to turn resolutely from them, and refuse to hear a word they have to say?

If you don't know, try it and see. Have you never enjoyed the luxury of hard thoughts against those who wronged you? Have you never known the joy of brooding over their unkindness? Of prying into their malice? Of imagining all sorts of wrong, uncomfortable things about them? It has made you wretched, of course. But, it is a fascinating sort of wretchedness that you cannot easily give up. And just like this is the luxury of doubting. Things have gone wrong with you in your experience.

Dispensations are mysterious. Temptations are odd. Your case seems unique. What could be more natural than to conclude that, for some reason, God has forsaken you? That he does not love you and is indifferent to your welfare? And how strong is the belief that you are too wicked for Him to care, or too difficult for Him to manage?

You do not blame Him or accuse Him of injustice. You feel that you deserve His indifference and rejection due to your unworthiness. This trick lets you doubt yourself while pretending to be humble.

But you are indulging in hard, wrong thoughts about your Lord, as much as you did of a human enemy.

He says He came not to save the righteous, but sinners. Your sinfulness and unworthiness are your best claims to His love and care.

The poor little lamb that has wandered and got lost in the wilderness might well say, “The shepherd does not love, care for, or remember me, because I am lost.” He only loves and cares for the lambs that never wander.” As well might the ill man say, “The doctor will not come to see me, nor give me any medicines, because I am ill. He only cares for and visits well people.” Jesus say s , “ Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are sick.”(Mathew 9:12) And again He says, “What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing. And when he comes home, he calls together his friends and his neighbors, saying to them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my sheep that was lost.”(Luke15:4 -6) Any thoughts of Him that differ from His own words are hard thoughts. To indulge in them is far worse than to indulge in hard thoughts of any earthly friend or foe. From the beginning to the end of your Christian life it is always sinful to indulge in doubts. Doubts are all from the devil, and are always untrue. And the only way to meet them is by a direct and emphatic denial. And this brings me to the practical part of the whole subject, as to how to get deliverance from this fatal habit. My answer would be that the deliverance from this can be by no other means than the deliverance from any other sin. It is to be found in the Lord and in Him only. You must hand your doubting over to Him, as you have learned to hand your other temptations. You must do just what you do with your temper, or your pride.

You must give it up to the Lord.

I believe the only remedy is to take a pledge against it. As you would urge a drunkard to do against drink. Trust in the Lord alone to keep you steadfast.

Like any other sin, the stronghold is in the will. You must surrender your will to doubt, just as you would to any other temptation. God always takes possession of a surrendered will. If we say we will not doubt and surrender our core to Him, His Spirit will work in us. We shall be kept from doubting by His great power. The trouble is, the soul often does not fully surrender. It reserves a small freedom to doubt, seeing it as sometimes necessary. “I do not want to doubt anymore,” we will say, or, “I hope I shall not.” But , it is hard to say, “I will not doubt again.””

But no surrender is effectual until it reaches the point of saying, “I will not”. The liberty to doubt must be given up forever. And the soul must consent to a continuous life of inevitable trust. I think, it is often necessary to end this doubt. We must reach a decision on it. I believe it is quite as necessary in the case of a doubter as in the case of a drunkard. It will not do to give it up by degrees. The total abstinence principle is the only effectual one here. Once surrendered, the soul must rest entirely on the Lord for deliverance in every temptation. It must lift up the shield of faith the moment the assault comes. It must hand the very first suggestion of doubt over to the Lord, and must tell the enemy to settle the matter with Him.

It must refuse to listen to the doubt a single moment. No matter how plausible or humble it seems, the soul must say, “I dare not doubt; I must trust.” The Lord is good, and HE DOES love me. Jesus saves me; He save s me now.” Those three little words, repeated over and over, -- “Jesus saves me, Jesus saves me,” -- will defeat the greatest army of doubts that ever attacked a soul. I have tried it times without number, and have never known it to fail. Do not stop to argue the matter out with your doubts, nor try to prove that they are wrong. Pay no attention to them whatever; treat them with the utmost contempt. Shut your door in their faces, and emphatically deny every word they say to you. Bring up some “It is written,” and hurl it after them. Look right at Jesus, and tell Him you trust Him, and you mean to trust Him. Let the doubts clamor as they may, they cannot hurt you if you will not let them in.

It may seem like you are shutting the door on your best friends. Your heart will long for your doubts more than the Israelites longed for the flesh-pots of Egypt. But deny yourself; take up your cross in this matter. Unmercifully refuse to listen to a word. A perfect army of doubts awaited my waking and clamored at my door for admittance. Nothing seemed real or true. Least of all, it seemed possible that I -- miserable and wretched -- could be the object of the Lord's love, care, or notice. If only I could let these doubts in. If I could invite them to sit and make themselves at home, what a luxury that would be! But years ago, I pledged against doubting. I would as soon violate my pledge against liquor as this one.

I dared not admit the first doubt. I lifted my shield of faith the moment I noticed these thoughts. I gave my whole army to my Lord to conquer. Then, I kept saying, “The Lord does love me.” He is my present and my perfect Saviour; Jesus saves me, Jesus saves me now!”

The victory was complete. The enemy came in like a flood. But the Lord raised a standard against him.

He was routed and put to flight. My soul sings the song of Moses and the children of Israel. It says, “ Then Moses and the people of Israel sang this song to the LORD, saying, I will sing to the LORD, FOR he has triumphed gloriously; the hor se and his rider he has thrown into the sea.” (Exodus 15:1) “The Lord is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father’s God, and I will exalt him. The Lord is a man of war; the Lord is his name. ”(Exodus 15:2 -3). It will help you to resist the assaults of this temptation to doubt, to see clearly that doubting is sin. It directly disobeys our Lord, who commands us, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John 14:27) The Bible everywhere commands us to trust, with no exceptions. Time and room would fail me to refer to one hundredth part of these. But no one can read the Psalms without being convinced. The man who trusts without question is the only one who pleases and is accepted by God. The “provocation” of Israel was that they did not trust; “Yet they sinned still more against him, rebelling against the Most High in the desert. They tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved. They spoke against God, saying, “Can God spread a table in the wilderness? He struck the rock so that water gushed out and streams overflowed. Can he also give bread or provide meat for his people? “Therefore, when the Lord heard, he was full of wrath; a fire was kindled against Jacob; his anger rose against Israel, because they did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power.” (Psalms 78:17 -22.)

In contrast, Isaiah says of those who tr ust, “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. “(Isaiah 26:3) Nothing wounds us like a friend's doubt. I am convinced, nothing grieves God more than our doubt.

One of my children, now with the Lord, said to me one evening as I tucked her in bed, “Well, mother, I have had my first doubt.”” “Oh, Ray,” I said, “What was it?” “Why,” she replied, “Satan came to me and told me not to believe the Bible, for it was not a word of it true.” “And what did you say to him?”

I asked. “Oh,” she replied, triumphantly, “I just said to him, Satan, I will believe it. So there!” I was delighted with the child's spiritual intelligence. She knew how to meet doubts. I encouraged her, explaining that all doubts and discouragements are from the enemy. He is a liar, so never listen to him.

The next night, I had forgotten all about it. So, I was surprised when she said, as I tucked her in, “Well, mother, Satan has been at it again.”” “Oh, Ray darling!” I exclaimed in dismay, “what did he say this time?” “Well,” she replied, “he just told me I was such a naughty girl that Jesus could not love me. It was foolish to think He did.”” “And what did you say this time?” I asked. “Oh!” she replied, “I just looked at him cross and said, Satan, shut your mouth!” And then she added, with a smile, “He can’t make me unhappy one bit.” A grander battle no soul ever fought than this little child had done, and no greater victory was ever won!

Dear, doubting soul, go and do likewise; and a similar victory shall be yours. As you lay down this book take up your pen and write out your determination never to doubt again. Make it a real transaction between your soul and the Lord. Give up your liberty to doubt forever. Put your will in this matter over on the Lo rd’s side, and trust Him to keep you from falling. Tell him of your weakness and your doubts.

Your enemy has you helpless. Commit the whole battle to Him. Tell Him you will not doubt again.

Then, keep your gaze on Jesus.

Turn away from yourself and your doubts. Hold on to your faith, for He is faithful who has promised.

If you stay confident to the end, you will, through Him who loves you, be more than a conqueror in this matter.

Least of all, it seemed possible that I -- miserable and wretched -- could be the object of the Lord's love, care, or notice. If only I could let these doubts in. If I could invite them to sit and make themselves at home, what a luxury that would be! But years ago, I pledged against doubting. I would as soon violate my pledge against liquor as this one. I dared not admit the first doubt. I lifted my shield of faith the moment I noticed these thoughts. I gave my whole army to my Lord to conquer. Then, I kept saying, “The Lord does love me.” He is my present and my perfect Saviour; Jesus saves me, Jesus saves me now!” The victory was complete. The enemy came in like a flood. But the Lord raised a standard against him. He was routed and put to flight. My soul sings the song of Moses and the children of Israel. It says, “ Then Moses and the people of Israel sang this song to the LORD, saying, I will sing to the LORD, FOR he has triumphed gloriously; the hor se and his rider he has thrown into the sea.” (Exodus 15:1) “The Lord is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation; this is my God, and I will praise him, my father’s God, and I will exalt him. The Lord is a man of war; the Lord is his name. ”(Exodus 15:2 -3). It will help you to resist the assaults of this temptation to doubt, to see clearly that doubting is sin. It directly disobeys our Lord, who commands us, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John 14:27) The Bible everywhere commands us to trust, with no exceptions. Time and room would fail me to refer to one hundredth part of these. But no one can read the Psalms without being convinced. The man who trusts without question is the only one who pleases and is accepted by God. The “provocation” of Israel was that they did not trust; “Yet they sinned still more against him, rebelling against the Most High in the desert. They tested God in their heart by demanding the food they craved. They spoke against God, saying, “Can God spread a table in the wilderness? He struck the rock so that water gushed out and streams overflowed. Can he also give bread or provide meat for his people? “Therefore, when the Lord heard, he was full of wrath; a fire was kindled against Jacob; his anger rose against Israel, because they did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power.” (Psalms 78:17 -22.) In contrast, Isaiah says of those who tr ust, “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. “(Isaiah 26:3) Nothing wounds us like a friend's doubt. I am convinced, nothing grieves God more than our doubt. One of my children, now with the Lord, said to me one evening as I tucked her in bed, “Well, mother, I have had my first doubt.”” “Oh, Ray,” I said, “What was it?” “Why,” she replied, “Satan came to me and told me not to believe the Bible, for it was not a word of it true.” “And what did you say to him?” I asked. “Oh,” she replied, triumphantly, “I just said to him, Satan, I will believe it. So there!” I was delighted with the child's spiritual intelligence. She knew how to meet doubts. I encouraged her, explaining that all doubts and discouragements are from the enemy. He is a liar, so never listen to him. The next night, I had forgotten all about it. So, I was surprised when she said, as I tucked her in, “Well, mother, Satan has been at it again.”” “Oh, Ray darling!” I exclaimed in dismay, “what did he say this time?” “Well,” she replied, “he just told me I was such a naughty girl that Jesus could not love me. It was foolish to think He did.”” “And what did you say this time?” I asked. “Oh!” she replied, “I just looked at him cross and said, Satan, shut your mouth!” And then she added, with a smile, “He can’t make me unhappy one bit.” A grander battle no soul ever fought than this little child had done, and no greater victory was ever won! Dear, doubting soul, go and do likewise; and a similar victory shall be yours. As you lay down this book take up your pen and write out your determination never to doubt again. Make it a real transaction between your soul and the Lord. Give up your liberty to doubt forever. Put your will in this matter over on the Lo rd’s side, and trust Him to keep you from falling. Tell him of your weakness and your doubts. Your enemy has you helpless. Commit the whole battle to Him. Tell Him you will not doubt again. Then, keep your gaze on Jesus. Turn away from yourself and your doubts. Hold on to your faith, for He is faithful who has promised. If you stay confident to the end, you will, through Him who loves you, be more than a conqueror in this matter.

fields.title: Practical Results
fields.body_html:
If all that has been said about the life hid with Christ in God is true, it should show in our daily lives.

Those who enjoy it should be a “peculiar people, zealous of good works.” My son at college once wrote to a friend that Christians must be God's witnesses. The world won't read the Bible, but they will read our lives. Their belief in our religion depends on the report our lives give. As we all know, this is an age of facts. Inquiries are shifting from theories to realities.

If our religion is to make any headway, it must be proved to be more than a theory. We must show, to our age's critical minds, the grand facts of lives transformed by God's mighty power working in us to do His will. “Show us 'forms of life,' say the scientists, and we will be convinced. When the Church presents to them, in all its members, a holy life, their last stronghold will be conquered.” I wish, before closing my book, to speak very solemnly of the fruits of a life of faith, such as I have been describing.

I believe they are necessary. I urge my readers to feel their duty to walk worthy of their high calling.

I would speak to some of you, as personal friends. I am sure that, through this book, a mutual longing has grown in your hearts, as it has in mine. We should show forth the praises of Him who has called us out of darkness into His marvellous light. As a friend, I may speak plainly to friends. Please pardon me if I discuss some vital details of life and character. They are important for true Christian growth.

The standard of holy living among Christians is low. Any real devotion in life and walk surprises, and often disapproves, many in the Church. Most professed followers of the Lord Jesus Christ are unlike Him. An outside observer would see little harmony between them.

But we, who have heard God's call to total devotion and trust, must do differently. We must come out from the world and be separate, and must not be conformed to it in our characters nor in our purposes.

We must no longer share in its spirit or its ways.

Our talk must be in Heaven. We must seek things above, where Christ sits at God's right hand. We must walk through the world as Christ walked. We must have the mind that was in Him.

As pilgrims and strangers we must abstain from fleshly lusts that war against the soul. As good soldiers of Jesus Christ, we must avoid the world's affairs as much as possible. This is to please Him who chose us to be soldiers.

We must abstain from all appearance of evil. We must be kind and forgiving to each other. God, for Christ's sake, has forgiven us. We must not resent injuries or unkindness. Instead, we should return good for evil and turn the other cheek to those who hurt us. We must take always the lowest place among our fellowmen; and seek not our own honor, but the honor of others. We must be gentle, and meek, and yielding; not standing up for our own rights, but for the rights of others. All that we do must be done for the glory of God. In summary, since He who called us is holy, we must be holy in our behavior. It is written, “Be you holy, for I am holy.””

Now, dear friends, this is all very practical. It surely means a life very different from most professors' lives. It means that we do really and absolutely turn our backs on self, and on self’s motives and self’s aims. We are a peculiar people, both to God and the world. Our Christ like lives and words will show that we follow the Lord Jesus Christ. We are not of the world, even as He was not of the world. We shall no longer feel that our money is our own, but the Lord’s, to be used in His service. We cannot use our energies only to seek worldly things. If we first seek God's kingdom and His righteousness, we will have what we need.

We will be forbidden to seek high places or worldly gains. We shall not be permitted to be conformed to the world in our ways of thinking or of living. We will have no desire to take part in the world's silly distractions. We should love heavenly things, not earthly ones. We will not serve ourselves, but our Lord. We will perform our duties better than ever. We will work “not with eye service as men pleasers, but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart.””

Clear standard of Christian life, we may not recognize His voice due to ignorance. So, I want to be very plain and definite in my statements. I have noticed that, where there is a faithful following of the Lord in a consecrated soul, several things follow, sooner or later. Over time, meekness and quietness of spirit become the daily life. There is a submissive acceptance of God's will, as it comes in the daily events.

There is also a pliability in God's hands to do or suffer His will. Next, there should be sweetness under provocation, calmness amid chaos, and yieldingness to others' wishes. There is an insensibility to slights and an absence of worry. Fear and care vanish. All these, and many other similar graces, are the natural result of that inward life which is hid with Christ in God.

As for their habits: We always see such Christians, sooner or later, giving themselves to some work for God and their fellowmen. They are willing to spend and be spent in the Master’s service. They become indifferent to their houses' furniture and their living style. They make all personal adornment secondary to the things of God.

The voice is dedicated to God, to talk and sing for Him. The purse is placed at His disposal. The pen is dedicated to write for Him, the lips to speak for Him, the hands and the feet to do His bidding. Year after year, such Christians grow more unworldly and heavenly-minded. They become more like Christ.

Their faces show a beautiful, divine life within them. All who look at them know they live with and abide in God.

I am sure you have each felt some Divine hints. They foreshadow the life I now describe. Have you not begun to feel, deep in your soul, the voice of God speaking to you about these things? Has it not been a pain and a distress to you of late to discover how much is wrong in your life? Hasn't your soul been troubled by doubt about some habits you once indulged in? Have you not begun to feel uneasy with some habits? Do you wish you could change them? Have not paths of devotedness and of service begun to open out before you, with the longing thought, “Oh that I could walk in them”?

All your longings, doubts, and distress are the Good Shepherd's voice. It seeks to call you away from all that is against His will. Oh! Let me entreat you not to turn away from His gentle pleadings. You little know the secret paths He means to lead you to by these very steps. You don't know the great blessings that lie at their end. If you did, you would eagerly obey all His requirements. You can reach the heights of Christian perfection. To do so, you must follow the Guide who will lead you there. He reveals your way one step at a time, through your daily life. He asks only that you yield to His guidance.

If you are convinced of any sin, it is the voice of your Lord. Surrender it at once to His bidding.

Rejoice that He has begun to lead and guide you.

Be completely soft in His wise hands. Go where He entices you. Turn away from all that makes you shrink. Obey Him perfectly. He will lead you swiftly and easily to a wonderful life of conformity to Himself. It will be a testimony to all around you, beyond what you will ever know.

I knew a soul who surrendered to follow the Lord wherever He led her. In three months, she went from deep despair to a blessed union with the Lord Jesus Christ.

In her darkness, she consecrated herself to the Lord. She surrendered her will to Him. She wanted Him to work in her, to do His good pleasure. He began to speak to her by His Spirit in her heart. He suggested small acts of service for Him. He called her away from all un-Christ ways.

She recognized His voice. She feared only disobeying Him. So, she followed Him, yielding to each of His requests, wherever He led her. He led her on, day by day. He conformed her to His will. Her life became a testimony to those around her. Even some who opposed and disbelieved were forced to admit that it was of God. They were won to a similar surrender.

After three short months of this faithful following, it came to pass. So swiftly had she gone that her Lord was able to reveal some of His deepest secrets of love to her wondering soul? He fulfilled the promise of ( Acts 1:5) “for John baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” baptising her with the Holy Ghost.

Do you think she has ever regretted fully following Him? Or that anything but joy fills her heart? She is grateful for the path that brought her to this amazing place. Some of those steps were difficult at the time, but she doesn't regret them. If you want a blessing, give yourself completely to the Divine Master, just like she did. Don't hold back from any surrender, He asks of you .

The perfect way is hard to flesh. It is not hard to love. If you were sick and in need of God, how swiftly would you move? Surely, you can trust Him! Some may call for things of little worth to you. They may seem unworthy of the Lord's attention. Remember, He sees not as man sees, what is small to you may be, in His eyes, the key to the deepest thing. To shape you to His will, He must have you soft. This flexibility is more quickly reached by yielding in small things than in greater ones. Your one great desire is to follow Him fully; canst thou not say then a continual “Yes, Lord!” to all His sweet commands, small or great, and trust Him to lead you by the shortest road to your fullest Blessedness?

My dear friend, this, and nothing less than this, is what thy consecration meant, whether you knew it or not. It meant inevitable obedience. It meant that the will of your God was henceforth to be your will under all circumstances and at all times. It meant that, from then on, you gave up your freedom. You surrendered completely to your Lord's control. It meant an hour of following Him, wherever He led you. No dreams of turning back. Now, I ask you to keep your word. Let everything else go. Live, in daily life, the Divine life within you. You are united to your Lord by a wondrous tie. So, walk as He walked. Show the world His power to save by letting Him save you completely. You need not fear to consent to this, for He is your Saviour, and His power is to do it all. He is not asking you, in your weakness, to do it. He only asks you to yield to Him. Then, He will use His power to make you want to do it and to do it. Your job is to yield yourself. His is to work. He will never give you a command without giving you the power to obey it.

Do not worry about tomorrow. Trust your loving Lord. He promised to lead His sheep on a safe and easy path. Take each onward step as He makes it plain to you. Bring all your life in each of its details to Him to regulate and guide. Follow gladly and quickly the sweet suggestions of His Spirit in your soul. And, day by day, you will find Him. He will bring you more into conformity with His will in all things. He will, as you can bear it, shape you. Then, you will be a vessel of His honor, sanctified and ready for every good work. You will have the joy of being a letter of Christ, known and read by all.

Your light will shine so brightly that, seeing your good works, men will glorify your Father in Heaven, not you.

We are predestined to be “conformed to the image” of God’s Son. This means, of course, not a likeness of bodily presence, but a likeness of character and nature. It means a similarity of thought, of feeling, of desire, of loves, of hates. It means we should think and act, as Christ would, under our circumstances.

A little girl was once questioned what it meant to be a Christian. She replied, “It means to be just what Christ would be, if He was a little girl and lived in my house.” Th e secret of Christ's life was His selfless love for others. If we are like Him, this will be our secret too. He saved others, but Himself He could not save. He “pleased not Himself.” So, we “not to please ourselves.” Instead, we should please our neighbor, if it is for his good.

A thoughtful Hindu, who recently visited England and America to study Christianity, said, “What Christians need is a bit more of Christ's Christianity, and a bit less of man's.” Man's Christianity teaches sacrifice to save oursel ves. Christ's Christianity teaches sacrifice to save others. Man’s Christianity produces the fruitless selfishness of too much of our religion. Christ's Christianity produces a blessed unselfishness. It comes from lives poured out for others, as was His. In short, our book teaches one thing: we are to be Christ like Christians. And all our experiences amount to nothing if they do not produce this result. “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the w ill of my Father who is in heaven.” (Mathew 7:21)
