fields.title: The Joy of Obedience
fields.body_html:
I once read: “Perfect obedience would bring perfect happiness if we had perfect confidence in the power we obeyed.” It struck me. It revealed a possible, yet undreamed-of, way to be happy. Later, despite my lawlessness, that saying haunted me. It promised a rest and a way to grow. It soothed and satisfied my yearnings.

I must say, I have discovered this rest, not as a vision, but as a reality. I have seen in the Lord Jesus, our Master. We can yield to Him and take His yoke upon us to find perfect rest. You, dear, hesitant soul, don't know the joy you are missing. The Master has revealed Himself to you. He calls for your complete surrender. You shrink and hesitate. A measure of surrender you are willing to make, and think indeed it is fit and proper you should. But you seem to think that an utter abandonment, without any reserves, is too much to be asked for. You are afraid of it. It involves too much, you think, and is too great a task. To be obedient in a measurable way is your desire; the idea of being completely obedient appalls you.

You see other souls, too. They walk with easy consciences in a wider path than the one marked out for you. You ask yourself, why is this? It seems strange, and perhaps hard, that you must do what they need not. And, you must leave undone what they have the liberty to do. Ah! Dear Christian, this very difference between you is your privilege, though you do not yet know it. Your Lord says, “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me. And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”(John14:21) You have His commandments; those you envy, have them not. You know the mind of your Lord about many things, in which, as yet, they are walking in darkness. Is not this a privilege? Is it regrettable that your soul is so close to your Master? He can tell you things that those farther away do not know. Do you not realize what a tender degree of intimacy this implies?

Many life relations require only a modest devotion from both parties. We may have great friendships.

Yet, we spend much of our lives in separate, differing pursuits. When together, we may enjoy each other's company. We may find many shared interests. But, we are not distressed by separation. Other, closer friendships do not interfere. We lack enough love to have the right or desire to share our most private affairs. A certain degree of reserve and distance is the suitable thing, we feel. But there are other relations in life where all this is changed. The friendship becomes love. The two hearts give themselves to one another, to be no longer two but one.

A union of souls takes place, which makes all that belongs to one the property of the other. Separate interests and separate paths in life are no longer possible. Things that were lawful before are now unlawful. It's due to the closeness of the tie that binds. The reserve and distance suitable for mere friendship become fatal in love. Love gives all, and must have all in return. One's wishes bind the other.

Each heart desires to know the other's secret wishes. It wants to fly on the wind to fulfill them.

Do people like this feel frustrated by the burden that love places on them? Do they envy the cool, calm friendships they see? Do they regret the closeness to their beloved because of the obligations it creates?

Do they not glory in these very obligations? And, with a tender, exulting joy, pity the poor, far-off ones who dare not come so near? Isn't every new revelation of each other's minds a delight? And, is any path hard that their love compels them to travel? Ah! Dear souls, if you've known this, even for a few hours; if you've ever loved someone enough to find joy in sacrificing for them; if you've ever longed to abandon your will to another as a sweet privilege, then, by all the love of your heavenly Master, I urge you to do the same for God!

He loves you with more than the love of friendship. As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so does He rejoice over you. Only a full surrender will satisfy Him. He has given you all, and He asks for all in return. The slightest reserve will grieve Him to the heart. He spared not Himself, and how can you spare yourself? For your sake, He gave all He had. For His, you must do the same. Oh, be generous in your self-surrender! Meet His measureless devotion for you, with a measureless devotion to Him. Be glad and eager to throw yourself headlong into His dear arms, and to hand over the reins of government to Him. Whatever there is of you, let Him have it all. Give up forever everything separate from Him. I resign my freedom of choice. I rejoice in our union. It makes my devotion not just possible, but necessary.

Have you never longed to love someone far away? You were not close enough for a more intimate approach. Have you not felt a burning desire to surrender yourself to them? Yet, you had no one to whom you could give that love. Have not your hands been full of very precious, alabaster boxes of ointment? You have never been near enough to any heart to pour it out. If you hear your Lord's sweet voice, He is calling you to a place of closeness to Himself. It requires a separation from all else. It will make your devotion not just possible, but necessary. Will you shrink or hesitate?

Will you find it hard that He reveals more of His mind to you than to others? He will not let you be happy in anything that separates you from Himself. Do you want to go where He cannot go with you, or to have pursuits which He cannot share?

No! No, a thousand times, no! You will spring out to meet His dear will with an eager joy. Even His slightest wish will become a binding law to you, which it would fairly break your heart to disobey. You will rejoice in the narrowness of the path He sets for you. You will pity, with infinite sorrow, the poor, far-off ones who have missed this joy. Love's obligations will be its sweetest privileges. Your right to give your all to your Lord will feel like a lift into a realm of unspeakable glory. Perfect happiness will come from perfect obedience. You will then know a bit of what Jesus meant when He said, “ I delight to do your will, O my God; your law is within my heart.”( Psalms 40:8 ) And do you think the joy in this will be all on your side? Has the Lord no joy in those who have thus surrendered themselves to Him, and who love to obey Him? Ah, my friends, we are unfit to speak of this. But the Scriptures reveal glimpses of the delight, satisfaction, and joy our Lord has in us. They ravish the soul with their wondrous hints of blessedness. That we should need Him is easy to comprehend; that He should need us seems incomprehensible. It is natural to desire Him. But that He should desire us is hard to believe. And yet, over and over, He says it, and what can we do but believe Him?

He has made our hearts able to feel this great love. He has offered Himself as its object. It is infinitely precious to Him. He says, “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves me.

And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him”(John 4:21). He knocks at every heart, seeking to be its supreme love. “Will you have me?” He says to the believer, “ To be your beloved, will you follow me into suffering and loneliness? Will you endure hardship for my sake? Ask for no reward but my smile and praise.

Will you throw yourself with an utter abandonment into my will? Will you give up to me the absolute control of yourself and all that you are? Will you be content with pleasing me and me only? May I have my way within you in all things? Will you come into so close a union with me as to make a separation from the world necessary? Will you accept me as your only Lord, and leave all others, to cleave only unto me?” In a thousand ways , He makes this offer of oneness with Himself to every believer. But all do not say “Yes,” to Him. Other loves and other interests seem to them too precious to be cast aside.

They do not miss Heaven because of this. But they miss an unspeakable joy.

You, however, are not one of these. From the very first your soul has cried out eagerly and gladly to all His offers, “Yes, Lord; yes!” You are more than ready to pour out upon Him all your richest treasures of love and devotedness. Your enthusiasm for self-surrender may disturb some moderate Christians.

Your love makes necessary a separation from the world, which a lower love cannot even conceive of.

Sacrifices and services are possible and sweet to you. They could not come from a less devoted heart.

The life upon which you have entered gives you the right to a lavish outpouring of your all upon your beloved One. Services, of which more distant souls know nothing, become now your sweetest privilege.

Your Lord claims from you, because of your union with Him, far more than He claims of them.

What to them is lawful, love has made unlawful for you. To you He can make known His secrets, and to you He looks for an instant response to every requirement of His love. Oh, it is wonderful! The glorious, unspeakable privilege upon which you have entered! It will matter little if men hate you. They may shun you, reproach you, and cast out your name as evil for His sake! “Rejoice in that day and leap for joy. Your reward is great in Heaven. If you share in His suffering, you shall share in His glory.” In you He is seeing of the travail of His soul, and is satisfied. Your love and devotedness are His precious reward for all He has done for you.

It is unspeakably sweet to Him. Do not be afraid then to let yourself go in a heart-whole devotedness to your Lord that can brook no reserves. Others may not approve, but He will, and that is enough. Do not measure your obedience or your service. Let your heart and your hand be as free to serve Him, as His heart and His hand were to serve you. Let Him have all there is of you, body, soul, and spirit, time, talents, voice, everything. Lay your whole life open before Him that He may control it. Say to Him each day, “Lord, how shall I regulate this day so as to please you? Where shal l I go? What shall I do? Whom shall I visit? What shall I say?” Give your intellect up into His control and say, “Lord, tell me how to think so as to please you?” Give Him your reading, your pursuits, your friendships. Then say, “Lord, give me the insi ght to judge these things with your wisdom.”” Do not let there be a day nor an hour in which you are not intelligently doing His will, and following Him wholly.

Serving Him will give your life a halo. It will gild even the dullest life with a heavenly glow.

Have you ever grieved that the romance of youth is so soon lost in the hard realities of the world? Bring God into your life and its details. A greater joy will thrill your soul than youth's brightest days could know. Nothing will seem hard or stern again. The meanest life will be glorified by this. As I watched a poor woman at her wash-tub, I thought of the disheartening aspects of her life. I wondered why such lives must exist. Then, with a thrill of joy, I recalled the possible glorification of it. I told myself, even this life, lived in and with Christ, following Him wherever He leads, would be glorious.

Every hour of it would be filled with enthusiasm.

I am comforted to know that God's greatest blessings lie with the poorest and most humble lives. “For,” says our Lord Himself, “whosoever,” whether rich or poor, old or young, bond or free.

Whosoever shall do the will of God, the same is my brother, and my sister, and my mother.

Pause a moment over these simple yet amazing words. His brother, sister, and mother! What would we not have given to have been one of these! Oh, let me beg you, beloved Christian. Come, taste and see how good the Lord is. He has wonderful things in store for those who “keep His commandments, and do what is pleasing in His sight.” “If you listen closely to the Lord your God and obey all His commandments today, He will elevate you above all the nations on earth. If you listen to the Lord your God, all these blessings will come upon you.”

“ Blessed shall you be in the city, and blessed shall you be in the field. Blessed shall be the fruit of your womb and the fruit of your ground and the fruit of your cattle, the increase of your herds and the young of your flock. Blessed shall be your basket and your kneading bowl. Blessed shall you be when you come in, and blessed shall you be when you go out. The LORD will cause your enemies who rise against you to be defeated before you. They shall come out against you one way and flee before you seven ways. (Deuteronomy 28:3-7) “T he LORD will command the blessing on you in your barns and in all that you undertake. And he will bless you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you. The LORD will establish you as a people holy to himself, as he has sworn to you, if you keep the commandments of the LORD your God and walk in his ways.” (Deuteronomy 28:8 -9) “ And all the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by the name of the LORD, and they shall be afraid of you. And the LORD will make you abound in prosperity, in the fruit of your womb and in the fruit of your livestock and in the fruit of your ground, within the land that the LORD swore to your fathers to give you. The LORD will open to you his good treasury, the heavens, to give the rain to your land in its season and to bless all the work of your hands. And you shall lend to many nations, but you shall not borrow. And the LORD will make you the head and not the tail, and you shall only go up and not down, if you obey the commandments of the LORD your God, which I command you today, being careful to do them,”(Deuteronomy 28:10 -13) For the Israelites, it was outward and temporary. For us, it is inward and spiritual. And, it is far more glorious. May our surrendered wills leap out to embrace it in all its fullness!

fields.title: Oneness with Christ
fields.body_html:
God's dealings with a believer's soul aim for oneness with Himself. This fulfills the Lord's Prayer: “that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me. The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one, I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one, so that the world may know that you sent me and loved them even as you loved me”(John 17:21-23) God's glorious purpose for His people, before the world's foundation, was a soul-union. It was the mystery hid from ages and generations. It was accomplished in the incarnation of Christ. It has been made known b y the Scriptures. And it is realized as an actual experience by many of God’s dear children. But not by all. It is true of all. God has not hidden it. But, many have dim eyes and unbelieving hearts. They fail to grasp it. The Lord is stirring up believers everywhere. He wants them to abandon themselves to Him. It is to bring them to a personal realization of this. He wants to work in them all the good pleasure of His will.

All the previous steps in the Christian life lead up to this. The Lord has made us for it. Until we know it, and choose to embrace it, His soul's travail for us is unsatisfied. Our hearts have not found their final rest.

The usual course of Christian experience is pictured in the history of the disciples. First, they awoke to their condition and need. They then came to Christ and pledged their allegiance to Him. Then they followed Him, worked for Him, believed in Him, and yet, how unlike Him! They sought to be above each other. They ran from the cross. They misunderstood His mission and words. They forsook Him in danger. Yet, He sent them to preach. He recognized them as His disciples, with power to work for Him. They knew Christ only “after the flesh,” is outside of them, their Lord and Master, but not yet their Life.

Then came Pentecost. These disciples then knew Him as revealed within. They were one with Him, their very indwelling Life. Henceforth, He was to them Christ within. He worked in them to will and to do of His good pleasure.

He, by the law of the Spirit of His life, delivered them from the bondage to the law of sin and death, under which they had been held. No longer was it between themselves and Him, a war of wills and a clashing of interests. One will alone animated them, and that was His will. One interest alone was dear to them, and that was His. They were made ONE with Him.

Surely, all can recognize this picture. But the final stage may not be fully reached. You may have left much to follow Christ, dear reader. You may have believed in, worked for, and loved Him. Yet, you may not be like Him. Allegiance, you know, and confidence you know, but not yet union. There are two wills, two interests, two lives. You have not yet lost your own life that you may live only in His.

Once it was I and not Christ. Then it was I and Christ. Perhaps now it is even Christ and me. But has it come to be Christ only, and not I at all? Perhaps you do not understand what this oneness means. Some believe it is a great emotion or a feeling of oneness. They turn inward, examining their emotions. They hope to find, in these, their union with God. But nowhere is the mistake of trusting to feelings greater than here.

Oneness with Christ must, by nature, mean a Christ-like life and character. It is not what we feel, but what we are that settles the question. No matter how strong our feelings, there can be no oneness without a likeness of character with Christ. We must share a unity of aim, purpose, and thought. Our actions must be similar, too.

This is common sense, and it is Scriptural too. We say two people are one. We mean their purposes, actions, thoughts, and desires are alike. A friend may express great love and unity. But if their aims, actions, and views are the opposite of ours, we can't feel any real oneness. This is true despite our affection for each other. To be truly one with another, we must share everything. Our likes and dislikes, joys and sorrows, hopes and fears, must all be the same. As someone says, we must look through one another’s eyes, and think with one another’s bra ins. This is, as I said above, only plain common sense.

And oneness with Christ can be judged by no other rule. It is out of the question to be one with Him in any other way than in the way of nature, character, and life. Unless we are Christ-like in our thoughts and our ways, we are not one with Him, no matter how we feel. I have seen Christians with few Christ-like traits. They were so emotional and ecstatic in their love for Christ that they believed they were justified in claiming a close oneness with Him. I scarcely know a sadder sight. Surely our Lord meant to reach such cases when He said, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” (Mathew 7:21.)

He w as not making here any arbitrary statement of God’s will, but a simple announcement of the nature of things. Of course it must be so. It is like saying, “No man can enter the ranks of astronomers who is not an astronomer.” Emotions will not make a man an a stronomer, but life and action. He must be one, not merely feel that he is one.

There is no escape from this inexorable nature of things, and especially here. We must be one with Christ in character, life, and action. If not, we cannot be one with Him in any other way. There is no other way. We must be “partakers of His nature” to share His life. His life and His nature are one.

But emotional souls do not always see this.

They feel so near to Christ and so united to Him that they think it must be real. They overlook the need for a Christ-like character and walk. So, they build their hopes on their delightful emotions and exalted feelings. They believe they must be one with Him to have such rich, holy experiences.

It is a fact that other causes can produce these emotions. They are not solely due to a divine influence.

The emotions depend largely on temperament and physical conditions. It is most dangerous, therefore, to make them a test of our spiritual union with Christ. It may result in just such a grievous self-deception as our Lord warns against in (Luke 6:46-49): “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell you? Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a foundation. When the stream broke against it, it immediately fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

Our soul delights in calling Him, “Lord, Lord.” But, are we doing what He said? He tells us this is the important point, after all.

If you are one with Christ, you will be sweet to those who are cross with you. You will bear everything and make no complaints. When reviled, you will not revile again. You will consent to be trampled on, as Christ was, and feel only love in return. You will seek others' honor rather than your own. You will take the lowest place and serve all, as Christ did. You will truly love your enemies and do well to those who spitefully use you. In short, you will live a Christ-like life. You will show and feel, a Christ-like spirit and walk among men as He did. This, dear friends, is what it is to be one with Christ. If this is not your life, you are not one with Him. Your feelings, no matter how ecstatic, do not matter.

To be one with Christ is too wonderful and solemn a thing. It is too mighty an experience to be reached by mere feelings. He was holy, and those who are one with Him will be holy also. There is no escape from this simple and obvious Fact.

When our Lord tried to show His oneness with God, He said, “And he who sent me is with me. He has not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.”(Joshua 8:29) “So Jesus said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you may marvel. For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son, just as they honor the Fat her. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him” (John 5:19-23) The test of oneness, then, was the doing of the same works, and it is the test of oneness now. If our Lord could say that, so must His disciples. He said to believe in Him only if He did the works of His Father. He asked for no belief based on His claims.

It is forever true that “So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. A healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseas ed tree bear good fruit” (Mathew 7:17 -18 ). It is not that they will not, but they cannot. A soul united with Christ will, for sure, bear a Christ-like life. A grapevine bears grapes, not thistles. I don't object to emotions, though. On the contrary, I believe they are very precious gifts when they are from God, and are to be greatly rejoiced in. I object to using them to test spiritual states, in ourselves or others. I don't want to base our faith on them. Let them come or let them go, just as God pleases, and make no account of them either way. But, we must have the vital marks of oneness with Christ. We must share a likeness in character, life, and walk. If we do, all will be well. fields.title: A Lesson in the Interior Life
fields.body_html:
At Christmas, many of our store windows show a significant picture. It is a dreary, desolate winter scene. There is a dark, stormy sky, bare trees, and brown grass and dead weeds, with patches of snow over them. On a leafless tree at one side of the picture is an empty and snow-covered nest, and on a branch near sits a little bird. It is cold, dark, and desolate enough to daunt any bird, and drive it to some fairer clime. But, this bird sits there, content. Its little head is bravely lifted to the sky, and a winter song is about to burst from its tiny throat.

This picture, which always stands on my shelf, has preached me many a sermon. And the test is always the same. It is in the two words at the head of this article, “Although” and “Yet.”

“ Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls,” (Habakkuk3:17). There come times in many lives when, like this winter bird, the soul finds itself without comfort. All seems dark and wrong. Everything we trusted fails us. Promises seem unfulfilled, and our prayers go unanswered. We find nothing left to rely on in earth or Heaven. And it is at such times as these that the brave little bird with its message is needed. Although all is wrong everywhere, yet there is one thing to rejoice in: God. He is the God of our salvation. He does not change. He is the same good, loving, tender God yesterday, today, and forever.

We can rejoice in Him always, whether we have anything else to rejoice in or not. By rejoicing in Him, I do not mean rejoicing in ourselves. I fear most people think this is what is meant. Their feelings, revelations, and experiences form the basis of their joy. If none are satisfactory, they see no chance of joy at all. But the lesson the Lord is trying to teach us all the time is the lesson of humility.

He commands us to look away from the self and its experiences. We must crucify the self and count it dead. We must cease to care about the self. We should know and want nothing but God.

The reason for this is that God has destined us for a higher life than the self-life. That, just as He has destined the caterpillar to be a butterfly, He has appointed its life to die. So, the butterfly may take its place. Likewise, He has appointed our self-life to die so that the divine life may be ours instead. The caterpillar destroys its grub form to become a butterfly. It dies that it may live. And just so must we.

So, the most essential thing now is to die to self and be reborn to a life in God. And it is for this reason that the lesson of joy in the Lord, and not in self, must be learned. Every advancing soul must, sooner or later, trust God. The bare God, if I may. It must trust Him for what He is, not for His promises or gifts. It must learn to have its joy in Him alone, and to rejoice in Him when all else in Heaven and earth shall seem to fail.

I believe the only way to reach this place is by the soul. It must face, in its own experience, the loss of all things, both inward and outward. I don't mean that all one's friends must die, or all one's money be lost. I mean that the soul shall find itself, from either inward or outward causes, abandoned, lost, and empty of all consolation. It must come to the end of everything that is not God, and must have nothing else left to rest on within or without. It must experience just what the prophet meant when he wrote that “Although.”

It must go through the mud, fall off the edge, and be covered by the water . It must, at last, find, among and below them, the present, living, loving, omnipotent God! Only then will it understand the prophet's exulting shout of triumph. It will be able to join it : “ yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation.”(Habakkuk 3:10) Then, and not until then, will it know the full meaning of the verse that follows: “ GOD, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the deer’s; he makes me tread on my high places .”(Habakkuk3:19) The soul often walks on what seem high places. They are, however, largely self-made and emotional, with little of God in them. In moments of loss and failure, these high places become edges. Their very foundations are laid in the midst of an utter loss and death of all that is not God.

Today's answered prayer may seem unanswered tomorrow. The once-fulfilled promises may no longer feel real. The spiritual blessing that once brought joy may be lost. All we may have left is a hungry, longing memory of it all. But when all else is gone, God is still left. Nothing changes Him. He is the same yesterday, today, and forever, and in Him is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.

And the soul that finds its joy in Him alone can suffer no wavering. It is grand to trust in the promises, but it is grander still to trust in the Promiser. The promises may be misunderstood or misapplied. When we rely on them, they may seem to fail us. But no one ever trusted in the Promiser and was confounded.

The God behind His promises is infinitely greater than them. He can never fail us in any emergency.

The soul that trusts in Him knows perfect peace.

The little child does not always understand its mother's promises. But it knows its mother. Its trust is based not on her word, but on herself. And just so it is with those of us who have learned the lesson of this “Although” and “Yet.” There may not be a prayer answered or a prom ise fulfilled to our own consciousness, but what of that? Behind the prayers and behind the promises, there is God, and He is enough. And to such a soul the simple words, “God is”, answer every question and solve every doubt.

To the little trusting child, the simple fact of the mother’s existence is the answer to all its needs. The mother may not make one single promise or detail any plan, but she is, and that is enough for the child.

The child rejoices in the mother, not in her promises, but in herself. To the child, as to us, there is joy.

It is the one unchangeable thing behind all that changes and can change. It is the mother's existence.

The child must be cared for while the mother lives. The child, instinctively if not intelligently, knows this and rejoices in it. And while God lives, His children must be cared for. They should know this and rejoice in it more than a human child would.

For what else can God do, being what He is? Neglect, indifference, forgetfulness, and ignorance are all impossible to Him. He knows everything. He cares about everything. He can manage everything. He loves us. What more could we ask? So, come what may, we will lift our faces to our God, like our brave little bird teacher. In our darkest “Althoughs,” we will sing our glad and triumphant “Yet.”

All of God’s saints in all ages have done this. Job said, out of the depths of sorrow and trial which few can equal, “ Though he slay me I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face .”(Job 13:15). In his deepest ang uish, David could say, “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.” (Psalm 23:4) And again, “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.”(Psalm 46:1). Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling. Selah there is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High. God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns.

In his sorrows, Paul could say, “We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; always carrying in the body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies.

For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus ’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may be manifested in our mortal flesh. So death is at work in us, but life in you.” (2Corinthianss 4:812).The soul that learned to rejoice in God alone can say all this and more.

Spiritual joy is not a thing, not a lump of joy, so to speak, stored away in one’s heart to be looked at and rejoiced over. Joy is the gladness from having something good or knowing something pleasant.

And the Christian’s joy is simply his gladness in knowing Christ, and in his possession o f such a God and Saviour. We do not on an earthly plane rejoice in our joy, but in the thing that causes our joy. And on the heavenly plane, it is the same. We must “ yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the God of my salvation. “(Habakkuk 3:18.) No man or devil can take this joy from us. No earthly sorrows can touch it.

A writer on the interior life says, in effect, that our spiritual journey has three very different regions.

Each is a necessary stage in our progress. First, there is the region of beginnings. It is a time of simple joys and delights, strong hopes, and deep feelings. Many secrets reveal God. Next is a vast wilderness, full of temptations and trials. It brings a loss of reason, dryness, and inner and outer darkness. If, after a long trial, you endure the desert, a region of mountain heights awaits. There, you will find a union with God, a detachment from earthly things, and a perfect contentment with His will. You will be transformed into the image of Christ.

I cannot discuss if this order is true. But, I am sure of one thing. Many souls, who found joy in the “Region of beginnings” here, later faced a desert experience that left them amazed and perplexed. And I cannot but think such might, perhaps, in this explanation, find the answer to their trouble. They are learning to detach from all that is not God. This is to unite their souls with Him, as shown in a picture of the third and highest region of bliss.

The soul’s pathway is always through death to life. The caterpillar must die to become a butterfly. It can only do so by giving up one life to live another. And neither can we. So, we may have to pass through this desolate, deadly region to reach the calm mountain heights beyond. If we know this, we can walk through the darkest times, sure that all is well, since God is God. Many who read this paper have at least one of these desert “Althoughs.” Some have many.

Dear friends, is the “Yet” there also? Have you learned the prophet’s lesson? Is God enough for you?

Can you sing and mean it, “You, O Christ, are all I want, more than all in you I find” If not, you need the little bird to speak to you.

His song, as he sits on that bare, leafless tree in the howling winter storm, must become your song too.

Though the rain may fall and the wind blow, And the chill is the wintry blast; Though the cloudier sky is still clouding, And the dead leaves tell that summer is passed; Yet my face I hold to the stormy heaven, My heart is as calm as a summer sea; Glad to receive what my God has given, Whatever it may be.

When I feel the cold, I can say, 'He sends it.' And His wind blows blessing, I surely know. For I've never wanted but that He attends it. My heart beats warm, though the winds may blow. The soft, sweet summer was warm and glowing. Bright were the blossoms on every bough. I trusted Him when the roses were blowing. I trust Him now.

My faith would be small and weak if it wavered just because the roses have stopped blooming . Frail was the trust that now should alter, doubting His love when the storm-clouds grow. If I trust Him once, I must trust Him ever. His way is best, though I stand or fall. Through wind or storm, He will leave me never, for He sends all.”

fields.title: How to Reign in the Interior Life
fields.body_html:
When the Pharisees asked him when the kingdom of God would come, he answered, “It does not come with observation.”” Neither shall they say, 'Look, here!'” or, look there! For, Behold, the kingdom of God is within you.” The phrases “kingdom of God” and “kingdom of Heaven” refer to the divine life in the soul. They are in Scripture. They mean simply the place or condition where God rules, and where His will is done. It is an interior kingdom, not an exterior one. Its thrones are not for human pomp and glory. They are for dominion over the things of time and sense. Its kings wear not royal robes of purple and fine linen. They wear instead the inner garments of purity and truth. And its reign is not in outward show, but in inward power.

Neither is it in one place rather than another, nor in one form of things above another. We should not seek Christ in this mountain or at Jerusalem. That is not where to find Him and enter His kingdom. It is not a matter of place at all, but one of condition. In every place, under every name, and in every form, all who seek God and do good will find His kingdom within them. But this is very little understood. Our childish literalism has led us to believe that a kingdom must be in a specific place. We expected the kingdom of heaven to mean an outward victory of heaven over earth in some particular location. We thought that to sit on a throne with Christ would mean to be publicly uplifted in power and glory.

But, as Scripture's inner sense unfolds, we see that this would be a poor, superficial fulfillment of the real meaning of these symbols. And the vision of their true significance grows before the “eyes that see.” At last, we know our Lord's words were truer than we had ever dreamed. The “kingdom of God comes not with observation; neither shall they say, lord here! or, lord there!” for, behold, the kingdom of God is wi thin you.”

Daniel 2:44 “And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people. It shall break in pieces all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, and it shall stand forever,” announces the kingdom. Isaiah 9:6-7 announces the King: -- “ For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace, there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this.”

This kingdom has the right to destroy all others. The law says the inward must rule the outward. If there is peace within, no turmoil can affect the soul. But outward peace can't calm an inner storm. A happy heart can walk, indifferent, through a sea of trouble. But internal anguish can't find joy in the best surroundings. A man's inner self makes or unmakes his joy, not his possessions. Someone told Diogenes, “The king has degraded you.” “Yes , ” replied Diogenes triump hantly, “but I am not degraded!” No act of kings or emperors can degrade a soul that retains its own dignity; no tyrant can enslave an inwardly free man.

So, to have this divine kingdom within means all other powers to conquer or enslave are broken. The soul reigns triumphant over them all. Men and devils may try to enslave one. But they are powerless before the might of this interior kingdom. No longer will fashion, convention, or fear of man rule a soul raised to a throne in this inward kingdom. Nor will the love of ease. Christians cringe and bow to many tyrants. No sin or temptation can overcome, no sorrow can crush, no discouragement can hinder.

Let a man or woman have been bound in ever so tyrannical chains of sinful habits, this kingdom will set them free. Circumstances may make men kings in the outside world. But, in the hidden life, men become kings over circumstances. And, the soul that was once a slave to a thousand things, now finds itself completely independent of them.

For the King in this kingdom is one whom nothing can affect or baffle. He it is who makes circumstances. Since the government is on His shoulders, we cannot doubt that He will rule with perfect justice. His subjects will want for nothing. The phrase “the government shall be upon His shoulder” holds the secret of this wonderful kingdom. Upon His shoulder, not upon ours. The care is His. The burdens are His. The responsibility is His. The protection is His. The planning, providing, controlling, and guiding are all in His hands. No one can question as to His perfect fulfilment of every requirement of His kingship. So, those in His kingdom are free from anxiety, burden, and trouble.

And by this deliverance they become kings. The government is not upon their shoulders, and they have no business to interfere with it. Their King has assumed all responsibility. If He sees His subjects happy and prosperous, He is content to bear all the weight and care of kingship. We often speak of the duties of earthly kings. We pity them for the burdens of kingship. We recognize, even on an earthly plane, that to be a king means, or ought to mean, the bearing of the burdens of even the meanest of his subject.

Even now, as I write, many hearts ache for the new Czar. He has taken on the heavy burden of the vast Russian Empire.

We can learn, from every human heart, of kingship's duties. It means to be in a kingdom where God is King. He has declared that all things shall be ordered with judgment and justice, forever. Surely no care or anxiety can ever enter here, if the heart but knows its kingdom and its King! In John 18:36, our King tells us the tactics of His kingdom: “ Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.”

Earthly kings and kingdoms gain supremacy through war. God's kingdom conquers by inward power.

Earthly kings subdue enemies; God subdues enmity. His victories must be interior before they can be exterior. He does not subjugate, but he conquers. Even we, on our earthly plane, know this principle.

We do not value any victory over another that only reaches the body and has not subdued the heart. No true mother cares for an outward obedience merely; nothing will satisfy her but the inward surrender.

Unless the center of the heart is conquered, the conquest seem worthless. And with God how much more so? We are told, “But the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not look on his appearan ce or on the height of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.” (1samuel 16:7) We speak of “subduing hearts.” We do not mean to force a surrender. We mean that they are won and willingly given to another. And it is after this fashion and no other that God subdues. So that to read that “His kingdom rules over all” means that all hearts are won to His service in a glad and willing surrender.

For again I repeat, His reign must be inward before it can be outward. And in truth, it is no reign at all, unless it is within. If we think for a moment, we will see this must be so. It is impossible to imagine God reigning in a kingdom where His subjects' actions are not controlled beyond their outward actions.

His kingdom is not of this world. It is a spiritual realm. Its power is over souls, not bodies.

So, it can only be set up once the soul is conquered.

Seen this way, all those declarations and prophecies become full of love and blessing. They say that God will subdue His enemies and will rule them in righteousness and power! And how glorious with hope does the voice of that great multitude heard by John sound out, saying, “Alleluia! For the Lord God omnipotent reigns” In confirmation of all this we have two passages descriptive of this kingdom, in (Romans.14:17) “ For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” , and (1 Corinthian s 4:20): “ For the kingdom of God does not consist in talk but in power.”

Not outward things, but inward. Not what a man eats or drinks. Not where he lives. Not his nationality or the customs of his race. Not even his thoughts or words. But what are the inward traits of his nature?

What is the power of his spirit? For these alone constitute this kingdom of God.

Not what I do, but what I am, is to decide whether I belong to it or not. This kingdom can be set up only when we have and experience, inward righteousness, peace, joy, and power. So, no external domination can achieve such results. Only the inner work of God's all-subduing spirit can.

I have learned a lot from the story of Odysseus and his journey, when he was sailing past the islands of the sirens. These sirens could charm anyone who listened to their songs. They lured them to leap into the sea. To avert this danger, Odysseus filled his crew's ears with wax. He did this so they would not hear the fatal music. He then bound himself to the mast with knotted cords. They passed the isle in safety. But, when Orpheus had to sail by the same island, he won a better victory. He made sweeter music than the sirens and enchanted his crew with more alluring songs. So, they passed the dangerous charmers, not only safely but with disdain. Wax and knotted cords kept Odysseus and his crew from a fatal leap. But, inward delights let Orpheus and his crew triumph over temptation itself. And just so is it with the kingdom of which we speak. It needs no outward law to bind it, but reigns by right of its inward life.

So that it is said of those who have entered it, “Against such there is no law. “For it is a kingdom of kings. The song we shall one day sing, nay, that we ought to be singing even now and here in this life, declares this: “ and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings on earth. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom, priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen (Revelation.1:5-6.)

We who have entered this kingdom, or, rather, in whom this kingdom is set up, sit upon the throne with our King and share His dominion. The world was His footstool, and it becomes our footstool also. He reigned above the things of time and sense. A life lived in a higher, superior plane gave him that power.

So may we. We all know the saying that someone “rises above his surroundings.” It means there is a hidden power in that person. It controls his surroundings instead of being controlled by them. Our King rose above His surroundings. We, who reign with Him, can do the same.

But, just as He was not a king in outward appearance, but only in inward power, so shall we be. He reigned, not in that He had all the world's riches. But that He had none, and could do without them.

And so shall our reigning be. We shall not have all men bow to us, nor do all things bend to our will.

With all men opposing us and all things adverse, we shall walk in a royal triumph of soul through them.

We shall suffer the loss of all things, and by that loss be set forever free from their power to bind. We shall hide in the King's will, an impregnable fortress. There, we shall reign in a perpetual Kingdom.

All this is contrary to man’s thought of kingship. The human heart can only grasp one idea. It is this: that outward circumstances must bend to the soul that is on a throne with Christ. Friends must approve, enemies must be silenced, and obstacles must be overcome. Affairs must prosper, or there can be no reigning. If man had ordered Daniel's business, or the three Hebrews in the fiery furnace, he would have said to win, they must change the kings' minds. Daniel should not have been cast into the lion's den, and the Hebrew children should have been kept out of the furnace.

But God’s way was infinitely grander. He allowed Daniel to be cast among the lions. He wanted to reign triumphant over them in their midst. He allowed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to be cast into a burning furnace. He wanted them to walk through it without even the smell of fire on them. He tells us, not to walk in paths without dragons and adders. But, we shall walk through the midst of them, and “tread them under our feet.””

And how much more glorious a kingdom is this than any outward rule or control could be! To be a king inside, but a slave outside, is a great triumph. It is the best our hearts can conceive. To be destitute, afflicted, and tormented. To be stoned, torn apart, and slain with the sword. To wander in sheepskins and goatskins, and in deserts, mountains, dens, and caves. Yet, through it all, to be kings in a kingdom of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. This is a kingdom that none but God could give, and none but God-like souls could receive.

We have seen or heard of a few such kings. All hearts have acknowledged their unconscious effect. I read about one of the members of the St. Cyr monastery. Their devotion made the monasteries and their superiors hate them. They were cast out as evil from their community. One was sent as a prisoner to a monastery where his enemies dwelt. There, he suffered cruel and degrading treatment. Although he came from a noble background and was a former leader, he had to do the simplest tasks . He was forced to carry a heavy burden on his back and made to beg with a sign on his chest saying he was the worst of the worst. But, through it all, the saint's spirit triumphed. Nothing disturbed his calm or soured his Christ-like sweetness.

For his persecutors, he never had anything but words of kindness and smiles of love. At last, by the divine kingdom's great power, he won all hearts. He became the trusted friend and adviser, and the beloved ruler of his former enemies who had once delighted in persecuting him. “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the earth” (Mathew 5:5) . By his meekness, he conquered and became king. At one time, a dangerous criminal was sent to the monastery for imprisonment. He was so violent that no bonds sufficed to bind him, and no strength could control him. At last, he was taken to the cell of a brother from St. Cyr. They were shut up together. Even the stolid monks recognized that divine meekness. It had a power to conquer that surpassed all they knew. The saint received the violent man as a beloved brother and smiled upon him with heavenly kindness.

But the criminal returned it with abuse and violence. He broke the monk’s furniture and destroyed his bed, he kicked him, beat him, and tore his hair, and spat upon him. He exhausted himself in his violence against him. Through it all, the monk resisted nothing.

He spoke only words of love. Finally, the criminal, worn out with fury, paused to catch his breath. The beaten and outraged man then smiled at his persecutor with deep love and compassion. It was as if he wanted to comfort him for his misery. It was more than the criminal could bear. Hatred, revenge, and anger he could repay in kind. But, he had no weapons against such love and meekness. His heart was conquered. He fell at the feet of the saint and washed them with his tears, as he entreated forgiveness for his cruelty, and vowed a lifelong loyalty to his service.

And from that moment all trouble with that criminal was over. He followed the saint about like a loving and faithful dog, eager to do or to be anything the other might desire. When his prison term ended, the gates opened. He could not be induced to leave, for he could not bear to leave the man who had saved him by love. Of such a nature is kingship in this kingdom of heaven. Each soul can make the application for itself, without need of comment from me.

In ( Mathew 5: 6-7), we have the King of this kingdom describing the characteristics of His kingdom and giving the laws for Hi s subjects. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy. “Not the rich, or great, or wise, or learned. But the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, those who mourn, and those who hunger and thirst. Also, the persecuted, reviled, and slandered. All such belong to this kingdom. These kings are gentle, yielding, meek, and charitable. They reign with that power.

One Christian asked anoth er, “How can I make people respect me?” “I would command their respect,” was the reply. This meant, not that he should demand, “Respect me!” But, he should act, live, and be, so that all would respect him. Men can win a show of respect by being tyrannical. But, to rule their hearts, they must try other methods.

Our Lord developed this thought to some who wished to share His throne. He called them to Him, and said, “But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it o ver them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.”(Mathew 20:25). But it shall not be so among you. Whoever wants to be great must be your minister. Whoever wants to be first must be the servant of all. For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.”

From a human view, only one man reigns. He is the one who can be lord over those around him.

From the divine standpoint the soul that serves is the soul that reigns.

Not he who demands most, receives this inward crowning, but he who gives up most. What greater leadership can be imagined than Christ's in the Sermon on the Mount? “But I say to you, do not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also . ” If someone sues you and takes your shirt, give them your coat too . And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go with him two miles. (Mathew 5:39) Surely only a soul that is in harmony with God can mount such a throne of dominion as this! But this is our destiny. We are made for this purpose. We are born of a kingly race, and are heirs to this Inexpressible kingdom; “ and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him .”(Romans 8:17) With that we could realize this, and, see in every act of service or surrender, an upward step. It would lead us to our kingdom and throne! I mean this in a very practical sense. I mean that our daily, humble tasks and small sacrifices, if done well, will be steps up a ladder to our thrones. If we are faithful over the “few things” of our earthly kingdom, we shall be made rulers over the “many things” of the heavenly kingdom.

He who serves and suffers for Christ will reign with Him. He will be the “chiefest” in His kingdom of love. Knowing this, who would hesitate to turn the other cheek? A kingdom and a throne are to be won.

Joseph was a type of all this. In slavery and in prison he reigned as king, as truly as when seated on Pharaoh’s throne or riding in Pharaoh’s chariot. (See Gen. 39:6) “So he left all that he had in Joseph’s charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food he ate. Now Joseph was handsome in form and appearance.”

(Genesis 39:22-23.) “ And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it. The keeper of the prison paid no attention to anything that was in Joseph’s charge, beca use the LORD was with him. And whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed.” He became the greatest by being the least, the chiefest by being servant of all.

Dear reader, are you ruling in this way, in this kind of kingdom? Are you the greatest in your small world — at home, church, or in your social circle? Then be the least. Be the servant of everyone. If not, your kingdom is not Christ’s kingdom, and your throne is not shared with Him. Accessing the secrets and power of this inner kingdom is not a fantasy . It’s not just an imagined victory. It’s a real and true way of reigning. It will make you rise above the world and its concerns. You will move through it, unaffected by its praise or criticism. You will live in a place of peace and victory that the world can neither give nor take away.

“For the kingdom of God is not in word but in power.” It is not a talk but a fact , and those who are in it recognize their kingship and prove it by reigning. But perhaps thou will say, “How can I enter into this kingdom , if I am not already in?” Let our Lord himself answer you: “At that time the disciples came to Jesus, saying, 'Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? ” (Mathew 18:1) “And calling to him a child, he put him in the midst of them and said , 'Truly, I say to you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.”(Mathew 18:2 -3) It is a kingdom of childlike hearts, and only such can en ter it. To be a “little child” means simply to be one. I cannot describe it better than this. We all know little children.

We delight in their simplicity, trust, and carelessness. We admire their unquestioning obedience to authority. To be the greatest in this divine kingdom, one must have the most of this child's trusting, tender, and obedient heart. It is guileless and self-forgetting.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Fa ther who is in heaven.”( Matthew 7:21 ) .It is not saying, but doing, that will avail us here. We must be a child, or we cannot sit on the child’s throne. And to be a child means to do the Father’s will, since the very essence of true childhood is the spirit of obedience united to the spirit of trust.

Become a little child. Set aside your greatness, self-assertion, and wisdom. Give up your strength and self-dependence. Consent to die to your old self. Be born again into the kingdom of God. The only way out of one life into another is by a death to one and a new birth into the other. It is the old story, therefore, reiterated so often and in so many different ways, of through death to life. Die, then, that you my live. Lose your own life that you may find Christ’s life.

They can only enter the butterfly's kingdom by dying to its caterpillar life, and then becoming a butterfly. Likewise, we can only enter God's kingdom by dying to the kingdom of self, and then rising to life in Christ. Let go of everything natural. This includes your ideas, plans, and thoughts. Instead, accept God's plans, ways, and thoughts. Do this faithfully and persistently. You shall, at last, sit on His throne and reign with Him in an eternal kingdom. It will break and consume all other kingdoms, and stand forever.

There is no other way. This kingdom can't be entered through pride, appearance, or power . It can only be entered by littleness, helplessness, childlikeness, babyhood, and death. To follow Him in the regeneration will, without fail, bring the soul that follows to His crown and throne. The Queen of England had sent him a medal through one of her earls. His friends pushed him forward to receive it, as he was shy and nervous and tried to step away.

Look at the honorable chairman. He had come from the House of Lords, where earls, dukes, and distinguished men like lawyers, judges, statesmen, and warriors were gathered. Royal princes were also there. Yet, all peer though he was, he was moved. He murmured, “I have the honor,” and pinned the lifesaving medal on the child's jacket. His heart was full. He paused to swallow down something that would rise in his throat before he could go on.

There is the 'glory and honor' of statesmen, warriors, and lawyers. But the glory of selfless lifesaving excels all. That was the wondrous glory won by this boy.” He had plunged into the stream and shared a drowning boy's risk. That little hand, look at it there, steadying him by holding the table, had come out holding the saved.

Why did that small body in its little breeches and jacket, wiping its tears on the rough little sleeve, grip thousands of hearts? Why did it make them, for a time, loyal subjects of its kingdom?

They say, “ saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and blessing!”( Revelations 5:12) .The Lamb that was slain is the mightiest King ever. All who share His spirit are in His kingdom. This kingdom is not a place, but a character. So, those without that character cannot be in it.

What is the kingdom of God but the rule of God? And what is the rule of God but the will of God? Therefore, when we pray, “Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven,” we have touched the secret of it all. A group of savages might take over a kingdom by force, but to truly control its civilization, they must follow its rules. The same is true for the kingdom of heaven. It only grants its power to those who obey its laws. “ The one who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father on his throne . ”( Revelation 3:21 ) “He always reigns who sides with God,” says an old writer. And again, “He who perfectly accepts the will of God, dwells in a perpetual kingdom.”

Are you reigning after this fashion and in this sort of a kingdom? Are you the most important by being the servant of all? Are you a king over your circumstances, or do your circumstances reign over you?

Do you triumph over your temptations, or do your temptations triumph over you? Can you sit on an inward throne in the midst of outward defeat and loss?

Can you conquer by yielding, and become the greatest by being the least? If you can’t answer yes to all these questions, then you can’t come into his kingdom. “Whatever yo ur lot or men's opinions, you are among those whom our Lord calls 'the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.'”

In every place, under every name, and in every form, all who seek God and do good will find His kingdom within them. But this is very little understood. Our childish literalism has led us to believe that a kingdom must be in a specific place. We expected the kingdom of heaven to mean an outward victory of heaven over earth in some particular location. We thought that to sit on a throne with Christ would mean to be publicly uplifted in power and glory. But, as Scripture's inner sense unfolds, we see that this would be a poor, superficial fulfillment of the real meaning of these symbols. And the vision of their true significance grows before the “eyes that see.” At last, we know our Lord's words were truer than we had ever dreamed. It shall break in pieces all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, and it shall stand forever,” announces the kingdom. Isaiah 9:6-7 announces the King: -- “ For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace, there will be no end, on the throne of David and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time forth and forevermore. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this.” This kingdom has the right to destroy all others. The law says the inward must rule the outward. If there is peace within, no turmoil can affect the soul. But outward peace can't calm an inner storm. A happy heart can walk, indifferent, through a sea of trouble. But internal anguish can't find joy in the best surroundings. A man's inner self makes or unmakes his joy, not his possessions. Someone told Diogenes, “The king has degraded you.” “Yes , ” replied Diogenes triump hantly, “but I am not degraded!” No act of kings or emperors can degrade a soul that retains its own dignity; no tyrant can enslave an inwardly free man. So, to have this divine kingdom within means all other powers to conquer or enslave are broken. The soul reigns triumphant over them all. Men and devils may try to enslave one. But they are powerless before the might of this interior kingdom. No longer will fashion, convention, or fear of man rule a soul raised to a throne in this inward kingdom. Nor will the love of ease. Christians cringe and bow to many tyrants. No sin or temptation can overcome, no sorrow can crush, no discouragement can hinder. Let a man or woman have been bound in ever so tyrannical chains of sinful habits, this kingdom will set them free. Circumstances may make men kings in the outside world. But, in the hidden life, men become kings over circumstances. And, the soul that was once a slave to a thousand things, now finds itself completely independent of them. For the King in this kingdom is one whom nothing can affect or baffle. He it is who makes circumstances. Since the government is on His shoulders, we cannot doubt that He will rule with perfect justice. His subjects will want for nothing. The phrase “the government shall be upon His shoulder” holds the secret of this wonderful kingdom. Upon His shoulder, not upon ours. The care is His. The burdens are His. The responsibility is His. The protection is His. The planning, providing, controlling, and guiding are all in His hands. No one can question as to His perfect fulfilment of every requirement of His kingship. So, those in His kingdom are free from anxiety, burden, and trouble. And by this deliverance they become kings. The government is not upon their shoulders, and they have no business to interfere with it. Their King has assumed all responsibility. If He sees His subjects happy and prosperous, He is content to bear all the weight and care of kingship. We often speak of the duties of earthly kings. We pity them for the burdens of kingship. We recognize, even on an earthly plane, that to be a king means, or ought to mean, the bearing of the burdens of even the meanest of his subject. Even now, as I write, many hearts ache for the new Czar. He has taken on the heavy burden of the vast Russian Empire. We can learn, from every human heart, of kingship's duties. It means to be in a kingdom where God is King. He has declared that all things shall be ordered with judgment and justice, forever. Surely no care or anxiety can ever enter here, if the heart but knows its kingdom and its King! Its power is over souls, not bodies. So, it can only be set up once the soul is conquered. Seen this way, all those declarations and prophecies become full of love and blessing. This kingdom can be set up only when we have and experience, inward righteousness, peace, joy, and power. So, no external domination can achieve such results. These sirens could charm anyone who listened to their songs. They lured them to leap into the sea. To avert this danger, Odysseus filled his crew's ears with wax. But, when Orpheus had to sail by the same island, he won a better victory. He made sweeter music than the sirens and enchanted his crew with more alluring songs.
