fields.title: The One Hundred and Thirty-ninth Psalm
fields.body_html:
Your great hospitality surrounds us like a boundless sea. We cannot lose ourselves where all is home, nor drift away from you.”

Very few of us understand the full meaning of the words in Matthew. 1:23, “Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel . ” This short sentence reveals the world's greatest truth. God, the Almighty Creator of Heaven and Earth, is not a distant god in a glorious Heaven.

He lives with us, in our poor, helpless lives, as close as we are to ourselves. This seems so incredible to the human heart that we are slow to believe it. But, the Bible teaches it as fact, from cover to cover.

Any honest mind cannot deny this.

In the very beginning of Genesis we read of the “presence of the Lord God amongst the trees of the garden.” Since then, He is always revealed to us. He has a daily, close relationship with His peop le everywhere. In Exodus we find Him asking them to make Him a “sanctuary that He might dwell among them.” He is recorded as having “walked” with them in the wilderness, and as “taking up His home” with them in the Promised Land. He taught them to rely on Him as an ever-present Friend and Helper.

They should consult Him about all their affairs and give Him their lives. And finally, He came in Christ in bodily form. He dwelt in the world as a man among men. He made Himself bone of our bone and flesh of our flesh. He took upon Him our nature. He revealed to us, in the most real way, a great and blessed truth. He intended to be with us always, even unto the end of the world.

Those who believe this truth will find its solution. It will solve all their life's troubles. As a little girl, I remember that, in trouble, my parents' arrival always relieved me. When I heard one say, “Daughter, I am here,” every burden dropped and every anxiety stilled. It was their simple presence that did it. They did not need to promise to relieve me. They did not need to tell me their plans. Their presence was all the assurance I required. It meant everything would be set right and all would go well for me.

After their arrival, I only wanted to see how they would do it.

They must be exceptional parents. Their children are very confident. I think they were. But our God is exceptional. So, the application is absolute. His presence is all we need.

It would be enough for us, even if we had not a single promise nor a single revelation of His plans. The Bible says, “I will be with you.” It has stilled all questions and fears. Who can doubt it? He meant to assure us that His infinite wisdom, love, and power are on our side. Over and over again in my childhood, have the magic words, “Oh, there is mother!” It brought me relief and comfort. In my later years, I've heard, “Oh, there is God!” spoken with reverence.” brought me a far more blessed deliverance. With Him present, what could I have to fear? He has said, “ Keep your life free from love of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, 'I will never leave you nor forsake you .”(Hebrews 13:5). So, I may boldly say, The Lord is my helper. I will not fear what man shall do to me. I still recall the inspiring sense of security that came with my father's presence. I never feared anything when he was by. And surely with my Heavenly Father by, there can be no possible room for fear.

I seek to make clear and definite the fact of “Emmanuel, God with us.” Its practical help and comfort inspire me. I am sure that few of God's own children truly believe it. They may say they do. They may repeat a thousand times, in a devout tone, “Oh, yes, we know that God is always present with us, but, and in this “but,” the whole story is told. There are no “buts” in the vocabulary of the soul that accepts His presence as a literal fact. Such a soul is joyously triumphant over every suggestion of fear or of doubt. It has God, and that is enough for it. His presence is its certain security and supply, always, and for everything.

I beg my readers to turn with me to the 139th Psalm. There, we will find a blessed revelation of this truth. The central thought of the Psalm is to be found in verses 7 to 12, “Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me. If I say, “Surely the darkness shall cover me, and the light about me be night,” even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright as the day, for darkness is as light with you.”

This passage is the strongest proof of His constant presence with us, wherever we are or whatever we do. People seek to be in the Lord's presence. But they cannot escape it. There is no place in the universe where He is not. Not in heaven, hell, or the farthest sea. No darkness can hide from Him, even for a moment. The reason is, He “has possessed our reins.” It means He is not only with us, but within us.

So, He must accompany us wherever we go.

We must accept it as true. Our Lord's words, “Look, I am with you always, even unto the end of the world,” were not just a beautiful sentiment. They are an undeniable fact. He is with us, and we cannot get away from Him.

In thick darkness, we may see nothing. We may think, often think that He does not see us. But our Psalm assures us that the darkness hides not from Him. In fact, darkness and light are both alike to Him. We are as present to His view and as plainly seen in our darkest spiritual depths as in our brightest light. The darkness may hide Him from us, but it does not hide us from Him. Nor does any spiritual distance or wandering take us from His presence. Not even if we sink into sin in our wandering. In the uttermost parts of the sea, or wherever we may be, He is ever present to hold and to lead us. There is not a moment nor a place where we can be left without His care.

Sometimes, confusion makes us unaware of the loving care of our nurses. A child in confusion might cry out for its mother, and its sad cries will break her heart. Meanwhile, she is holding the child's hot hand, cooling its fevered head, and caring for it with a mother's love. The sickness may hide the mother from the child, but it doesn't hide the child from the mother.

And just so it is with our God and us. Our doubts, fears, sorrows, and sins cannot hide us from Him.

But they often hide Him from us. He has said that the darkness and light are alike to Him. If our faith accepts this, we can trust in dark times. Though we cannot see or feel Him, our God cares for us. He will never leave us.

Whether, however, this abiding presence of our God will be a joy to us or a sorrow will depend upon what we know about Him. If we think of Him as a stern tyrant, intent only on His own glory, we shall be afraid of His continual presence. If we see Him as a loving Father, we'll be glad. He wants only our happiness. So, we'll be thankful to have Him with us always. For the presence and the care of love can never mean anything but good to the one beloved.

The Psalm we are considering shows us that God's presence is love. It brings us infinite comfort and rest. He says in verses 1 to 5, “O Lord, you have searched me and known me! You know when I sit down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying down and are acquainted with all my ways. Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O Lord, you know it altogether. You hem me in, behind and before, and lay your hand upon me.”

Our God knows us and understands us, and is acquainted with all our ways. No one else in all the world understands us. People may misinterpret our actions and misjudge our motives. Our natural characteristics are not taken into account, nor our inherited tendencies considered. No one makes allowances for our ill health; no one realizes how much we have to contend with. But our Father knows it all. He understands us. His judgment considers every part of our character, both conscious and unconscious. It also considers what controls our actions. Only an all comprehending love can be just, and our God is just. No wonder Faber can say: Nowhere on Earth are its sorrows felt more than in Heaven. Nowhere are its failings judged more kindly. Some of you may fear His justice, thinking it would be against you. But do you not see? It is all on your side, just as a mother's justice is, because He knows our frame and remembers that we are dust. No human judge can ever do this, and to me, this comprehension of God is one of my most blessed comforts. Often, I do not understand myself; all within looks confused and hopelessly tangled. But I remember that He has searched me. He knows me. He understands my perplexing thoughts. So, I may leave the whole mess to Him to unravel.

And my soul sinks at once, as on downy pillows, into a place of the most blissful rest. Then, because of His complete knowledge of our needs, what comfort it is to be told that He knows our down sitting and our uprising. He compasses our path, and takes note of our lying down. Our God does for us what a mother does for her foolish, careless, ignorant, but dearly loved little ones. When a mother is with her children, she thinks of their comfort and well-being always before her own. They must have comfortable, draught-free seats. She must endure any discomfort. Their beds must be soft and their blankets warm, let hers be what they may.

Their paths must be smooth and safe, even though she is obliged to walk in rough and dangerous ways.

Her own comfort, as compared with that of her children, is of no account in a loving mother’s eyes.

Surely, our God is not less capable of a self-sacrificing love than the mothers in this world. He must be better and greater on the line of love and self-sacrifice than any mother He ever made. He has assured us that He knows our down sitting and uprising. He compasses our path and our lying down. So, we can be sure, in all the little details of our lives, we get the very best that His love, wisdom, and power can provide. I mean this in a very literal sense. I mean that He cares for our seats and our beds. He sees that we each have the best kind for our highest development.

And just on this last point is where He is so much better than any mother can be. His love is a wise love that sees the outcome of things and cares more for our highest good than for that which is lower. A mother's weak love can't see beyond a child's comfort. It can't bear to cause any discomfort. But God's strong, wise love can permit some pain. It is for the sake of the future glory that will come from it.

At home and abroad, let us trust God. He knows all about our daily lives. So, let Him choose our seats, beds, and other small things.

For we are told in our Psalm that He “besets” our path. We have some of us have known what it was to be “beset” by unwelcome and unpleasant people or things. But we never thought, perhaps, t hat we were beset by God. He loves us so much that He cannot leave us alone.

No coldness or rebuffs can drive Him away. Yet it is gloriously true! Moreover , He besets us “behind” as well as before. Just as a mother does. She goes after her children. She picks up all they dropped and clears away their rubbish.

We mothers start this in the nursery with the blocks and toys. We do it all our lives. We try to fix what our children have left undone or wrong. It takes a lot of effort and trouble, but our love makes that effort seem small compared to caring for our children. What good mother would ever turn away a sad, crying child? Or refuse to help a boy untangle his kite strings? Even if the knots and tangles are his fault, her love understands and feels for those mistakes. So, she works even harder to help fix them.

Our God does all this, and more, for us from infancy. He does it long before we are aware of it, until the end of our earthly lives. We have seen Him before us, perhaps, but we have never thought of Him as behind us as well. Yet, it is a blessed fact. He is behind us. He longs to make crooked things straight, untangle our knots, and atone for our wrongs. If any of us has a troubling past, let us be happy. The God who is behind us will set it all straight if we commit it to Him. He can even make our mistakes work together for good. Ah! It is a grand thing to be surrounded by God.

Then again, what comfort in verses 14 to 16: “I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.

A Wonderful work are your works; my soul knows it very well. My frame was not hidden from you when I was being made in secret, intricately woven in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me, when as yet there was none of them.”

We often dislike, more than we admit, how we were made. Our mental or moral “make - up” does not suit us. We think that if we were created with less of this or more of that, we'd be more successful. If we were less impulsive or more enthusiastic, we could better serve God. We could also be more satisfactory to ourselves and to Him. We believe that if we were more like someone we admire, it would help too. And we are tempted sometimes to think that with our miserable make-up, it is hopeless to expect to please Him.

If we truly realized that God made us, we would see the folly of all this at once. But, we feel that He had little hand in it. We think we were put together haphazardly, leaving our characters to chance. We believe in creation in the general, but not in the particular, when it comes to ourselves. This Psalm shows that God oversaw our creation. He managed even the smallest details. Figuratively, he wrote down what each “member” was to be when none existed yet. So, we are, by nature, what God wants.

He made us do a special work. I mean, of course, our natural characteristics, not the perversion of them by sin on our parts.

There is something very glorifying to the Creator in this way of looking at it. Genius always seeks to express itself in many ways. No true artist repeats himself. Each painting or statue is a new expression of his creative power. An art exhibition should not have two identical pictures. If it did, it would lower the value of art. The same is true for us, as we are “God's workmanship.” His creative power expresses itself differently in each one of us.

And in the individual “make-up,” which sometimes troubles us, there is a unique power. Without it, the day of the exhibition, when we are to praise His glory, would be incomplete. He asks only this: since He made us, He should manage us. He alone understands us, so only He can do it.

The man who makes an intricate machine is best suited to manage and repair it. Anyone else who meddles is likely to spoil it. Given our complex minds and our poor control of them, we should be thankful to hand them to their Creator and leave them in His hands. We can be sure He will make the best of us. Even with our “peculiar temperaments” and flaws, we will be made into vessels of honor.

We will be sanctified and fit for the Master's use, ready for every good work.

I once read a saying from an old Quaker writer that stayed with me: “Be content to be just what God made you.” It helped me understand my thoughts. I believe that to truly submit to God, we must accept ourselves as He created us, just as we accept our daily circumstances. If we did not exist, a part of God’s creation would be missing. His work would be incomplete. Besides, com plaining about ourselves is like complaining about the One who made us, which must hurt Him. Let’s be content and trust the Divine Potter to shape us as He sees best and use us as He chooses.

Verses 17 and 18 bring out another view of God’s continual pr esence with us, and that is, that He is always thinking about us, and that His thoughts are kind and loving thoughts, for the Psalmist calls them precious. “How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! How great is the sum of them!

If I should count them, they are more in number than the sand: when I awake, I am still with thee.”

So many people are tempted to think that God is not paying any attention to them. They believe their interests are beneath His notice. They feel too unworthy to hope for His attention. But they wrong Him grievously by such thoughts. A mother pays as much attention to her smallest infant as to her oldest children. She is as interested in its little needs and pleasures as in theirs. I am not sure, but she is more.

She thinks of the one who needs them most. He who made the mother's heart will care for His most helpless creatures. He hears the young lions when they cry. Not a sparrow can fall to the ground without Him. We are worth more than many sparrows. So, we need not fear neglect for a moment.

Creating anything requires constant care from the Creator. Omnipotence's glory is that it can do everything at once. It can tend to the smallest details and the grandest tasks. “Only an infinite greatness can hold all things. A greatness less than infinite would crush us.”

I don't know why we see a man or woman as weak for neglecting small details in favor of big tasks.

Yet, we accuse our God of doing the same thing. But if any of my readers have been guilty of this folly, let it end now. “How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!

If I were to count them, they would be more than the sand. I awake, and I am still with you.”

The rest of the Psalm shows a perfect harmony between the soul and God. It is where this life of simple faith has begun. The soul unites with God, knowing that He is always present and cares. It loves what He loves and hates what He hates. It eagerly asks Him to search and test it, so no part of it is out of harmony with Him.

In His presence, darkness must flee. The heart will feel it cannot endure having any corner hidden from His light. “For, you make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your right hand are pleasures forevermore.” (Psal m 16:11 ) An old woman, in a desolate part of England, made a lot of money selling ale and beer to travelers at her lonely cottage. But her conscience troubled her about it. She wanted to be a Christian and go to Heaven when she died. But, she felt that, if she did, she'd have to give up her profitable business. She thought that would be too much to bear. So, she was torn between the two.

One night, at a meeting she attended, a preacher spoke about the joy of God's constant presence. He said knowing this truth brings great happiness. Her heart was filled with excitement at the thought that this could be true for her. Forgetting all about the beer, she simply and sincerely accepted it as a wonderful reality. As the preacher kept speaking, she cried in her he art, “Lord Jesus, I didn’t know you were always with me! Lord, how amazing it is to know that you are always here with me, taking care of me! I will never feel lonely again !

When the meeting ended, she walked home across the fields. The joyful thought kept repeating in her heart, “Ah, Lord Jesus, you are coming home with me tonight.” She said, “Never mind, Lord Jesus, old Betty won’t ever let you go again now. I know you are here with me.

Her faith in God’s presence grew stronger, and she felt more joy ful with each step. By the time she reached her cottage door, her heart was full of happiness. As she walked in, the first thing she saw was a big pot of beer on the table, ready to be sold. A thought came to her: “The Lord won’t like that pot of beer.” Her heart quickly responded, “Then it must go.” The pot was heavy, so she knelt beside it and prayed, “Lord, You have come home with me. You will live in this cottage, and I know you don’t want this beer here. Please give me the strength to pour it out.” God gave her strength, and soon the beer was running down the road. Then she went back inside, knelt, and thanked the Lord for helping her. She added, “Now, Lord, if there is anything else in this cottage that you don’t like, show me, and I will get rid of it too. Isn’t this a perfect example of the message at the end of our Psalm?

“Lord, don’t I hate those who hate you? Am I not troubled by those who oppose you? I hate them completely and see them as my enemies.

Search me, O God, and know my heart. Test me and know my thoughts.

If there is anything wrong in me, show me, and lead me on the right path forever Just as light drives out darkness, so does the realized presence of God drive out sin. The soul that by faith abides in His presence knows a very real and wonderful Deliverance.

And now I trust that some will ask, “How can I find this presence to be real to myself?” I will close, so, with a few practical directions. First, convince yourself from the Scriptures that it is a fact. Facts must always ground our experiences. Without them, the experiences are worthless. It is not the feeling that causes the fact, but the fact that produces the feeling. What every soul needs, first of all, is this.

God's own words must convince them, beyond question. They must know, as an unalterable fact, that His presence with us is constant.

Then, this point settled, we must make it real. We must “practice His presence,” as an old writer said, always and everywhere, in everything. You must obey the Scripture command. It says, “In all your ways acknowledge Him.” So, at every hour and moment, say, “The Lord is here.” Do everything, even eating and drinking, in His presence and for Him. Literally, “whether, therefore, you eat or drink, or whatsoever you do, do all to the glo ry of God.” By this continual “practice of His presence,” the soul gains a habit of faith. It becomes, finally, as hard to doubt His presence as it was to believe it at first.

This requires no great effort, just an unwavering faith. It is not studied reasoning or elaborate meditations that will help you here. The soul must, by simple faith, recognize that God is present. It must then, in freedom and simplicity, talk to Him about everything, all the time. He does not need great things of us. He asks for so little. A little remembrance of His presence. A few words of love and confidence. A brief lifting of the heart to Him as we go about our daily tasks. A constant appeal to Him, a present and loving friend. A desire to live in a sense of His presence, and to let our hearts “dwell at ease” because of it. The least remembrance is welcome to Him. It helps make His presence real to us.

Whoever remains faithful in this exercise will soon discover a blessed realization. Of all I've tried to tell in this book, and of far more that I cannot, I hope you will understand, beyond words, those wonderful words about our Lord: “They must call Him Emmanuel, which means, 'God with us.”

THE END

He has a daily, close relationship with His peop le everywhere. He taught them to rely on Him as an ever-present Friend and Helper. They should consult Him about all their affairs and give Him their lives. And finally, He came in Christ in bodily form. He dwelt in the world as a man among men. He made Himself bone of our bone and flesh of our flesh. He took upon Him our nature. He revealed to us, in the most real way, a great and blessed truth. It meant everything would be set right and all would go well for me. After their arrival, I only wanted to see how they would do it. They must be exceptional parents. Their children are very confident. I think they were. But our God is exceptional. So, the application is absolute. His presence is all we need. You will live in this cottage, and I know you don’t want this beer here. Please give me the strength to pour it out.” God gave her strength, and soon the beer was running down the road. Then she went back inside, knelt, and thanked the Lord for helping her. She added, “Now, Lord, if there is anything else in this cottage that you don’t like, show me, and I will get rid of it too. Isn’t this a perfect example of the message at the end of our Psalm? “Lord, don’t I hate those who hate you? Am I not troubled by those who oppose you? I hate them completely and see them as my enemies. Search me, O God, and know my heart. Test me and know my thoughts. If there is anything wrong in me, show me, and lead me on the right path forever Just as light drives out darkness, so does the realized presence of God drive out sin. The soul that by faith abides in His presence knows a very real and wonderful Deliverance. And now I trust that some will ask, “How can I find this presence to be real to myself?” I will close, so, with a few practical directions. First, convince yourself from the Scriptures that it is a fact. Facts must always ground our experiences. Without them, the experiences are worthless. It is not the feeling that causes the fact, but the fact that produces the feeling. What every soul needs, first of all, is this. God's own words must convince them, beyond question. They must know, as an unalterable fact, that His presence with us is constant. Then, this point settled, we must make it real. We must “practice His presence,” as an old writer said, always and everywhere, in everything. You must obey the Scripture command. It says, “In all your ways acknowledge Him.” So, at every hour and moment, say, “The Lord is here.” Do everything, even eating and drinking, in His presence and for Him. Literally, “whether, therefore, you eat or drink, or whatsoever you do, do all to the glo ry of God.” By this continual “practice of His presence,” the soul gains a habit of faith. It becomes, finally, as hard to doubt His presence as it was to believe it at first. This requires no great effort, just an unwavering faith. It is not studied reasoning or elaborate meditations that will help you here. The soul must, by simple faith, recognize that God is present. It must then, in freedom and simplicity, talk to Him about everything, all the time. He does not need great things of us. He asks for so little. A little remembrance of His presence. A few words of love and confidence. A brief lifting of the heart to Him as we go about our daily tasks. A constant appeal to Him, a present and loving friend. A desire to live in a sense of His presence, and to let our hearts “dwell at ease” because of it. The least remembrance is welcome to Him. It helps make His presence real to us. Whoever remains faithful in this exercise will soon discover a blessed realization. Of all I've tried to tell in this book, and of far more that I cannot, I hope you will understand, beyond words, those wonderful words about our Lord: “They must call Him Emmanuel, which means, 'God with us.” THE END
